sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
Europe runs from Lisbon to the Urals and from Sicily to the North Cape, and everywhere magic is licensed. What divides it is who holds the pen. In the west four crowns license magic through ministers and a republic through its cities, and in 1668 each has just learned that it is behind Mutapa. East and south of them authority is elected or divided: an elected emperor, an elected Polish king, a Swedish regency, Venice's councils and Russia splitting over how to cross oneself. This is the setting's front door and the home of the Great Game.

**The one thing to remember:** in Europe nobody asks whether you can do magic, only who signed for it. Where one hand writes the license, the license is a weapon; where authority is divided, every prince, bishop and village court decides for itself, and the witch hunts burn.

sections.heading: Playing Here
What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The red alert.** The ministries have reached their conclusion about Mutapa (see The World in 1668, The Mark), and the spies are moving.
- **The platina.** Spain threw the Chocó's platinum away until 1667 and now means to mine it, by way of the gate at Toledo. Spain's hold on the Chocó is thin, so a crown that learns where the gate's far circle stands, or the sigils that open it, can take the metal with a single fleet (see Adventures and Hooks, The Great Game).
- **The Treaty of Lisbon** was signed in February: Spain recognizes Portugal's independence, and the Council of Portugal's papers are leaving Madrid.
- **Candia** is in the last full year of its 21-year siege; Venice is desperate, and the Ten are selling what they can (see Adventures and Hooks, The Venice Job).
- **The Blåkulla panic begins.** In Härjedalen, Märet Jonsdotter's trial starts rumors that witches are carrying children to a sabbath at Blåkulla. In our history it runs eight years and kills about 280 people.
- **Russia's schism.** The Solovetsky Monastery refuses the new rite, and in summer the tsar's siege will begin.
- **Poland's king,** John II Casimir, will abdicate in September, and an election is coming.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
The western lowlands were cleared centuries ago; what woodland is left is coppice or royal forest under its own law. The Hidden wait at the hedge, the ringfort, the parish edge and the forest's edge.

- **The cold.** The Little Ice Age is at its depth, and the Thames freezes in hard winters.
- **The plague's tail.** London's Great Plague was 1665–66, and Basel's is running now. Healers are few, so magic blunts an epidemic without stopping it.
- **The timber.** The Black Forest goes down the Rhine to Dutch shipyards on rafts over 1,000 feet long.
- **Ireland**, England's conquest nearest home, is being remapped. Catholics held about 60% of its land before Cromwell's conquest; the Down Survey's maps, kept in Dublin, decided who got what was forfeited.
- **The north.** Sápmi's fells are reindeer country over three crowns' borders, and Denmark–Norway's fishing stations reach out to Hammerfest and the long winter dark.

> **Further in.** A Black Forest fir felled in 1668 can end up as a pile under an Amsterdam canal house. Nobody asks the forest. Something in it is keeping count.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
Crowns that own their churches absorb magic, church-run states regulate it and divided lands leave it to whoever holds the ground (see Powers and Factions, The Crowns and the Churches).

- **France absorbs.** Colbert's clerks in Paris keep the register of licenses; to them, magic is one more manufacture. *The license:* a royal patent entered in Colbert's register. *It pays for:* foreign craftsmen brought to Paris with their secrets, as it paid for Murano's mirror-makers three years ago.
- **England absorbs.** Charles II inherits John Dee's legacy. Magic belongs to a committee of the Privy Council, which borrows Royal Society Fellows for an expert eye. Scotland keeps its own Privy Council in Edinburgh, and its Kirk has its own ideas about who may practice. *The license:* a Privy Council warrant, and in Scotland the Kirk session's silence. *It pays for:* very little in coin, since the Dutch war emptied the Treasury; the usual fee is a warrant, a pardon or a place.
- **Spain regulates.** The Inquisition's *Suprema* has required material evidence in witchcraft cases since 1614. *The license:* an entry in the Inquisition's register, which the crown then taxes. *It pays for:* silence about the Chocó, and news of any fleet fitting out to go there.
- **Portugal regulates.** Portugal is independent again under the Braganzas and, in Euphonia, has lost Sofala to Mutapa. *The license:* the Portuguese Inquisition's, as in Spain. *It pays for:* titles and trading rights, for anything that loosens Mutapa's hold on Sofala.
- **The Dutch Republic is pragmatic.** Its weapons are the Amsterdam Wisselbank, whose bank guilder is Europe's unit of account, and the VOC and WIC, companies licensed to make war. *The license:* a city's, granted through a guild, and cheap. Here the VOC never built its Cape station; Dutch ships call at Mauritius and, when they must, at Mutapa's harbor under Table Mountain. *It pays for:* cargo delivered and news that moves a price, in bank money and on the day agreed.
- **The Empire.** An elected Habsburg emperor in Vienna and a standing Diet at Regensburg. Licensing goes territory by territory, and Vienna answers only for the Habsburg lands. *The license:* a prince's or a prince-bishop's patent, good in his territory and nowhere else. On the Ottoman border, the Military Frontier is a belt of armed Vlach and Serb colonists holding land for border service. *It pays for:* the job at hand; each prince hires by the job, so a party's papers start again at every border.
- **Venice.** The councils rule; the doge presides. The Council of Ten runs espionage, with "lion's mouth" boxes for denunciations and Europe's best cipher bureau. *The license:* the Ten's, and a denunciation is how it is lost. *It pays for:* denunciations that prove true, and men, powder and engineers got into Candia.
- **Rome** is a court among courts. The Holy Office has prosecuted learned magic since 1586 and keeps scholars who study what it bans, on the grounds that someone must. Naples and Sicily (from Palermo) have Spanish viceroys, Milan a Spanish governor. *The license:* a faculty from the Holy Office, granted to scholars and confessors and never to practitioners. *It pays for:* banned books delivered unread, and independent reports of what its missionaries are doing in Beijing, Kongo and the Americas.
- **The north.** Sweden's empire is governed from Stockholm by a regency for the boy king Charles XI. *The license:* a royal patent from Stockholm or Copenhagen, entered by the state church. *It pays for:* little in coin; the regency sells Sweden's alliance for subsidies, and an envoy who brings the money can name the enemy. Sápmi, the Sámi north, is taxed by Sweden, Denmark–Norway and Russia, sometimes all three in one winter; Sweden's church has begun questioning noaidi and taking their drums (see Places, Jokkmokk).
- **Poland–Lithuania.** The *szlachta* rule through the Sejm at Warsaw, where one deputy can void a session. South lie the Cossack Hetmanate, in the years called the Ruin, and the Crimean Tatars' slave raids. *The license:* whoever holds the ground grants it: a magnate on his estates, a starosta in a royal town. *It pays for:* votes, with an election coming, and ransoms: families and brotherhoods hire go-betweens to buy captives back from Crimea.
- **Russia.** Tsar Alexei rules from Moscow. *The license:* the Church's blessing, entered by the Apothecary Chancery, which also hires the tsar's foreign physicians. The Old Believers would rather burn than change how they cross themselves. Siberia, over the Urals by the road from Solikamsk, runs on river forts and forced fur tribute (see The Steppe and the North). *It pays for:* foreign officers, gunners and physicians, hired on contract and housed in Moscow's Foreign Quarter.

**The Romani** hold none of this power and live under all of it. In the west they are hunted as vagrants and sent to the galleys or the gallows. In Wallachia and Moldavia they are enslaved, to princes, boyars and monasteries. In Hungary and Transylvania princes and towns give their smiths and their voivodes letters of protection, because the fortresses need the iron (see Places, Hermannstadt).

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
European wizardry follows the Children of the Emerald Tablet, whose Hermetic schools hold the universities (see Powers and Factions).

- **The minister of magic** decides who may practice, teach, sell and heal. A licensing examiner carries *Detect Magic* and a list. Mutapan curiosities don't show up on it, which is one reason the examiners are worried.
- **The hunts** (see Powers and Factions, The Witch Hunts). Germany has about half of Europe's witch trials, worst in lands ruled by bishops, where the man who licenses magic and the man who judges it are the same man. Here the hunts find real witches, and also anyone a neighbor names.
- **Cunning folk** are on the examiners' lists here. Their charms are folk magic, but many work from written charm books and for fees, so the examiners class them with learned magic practiced out of the license's reach.
- **Clerics** need a bishop's faculty to heal, on either side of the Reformation, and get the same spells on both (see Magic, Faith and Wisdom).
- **Prague's legacy.** Rudolf II's court kept Dee and Kelley, and here Dee's crystals worked.
- **The night battles.** In Venetian Friuli the caul-born *benandanti* fight witches in spirit over the harvest, and the Inquisition is slowly turning them into witches.
- **Kabbalists** keep their own learning (see Magic, Learned Magic). Venice's ghetto has its golem and its reader of an angel's book (see Places, Venice).
- **The noaidi's drum** is a working instrument of divination: rings on the skin, a bone hammer, a trance and a report. Denmark–Norway made Sámi drumming a capital crime in 1609. The hunts class it as unlicensed magic rather than a fae gift.

> *"The bishop's court wanted names. I gave them the woman who sold me a charm that worked. They burned her, and I still have the charm."* (a Franconian miller)

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Europe's Hidden go by many names, and people avoid saying any.

- **The Good People.** The Good Neighbors, the Gentry; in Irish, the *aos sí*, the people of the mounds. Farmers leave Ireland's tens of thousands of ringforts, their houses, unplowed. "Seely," an old Scots word for blessed, names kinds of fairy and was never the name of a government.
- **In the witch trials,** the good people become the Devil in the clerk's hand, in Scotland above all (see Peoples, Mixed Ancestry in 1668).
- **The taken.** Fairies take infants, and new mothers to nurse fairy children, and leave a sickly substitute. When a child vanishes, look to the Hidden, not the Romani family the village blames.
- **The mine folk.** Kobolds help and hinder in houses and mines; Agricola's *Bergmännlein* look like old miners and throw pebbles.
- **The leshy** is the master of a Slavic forest. The forest's edge is the edge of his power, which makes the village edge literal here. The *domovoi* by the oven must be invited along when a family moves.
- **The north.** The forest *huldra*, the fiddling *näck*, the farm's *tomte*. The Sámi have no village edge, and their underground people, the *gufihtar*, keep herds and move with the seasons too. They take children, and a taken child who refuses their food comes home.
- **Goblins** march in the Hunt's foot ranks (see Appendices, Appendix A: Bestiary).
- **The Wild Hunt** rides as Herne the Hunter in England, the *Mesnie Hellequin* in France, the *hueste antigua* in Castile, Wodan's *Wütendes Heer* and the *Åsgårdsreia* in Norway.
- **The Black Forest** has a giant, its name unknown, out of the oldest tales, fae-touched and remembering (see Adventures and Hooks, The Giant of the Black Forest).
- **Protections.** Iron in the cradle and the doorway; St John's wort and yarrow against them. Hawthorn and foxglove are theirs, and harming them invites revenge. Every parish has its Hidden Killer, who keeps the village against them, and its own word for one.

> **Further in.** Old families on both sides of the Channel count a fairy among their forebears, and have reasons to keep the licensing office friendly.

sections.heading: Life Here
sections.text:
Away from the courts, a European year runs on bread and beer, the church bells and the weather, and on the neighbors who turn up when they're needed.

**A day in Leiden.** Holland's cloth town wakes to the Pieterskerk bells and the clack of looms in front rooms, where whole families weave by the piece for a draper. About half the town lives on cloth, and many of its weavers are the grandchildren of refugees from Flanders, France and England. By eight the fishwives are crying herring at the fish market on the Rhine, students from the university are arguing in Latin over small beer and the inspectors at the cloth hall are sealing each finished piece in lead. The fullers tread cloth in tubs all day for a wage and a beer ration. At dusk the doorsteps fill, somebody has a fiddle and the children play tag along the canals until the lamps are lit; in the dark half, every door gets its horseshoe checked before bed. The city licenses magic through its guilds, and cheaply, so the dyer who sings madder into a deeper red has a paper for it, and a Mutapan Cold Box sits in a brewer's widow's cellar beside the butter.

**Food and drink.** Everyone drinks beer, children included: small beer at breakfast and stronger at night, because the canal water isn't safe. Rye bread for working families, wheat for feast days and the comfortable, cheese (Leiden's is spiced with cumin), herring, peas and whatever the market boat brings. Tea is new, dear and sold by apothecaries as a medicine.

**The year.**

- **3 October** is Leiden's own day: the relief of the Spanish siege in 1574, kept with thanksgiving sermons, a fair and herring and white bread, the food the relief fleet brought. In 1668 it falls at the ebb and in the light half, the safest fair of the year.
- **Sinterklaas.** On the eve of 5 December a child's shoe by the hearth fills overnight with sweets, or a birch rod. The preachers disapprove and the households do it anyway; Leiden's own Jan Steen, working in Haarlem, has just painted one family's morning after. This year the eve falls the night after the new moon, at the ebb: the one dark-half night parents let the children stay up.

**Who helps.**

- **The hofjes.** Behind a plain street door in Leiden is a ring of small houses around a garden and a pump: an almshouse, endowed by a dead merchant or his widow, where old women live rent-free with peat and bread and a regent who looks in on them. A party meets one as the quietest refuge in town; the gate shuts at nine, and nobody searches a hofje.
- **The neighborhood** (*gebuurte*). Every few streets in Leiden form a sworn neighborhood, with its own officers, its own box and the city's leave to make its own rules. Members pay into the box at a birth or a wedding, and the neighborhood finds the men to carry its dead, looks after the children they leave and settles a quarrel over a gutter before it reaches a magistrate.
- **The black hoods.** In Catholic Europe the brotherhoods carry the sick and bury the dead, Florence's Misericordia first among them; a wool-carder and a grand duke's cousin can carry the same litter.

**What people love.** The ice. When the canals freeze all Holland skates, magistrates, lovers and fishwives together, with *kolf* sticks and sledges, and at every bend a *koek-en-zopie* stall sells pancakes and *zopie*, a hot beer drink. In summer it's the fair, the towers that play tunes on the quarter-hour and the long evening on the doorstep.

#### Hooks

- **The ice fair.** The Rhine freezes in January, the whole town is on it and Leiden's ice-reader says it will hold until the full moon on the 17th. Something under the ice disagrees, and the children's sledge race is on the 16th.
- **The banns.** A Leiden weaver's daughter and a Walloon fuller's son mean to marry, and their two churches and their two mothers won't speak. The banns are read three Sundays running, and the party has until the third to get both families to one table.
- **The lute.** The Misericordia buried a foreign student last winter with no name and a lute. A brother wants the lute taken home, and the only clue is a song inside its lid, in a language nobody in Florence reads.

sections.heading: Places
sections.text:
Each of the setting's own people here stands in the place where a party meets them, with what they want and how a table uses them. The cast of the Great Game and the Venice Job comes first. Each has a pregen sheet except Máhte Ingá, Dorka Lakatos, Zofia Lipska and Don Gaspar de Rojas. The sheets are on the site, perceptualmechanics.com/euphonia.

#### Venice

The Republic's councils rule and the Ten listen (Who Holds Power), with Candia in the last full year of its siege. The Venice Job begins here (Adventures and Hooks, The Venice Job), and in the ghetto a golem walks after dark.

**Ser Marin Zorzi.** One of Venice's three State Inquisitors, a tiefling of an old patrician house who has worn a plain white mask in court since his horns came in. You meet him only in the Ten's windowless courtroom, or by posting a denunciation in a lion's mouth: he reads them himself at night and can tell spite from fear by the handwriting. He wants to see the face of the halfling whose file he has read more often than his breviary. The Venice Job's villain, or its most dangerous patron; the brass figure at his elbow turns its head when you lie.
<!-- @at Venice, Italy -->

**Zanetta Bon.** A halfling carnival masker of the Giudecca who forged health passes, went into the Hidden and came home able to fold space. In Carnival she sits masked in a bauta at the Ridotto's faro table, losing small sums to a sergeant of the Ten's men. She wants her own file out of the Ten's archive, to read what they think she is. The Venice Job's way in and its way out, and the Crossing Danae on Venice's rooftops; what she owes the Hidden for the doors, she keeps to herself.
<!-- @at Venice, Italy -->

**Simon Horowitz.** The ghetto's Kabbalist, reading a book the angel Raziel gave him, a page at a time. The Venice Job's way into the ghetto, its reader of the scryers' hand and the one who knows the golem's word.
<!-- @at Venice, Italy -->

He is a Warlock (Envoy), about thirty-five, and a Horowitz of Prague, of the Levite family that built a synagogue there; his grandfather brought the household to Venice, and he lives on the fourth floor above a German congregation's synagogue door. He earns his living by reading: contracts, old deeds and, for the Council of Ten, any hand their own clerks can't make out. The Republic locks the ghetto's gates from sunset to dawn, so he works at night, by a candle-end.

Two years ago much of the ghetto believed Sabbatai Zevi was the messiah, and some families sold their leases and furniture to be ready. Then Sabbatai Zevi took the turban before the sultan. Simon hadn't believed, and being right didn't make him kinder: he trusts no one who promises anything. In March 1668 the messiah's prophet, Nathan of Gaza, lands at Venice, and the rabbis and the city make him sign that his prophecies were his own imagination. Simon is asked to read the hand of the confession.

**The book.** An angel gave Simon a book and told him to read it. By default the angel is Raziel, the keeper of secrets, who in Kabbalist tradition gave a book to the first man; that is why the gift came as a book. Simon can read the script and can't yet read the language. Each page gives way after weeks of work, and each page he reads is something he can then do, which is how he comes by an Envoy's powers (*The Classes*, Warlock, Envoy). He is eleven pages in. What the book is for belongs to the table; by default it is the book Raziel gave the first man, and its last page opens a door the angel wants opened.

**The golem.** By default the ghetto's golem followed its word from Prague to Venice: Simon's grandfather knew the word that stops it. The burial society knows the word now, and so does Simon. The golem itself is in Adventures and Hooks, The Venice Job.

**At the table.** Simon is young, sleepless and sharp-tongued. He is a contact first: he reads what nobody else can, he knows how the Ten lock their rooms and he can walk a party past the golem. As a teacher he takes an Envoy or a Wizard who will work, and he asks to be paid in texts: a copied page, a borrowed manuscript, a letter carried to Prague or Amsterdam and the answer brought back. As a patron he hires for whatever he can't do from behind locked gates. A party that says plainly what it wants from him, and what it will take, gets further than one that flatters or promises.

*Hooks:*

- The twelfth page names a house in Venice outside the ghetto, and Simon can't go there after dark. He wants someone to go, and to tell him exactly what is over the door.
- The Ten send him a letter to read. It is in his own hand, and he never wrote it.
- The golem has started stopping at Simon's door each night and waiting. It last did that the week his grandfather died.
- Nathan of Gaza is being sent on to Livorno under escort. One family in the ghetto wants him to slip the escort, the rabbis want him delivered and Simon wants ten minutes with him first, to ask what he saw.

#### Candia

Venice's city on Crete, in the last full year of its 21-year siege (What's Happening in 1668). Its fall frees an Ottoman army (Trouble Brewing).

**Fra Bertrand de Montclar.** A gold-scaled dragonborn knight of the Order of St John, a younger son of the Langue of Provence, holding Candia's breaches in the siege's last full year. After dark he loses at dice to Venetian sappers in a casemate on the Sant'Andrea bastion, and confesses it on Saturdays. In the breach his sword lights like a church window and the men beside him can't be afraid. An ally or patron for anyone who wants something out of Candia before it falls.
<!-- @at Candia = Iraklio, Greece -->

#### Toledo

Spain means to mine the Chocó's platina by way of the gate at Toledo (What's Happening in 1668), and the Great Game turns on what the city keeps (Adventures and Hooks, The Great Game).

**Don Gaspar de Rojas.** A canon of Toledo's cathedral and keeper of the chapter's archive, who holds the list of keys to the vaults under the city and has never been told what lies at the bottom of the deepest one. He works in the archive off the cloister from the morning office to noon, and walks the Zocodover in the evening, where every court's agent in Toledo has tried to buy him a drink. Since the winter the Archbishop's guards have taken a lantern down past his last door every Friday, and he wants to know why; he is a scholar, and not knowing is the one thing he can't bear. The Great Game's way into Toledo, or the man a rival court tries to buy.
<!-- @at Toledo, Spain -->

#### Warsaw

The Sejm sits here, where one deputy can void a session (Who Holds Power).

**Zofia Lipska.** A deputy to the Sejm from the Sandomierz gentry, who has ended one session with a single word of protest and knows what that word is worth. The king abdicates in September, and the election that follows is open to every foreign purse: the agents of a French prince, a Neuburg and a Lorrainer have each offered to pay her debts. She lodges at an inn near Warsaw's castle when the Sejm sits, and has taken nobody's money yet. One of the three offers came with a spell on it, and she will hire a party to find out which before she votes. A patron for a Great Game in the east.
<!-- @at Warsaw, Poland -->

#### Vienna

The elected Habsburg emperor's city. Licensing in the Empire goes territory by territory, and Vienna answers only for the Habsburg lands (Who Holds Power).

**Matthias Kessler.** A taster and apothecary's man at the Habsburg court in Vienna, paid to keep his masters alive, and by some of them for the other thing. He works the kitchens under the Hofburg at the dinner hour, and witnesses afterward can't describe his face. A Hollowed Counsellor, a poisoner who computes and feels nothing, he wants to hold on to the one thing he kept from before, and to keep anyone from knowing what it is. A villain or a contact for a Great Game in Vienna; agree at the table how much poisoning and coldness is shown before he appears.
<!-- @at Vienna, Austria -->

#### Regensburg

The Empire's standing Diet sits here (Who Holds Power).

**Gottlieb von Schleich.** A Counsellor (Spymaster) and Wizard, about fifty, and the man nobody invites. He's a Freiherr from a corner of Franconia, and envoy to the Perpetual Diet at Regensburg for an imperial county so small that it shares one vote with a whole bench of counts. The Diet opened in 1663 and never closed, so Schleich has had five years with nothing to do, and he has filled them by going everywhere.
<!-- @at Regensburg, Germany -->

He is at every reception in Regensburg and Vienna, every wedding, every lying-in-state, every opera and every hunt, at the edge of every conversation that matters, holding a glass he never drinks. Three courts have licensed him as a wizard, because none of them could find a reason not to. He's damp, attentive and agreeable; he laughs a moment after everyone else; he remembers your mother's name and your debts. He writes it all down in a small green book. He is never quite rude enough to be shown the door, and he always knows which door you came in by.

**At the table.** The party meets him in every city, and he has always heard. He offers help nobody asked for, and it's always good. The table's slow discovery is that he is never wrong, and that somebody is paying for the green book: his county can't afford his coat.

*Hooks:*

- Schleich greets the party by name in a city they arrived in that morning, and congratulates them on a job they haven't taken yet.
- The green book has been stolen. Half of Vienna is relieved; the other half has started to worry about who has it now. Schleich asks the party to get it back, and to not read it.
- Someone has finally poisoned Schleich, not fatally, and he wants to know who. He has a list, and it's long.
- A minister offers the party a fortune to find out who Schleich reports to. The first clue is a bill for the coat.

#### Naples

Spain rules Naples through a viceroy (Who Holds Power).

**Gennaro Esposito.** Majordomo to a Neapolitan family, a foundling with the foundlings' surname, who keeps the books, hires the crews and decides who knows what, from a back room above a chandler's shop. He wants to stay the one person the family can't do without, and keeps three ledgers to manage it, one of them true. A patron who hires a party and already knows what it knows.
<!-- @at Naples, Italy -->

#### Saint-Germain

The French court and the king's high play are at Saint-Germain, and at Versailles when the king takes the court to his pleasure house there. Colbert's clerks keep the register of licenses in Paris (Who Holds Power).

**Anselme Lafrenaye.** The graying halfling Gamester of the French court, with his own chair at the end of the lansquenet table at the king's high play, at Saint-Germain most weeks. He knows what Pascal and Fermat wrote to each other about dice, and generals who won't be seen asking a card player the odds lose to him first. A Counsellor's patron, rival or model.
<!-- @at Saint-Germain = Versailles, France -->

He knows the odds on everything and a few of the corridors anyway.

*Hooks:*

- He wants the man who beat him at a hand he couldn't lose found and brought to the table again.
- A general who lost a dispatch to him at lansquenet wants it won back before the king hears it was staked.

#### London

The Thames freezes in hard winters, and the Great Plague of 1665–66 is just behind the city (The Lay of the Land). Magic belongs to a committee of the Privy Council (Who Holds Power).

**Kit Harrow.** The Sharper of the pair called the Sharper and the Wit: a Cavalier baronet's daughter who plays hazard at the Groom Porter's in winter and the card rooms of Tunbridge Wells in August. She wants her father's estate back or, failing that, to be owed more than anyone in England. A player character as written, an ally or a rival.
<!-- @at London, United Kingdom -->

**Ned Ashcombe.** The Wit: Kit Harrow's husband, a Royalist colonel's younger son whose lampoons all London sings and whose couplets are signals to her across the room. He wants the place at court the Restoration promised his father's son, on terms that don't cost him Kit. A player character as written, an ally or a rival.
<!-- @at London, United Kingdom -->

**The Sharper and the Wit.** A Gamester and a Courtier who work as a pair: English, in their twenties, banned from more houses than most people have visited, very funny about the English and much better brought up than they let on. They're written as player characters a table can take as they are, or meet as rivals across a gaming table.

**Kit Harrow**, Counsellor (Gamester), 24. A Cavalier baronet's daughter whose father came home with the king in 1660 and lost the estate at hazard at the Groom Porter's inside two years. Kit learned the game to win it back, and found she was better at it than anyone she'd ever met. She plays in breeches, does the season like a campaign (Whitehall in the winter, Tunbridge Wells in summer, Paris when London gets too hot) and keeps a pocketbook of every debt anyone owes her. Two earls and a bishop owe her money. She owes it to one moneylender in Lombard Street, who is very patient, and very frightening.

**Ned Ashcombe**, Courtier (College of Verse), 26. The younger son of a Royalist colonel killed at Worcester, raised on a promise the Restoration hasn't kept. His lampoons are portraits of types that all London sings, and everyone is sure the next verse is about the man beside them; one got him banished from court for a season. He fences well and insists he doesn't, and has fought five duels and lost none, mostly because he made his opponents laugh.

**The couple.** They met across a hazard table, where Ned tried to cheat her and Kit let him, to see how good he was, and they were married a year later in the Fleet, on a bet Kit won. Ned maintains it doesn't count and has never once tried to prove it. They fight in public, in verse and in arithmetic; nobody has ever seen either of them take a side against the other.

**The act.** Kit plays, and Ned works the room. A couplet in his mouth is a signal to her (a rhyme on the king means the bank is weak; a line of Donne means the man on her left is cheating), and nobody in Europe listens to Ned closely enough to notice. When the house turns ugly, she counts, he ripostes and they leave by the window. They're banned from the Groom Porter's for a season, the Duke of York's apartments for a lampoon and two Paris *académies de jeu* for winning; Venice's Ridotto still lets them in, masked like everyone else.

**At the table.**

- *As player characters,* both are level 8, and their sheets are on the site (perceptualmechanics.com/euphonia). They're the pair for an intrigue game: Kit's Everyone's a Mark finds the tell, and Ned's Read finds who holds the power. In a fight, Kit's Big Player puts Ned where he needs to be, and her Know the Odds tells him exactly how much is left to cut.
- *As NPCs,* they're the party's best friends or its worst rivals at any table in Europe (cross one of them and you've crossed both), and the people every Back Stair agent would like to recruit, since no one notices who they talk to.
- *As a team,* every debt is a hook.

*Hooks:*

- Kit has won a sealed dispatch case at ombre from a drunk envoy, and has no idea what is in it. Someone does, and is already at her lodging.
- Ned's latest lampoon names no one, and everyone at court thinks it's about them. A duke wants the author's name; the author wants the party to find out which duke.
- The patient moneylender in Lombard Street has finally called Kit's debt, and he doesn't want money. He wants her to lose one game, on purpose, at the Ridotto, to a man who has never lost.
- A rival offers Ned a place at court, a pension and a wife with an estate, if he'll swear the Fleet marriage was a joke. He's asked the party to find out who's paying for the offer, and he hasn't told Kit.

#### Lanternhall

Lanternhall, in Basel, is the home of the Physician (see Powers and Factions, Lanternhall and the Healers). Basel's plague is running now (The Lay of the Land).

**Ilyanor Sael.** Lanternhall's elf, Attending Physician and Chair of Vital Studies. He is on rounds on the Long Ward at the sixth bell, or in his office above the Library of Cases at any hour; he doesn't leave the Hall. He wants his graduates licensed in the countries they go home to: a patron for any Physician party and a problem for every licensing office in Europe.
<!-- @at Lanternhall = Basel, Switzerland -->

He is one of the high Hidden holding a shape, who crossed with something of the Hidden still in the soul, and so remembers. A teacher, a licensing problem for every church and a reason for a Physician party to exist.

*Hooks:*

- A Lanternhall graduate hanged at Lyon left a letter saying Ilyanor taught her everything she did.
- A canon of Basel's cathedral wants proof that the Chair of Vital Studies remembers being Hidden, and has hired someone to get it.

**Sister Ondine.** The senior night sister on Lanternhall's Long Ward, who can't cast a spell and is the one person in the Hall every Physician obeys. She has threatened Ilyanor Sael with a blanket, and wants to see him sleep in a bed, once, with his eyes shut. She knows which patients will die by the way they ask for water. The ward's conscience and its comedy, and the one who sends an exhausted student to bed.
<!-- @at Lanternhall = Basel, Switzerland -->

#### Lisbon

Portugal is independent again: the Treaty of Lisbon was signed in February (What's Happening in 1668). It has lost Sofala to Mutapa, and pays for anything that loosens Mutapa's hold there (Who Holds Power).

**Brites Fagundes.** A halfling baker of the Alfama, Lisbon's old quarter, whose bread is as good on the third day as the first; a sailor from Sofala paid a debt with the Mutapan Cold Box in her back room, and she has never asked what it's worth. She wants someone to stop the Holy Office's familiar who has started buying a loaf every day and taking it away uneaten. A host, a safe kitchen and a quiet thread to Mutapa.
<!-- @at Lisbon, Portugal -->

#### Leiden

Holland's cloth town, on the Rhine. Life Here spends a day and a year in it, and its ice fair is that section's first hook.

**Neeltje Claesdochter.** Leiden's ice-reader, who walks the frozen canals at dawn with a pole, an auger and a hedge charm her mother taught her, and says which ice will bear; the city licenses her through the fishmongers' guild. She runs her own *koek-en-zopie* stall on the Rhine, can't read and has never been wrong about ice. She wants her granddaughter to have the license before the guild gives it to a man with a book.
<!-- @at Leiden = The Hague, Netherlands -->

#### Florence

The grand duke's city, where the Misericordia's black hoods carry the sick and bury the dead (Life Here).

**Piero Neri.** A wool-carder of Santo Spirito and a captain of the Misericordia, who has carried Florence's sick to the hospital under a black hood for nineteen years. The man to ask who in Florence is sick, poor, dying or newly arrived, and the brother who wants the lute taken home (see Life Here).
<!-- @at Florence, Italy -->

#### The Welsh border

Border country: the Hidden wait at the parish edge (The Lay of the Land), every parish has its Hidden Killer and in England the Wild Hunt rides as Herne the Hunter (The Hidden Here).

**Étaín of the Ford.** A wild elf of the Bordermarches, the shifting country where the Hidden Realm and the world overlap, who has ridden with the Wild Hunt since before the parish churches were built. A village meets her at the ford below it on the first dark night after Samhain, hounds ahead of her, her body turned in its skin by the ríastrad. She has never been able to throw away a child's wooden horse from a raid three hundred years ago, and wants to know whose it was. A villain for a game on the Border, or a foil someone patient could talk to in the light half.
<!-- @at the ford = Chester, United Kingdom -->

**Morfudd Prys.** A dwarf of the old mines on the Welsh border who keeps the gate against the Hidden for her village, walking the boundary at dusk through the dark half with a mastiff, an iron bell and her buff coat worn inside out. She wants to find the last Killer, her parent, taken on a Samhain night when she was twelve. An ally or teacher on the Border; the new magistrate thinks she's a cunning woman and would like to see her license.
<!-- @at the Welsh border = Chester, United Kingdom -->

#### Connacht

The west of Ireland, in a country being remapped by the Down Survey (The Lay of the Land), where farmers leave the ringforts, the houses of the *aos sí*, unplowed (The Hidden Here).

**Tadhg Ó Laoi.** A Connacht fiddler of Queen Elizabeth's time who played one night under the hill and came home a century late, to the Ireland of the transplantation. Hear him at a wedding, or in a shebeen on a fair night where an old woman has started to cry at a tune nobody alive should know. He wants to learn what he owes the Hidden before they come to collect it. An ally and a contact, with a purse of harp shillings no one will take.
<!-- @at Connacht = Galway, Ireland -->

#### Hermannstadt

A Saxon town of Transylvania. Here princes and towns give the Romani smiths letters of protection, because the fortresses need the iron (Who Holds Power).

**Dorka Lakatos.** A Romani nail-smith in the quarter outside the walls of Hermannstadt, in Transylvania, whose family forge works under the town's letter of protection. She makes the nails the Saxon villages drive into their gateposts for the dark half, and the same villages name her people when a child goes missing. She keeps a count of which villages bought no iron this year, and needs someone a magistrate will listen to, to carry it before the autumn open night. The source of iron for any Border game east of Vienna.
<!-- @at Hermannstadt = Sibiu, Romania -->

#### Jokkmokk

In Sápmi, the reindeer country over three crowns' borders (The Lay of the Land), where Sweden's church has begun questioning noaidi and taking their drums (Who Holds Power).

**Máhte Ingá.** A noaidi of the Lule Sámi: Ingá, Máhtte's daughter, who reads the drum for three *siidas*, the herding communities of her district. A party meets her at the winter market at Jokkmokk, where the crown's bailiff takes the tax and the priest counts who came to church. A priest took her uncle's drum to a cabinet in Stockholm, and she will read the drum for a party's road in exchange for word of where it is now. A guide and an ally in the north; to the hunts, what she does is unlicensed magic.
<!-- @at Jokkmokk = Kiruna, Sweden -->

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The first fleet to the Chocó.** Which crown sends it, under what flag and whether Spain can stop it.
- **The license war.** The Children of the Emerald Tablet, the Invisible College, the Agitators and the anti-monarchists each want the pen that writes the licenses. A single revocation can tip a court, and the Polish election can be bought with magic.
- **The Dutch reckoning.** The Republic is rich, unloved and allied only for as long as it pays, and whoever breaks the Wisselbank breaks everyone's credit.
- **The Ottoman frontier.** Candia's fall frees an Ottoman army, and the next place it looks is Hungary.
- **Lanternhall's graduates** are going home, most of them unlicensed there, and the first hanging of a Lanternhall doctor will be a diplomatic incident.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The ringfort.** A Down Survey grantee has ordered a ringfort plowed, and the plowman has walked off the job. The grantee pays well for hands who don't believe in anything.
- **The register.** A clerk in Colbert's licensing office has been selling entries, and one is in a dead man's name. The license is still being used.
- **The coffeehouse.** A Mutapan stove in a London coffeehouse has stopped working, and the man who came to retune it was seen leaving with the owner's ledger.
- **Blåkulla.** A Swedish commissioner rides to Härjedalen to take the children's testimony and needs people who can tell a witch from the Hidden from a frightened child. What carries the children off, if anything, is each table's to decide; by default nothing does, and the danger is the commissioner's list.
- **The drum in the cabinet.** A seized Sámi drum sits in a prince's cabinet of curiosities, and its owner's family can't make decisions without it. The drum has started moving its own rings.
- **The vote.** A Polish elector has been offered a Mutapan lamp, a French pension and a Swedish license, and has started asking which is worth most.

across the Cape Flats to the mountains

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
Mutapa is the Shona empire of the high plateau between the Zambezi and the Limpopo. In our history a Mutapa king ceded its mines to Portugal in 1607; here he didn't. Sixty years on, his heirs rule Africa's richest state, run it like a counting house and power it with platinum, which no one else can work. It is the other player at the table in the Great Game. Its sea is the Indian Ocean. Europeans hold forts there but not the water, which Asian, Arab and Swahili ships work too, and Mutapa holds the ocean's southern gate at the Cape. The trade ties the region together; everything else divides it, from Shona plateau to Swahili coral town to Gujarati counting house. This chapter covers the ocean from the Cape to India's ports and the ships that cross it. The Malay straits, Java, the spice islands and the Philippines are in East and Southeast Asia.

**The one thing to remember:** Mutapa isn't a hidden kingdom; it's an open one with a secret. Everyone trades with it, and no one can copy it. In 1668, the people whose job it is to notice have noticed.

> **Further in.** What Mutapa sells is not what it has.

sections.heading: Playing Here
What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The red alert,** from the other side. Mutapa's spymaster, whom her agents call **Shiri**, is reading Europe's services from a room above the House of the Bird, Mutapa's bank.
- **The platina.** Spain now knows the same metal lies in its Chocó, in New Granada; the question is who moves first.
- **The Cape.** Mutapa holds Hoerikwaggo, its town under Table Mountain: the gate every European fleet must pass to reach the Indies, and the great flashpoint.
- **The go-between.** **Tsitsi**, who speaks four languages, is the most useful person at the Cape to four powers (see Places, Hoerikwaggo).
- **Sofala** is growing faster than anyone can govern it, over the Swahili and Portuguese town it took. The rumor that the court is moving to Sofala sells houses, buys votes in the merchant houses and keeps the royal mediums up at night.
- **The sickness.** In our history, from the late 1660s to about 1680, locusts, smallpox, measles and plague emptied the Mutapa lands. Here the first outbreaks are reaching the plateau, and where the healers choose to go decides who stays loyal, on the plateau and at the Cape.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
Mutapa is a high plateau between the Zambezi and the Limpopo, mostly over 3,000 feet up: open woodland that goes bare in the dry season, not jungle or savanna. People have farmed, herded and mined it for over a thousand years; none of it is wilderness. ✦ The map's Mutapa and its tributaries are the book's: in ours the king gave up the mines in 1607, and no atlas draws the empire that kept them.

- **Seasons.** Cool and dry (April to early August), hot and dry (to October) and the rains (November to March), which decide the year.
- **The miombo and the granite.** Msasa woodland over thin grass, with grassy wetlands along the streams and granite domes and boulder hills, whose slabs built Great Zimbabwe without mortar. In the Matobo Hills, near Khami, the boulders go on like a sea.
- **The Great Dyke.** A ridge of ultramafic rock runs about 340 miles down the country's spine. Only a few specialist plants grow on it, and they are how Mutapa found what is under it.
- **The lowlands.** Tsetse fly and malaria in the Zambezi and Limpopo valleys kill cattle and strangers, and anyone after Mutapa's metal crosses them to reach the healthy plateau.
- **The court and the city.** ✦ The king rules from the plateau, from the old court in the north, near the royal graves and their mediums and above the mines and forges of the Dyke; each new king is installed there and lights the new fire. Sofala, taken from the Portuguese in the 1640s, is where the gold, the credit and the ships meet: the empire's great city, its workshops, its bank and its door to the world. The court governs and Sofala pays, as the Dutch Republic's governors sit at The Hague while Amsterdam keeps the money. Everyone in Sofala knows the court is moving there next year, and has known it every year since the 1650s.
- **The Cape.** A different country well over a thousand miles away by sea, of winter rain and Khoekhoe grazing. ✦ The map draws the Cape as Mutapa's harbor and its tributaries' country. Mutapa took it in 1650, by sea and by treaty. A fleet from Sofala's yards, built by Swahili and Gujarati shipwrights and piloted by men who had sailed for the Portuguese, rode the Agulhas current down the coast in the southern summer. Its captain came ashore in Table Bay with copper to give before he showed a gun. The Goringhaiqua and their neighbors on the Peninsula, who had killed a Portuguese viceroy on that beach in 1510 in a fight over cattle, made terms: a harbor and a town for Mutapan copper and protection from the ships that raided their herds. The Gunners' walls went up the next year, and by Mukombwe's accession in 1663 the terms had become tribute. In ours the Dutch built a station there in 1652; here the Company's survey ship found the bay already taken.
- **The monsoon.** Dhows ride the dry northeast monsoon to East Africa in winter and come back to Arabia in late spring. At the southwest monsoon's height, roughly June to August, much of India's west coast is closed to shipping. A ship that misses the wind waits months.
- **The spices grow in tiny places.** The Dutch restrict cloves to Ambon and nutmeg to the Banda Islands, which they conquered in 1621, killing or enslaving nearly all their people; the Treaty of Breda (1667) has just handed them Run, the last nutmeg island outside their grip. Coffee grows commercially almost only in Yemen and ships from Mocha.
- **The islands.** Swahili towns from Mombasa to Zanzibar are built of coral stone; the dodo of Mauritius is nearly gone.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
Powers and Factions (Mutapa's Institutions) has the crown, the mediums, the House of the Bird, the Mhizha Guild and the spymaster in full; here is how they sit on the ground, then around the sea.

- **The crown.** The paramount ruler is the *Mwenemutapa*, and his commander, the *mukomohasha*, is also "captain of the gates." Mukombwe holds the throne, as he did in our history. The merchant houses steer him (see Powers and Factions).
- **The mediums** (*svikiro*) speak for the royal dead, the *mhondoro*, each guarding a province and its rain; here the dead answer. In the southwest, petitioners climb to the Matobo shrines, where Mwari, the creator, is said to speak from the rocks.
- **The great artificer**, Simbarashe Moyo, is alive and unhappy with how the court stewards his work (see Places, Sofala).
- **The tributaries.** Mutapa's overlordship is a relationship, renewed with tribute and the new fire. Uteve, Manyika (in the eastern highlands) and Barwe keep their own dynasties and pay in grain, gold, labor and one tusk of every elephant killed. Royal officials put out every hearth and relight it from the king's fire; refusing the new fire is rebellion.
- **The Torwa** rule Butua, to the southwest, from a court that has left Khami, and are no one's tributary.
- **The Portuguese remnant.** The prazo heirs on the Zambezi around Tete lost their leases when Mutapa kept its mines; some kept their private armies of enslaved soldiers and sell them to anyone. The old plateau fairs, the *feiras* (Dambarare, Masapa), are Mutapa's customs posts now, where foreign traders live and pay by the king's leave. Sofala's harbor carries the gold to sea.
- **The Cape's own people.** The Khoekhoe chiefdoms nearest the harbor are Mutapa's tributaries, held with the same tools: lent cattle, the new fire lit each reign from the king's own and a tax on every trade. Further out, the Cochoqua and the Chainouqua take Mutapa's terms when it suits them and a Dutch or English captain's when it doesn't. The San hold the mountains and the dry country, in no one's ledger.
- **The Swahili city-states** are Muslim trading towns, each with a foreign patron. Mombasa and Pate have asked Oman for help against Fort Jesus, and any town pays for news of whose fleet is coming.
- **The Portuguese at sea** hold Mozambique Island, Fort Jesus at Mombasa and Goa. They have lost Hormuz, Malacca and Muscat. They sell passes, *cartazes*, to other people's ships, and pay for any way to hold Fort Jesus without a fleet.
- **Oman.** The Ya'rubi imams took Muscat from the Portuguese and raid their posts down the Swahili coast. The imam, Sultan bin Saif, hires shipwrights, gunners and pilots, and buys news of Portuguese garrisons.
- **The Dutch East India Company** holds Ceylon's cinnamon coast from Colombo (Kandy keeps the highlands) and the pepper ports of Malabar (see Powers and Factions, The Chartered Companies). Its seat at Batavia and its spice islands are in East and Southeast Asia. *It pays for:* charts, pilots and news of anyone selling spice outside its contracts.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Mutapan magic is artifice, and it runs on platinum. It isn't stronger than other magic. It's better made. Magic, Artifice and Electricity has the theory; Characters has the seven curiosities.

- **The catalyst.** Platinum isn't used up and holds its calibration, so Mutapa makes magic in workshops rather than by lone geniuses.
- **Small work for anyone, big work for the trained.** A lamp lights for anyone who touches it, and drifts until a Mhizha's hands retune it; a weapon, a flight pack or an Arc Gun needs a **Mhizha**, and Mutapa doesn't sell them.
- **Shewstones** go abroad only as the king's gifts (see The World in 1668, Words Across Distance). Other devices, and platinum, come up the coast as cargo.
- **The older magic.** Mutapa's healers, mediums and readers of plants work Wisdom magic, the crown's by custom, as artifice is the guild's.
- **The sea's healers.** Most shores are Muslim, and their learned magic is the science of letters (see Magic, Learned Magic). The Swahili *mganga* heals by the book (Islamic texts), the spirit, the head or plants.

> **Further in.** The platinum came to Mutapa through a druid reading the plants on the Dyke. What else the plants know is anyone's guess.

> **Further in.** On the Swahili coast, some *jini* are kept in rooms, chests or bottles for their owners' gain, and demand blood. Not every device on the Monsoon Road that runs by itself is Mutapan.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
The Hidden here go by their own names. Most of the record is 19th- and 20th-century and projected back; Mutapa's royal mediums are the exception. On the sea, most peoples see their spirits as part of their faith.

- **The water-takers.** Shona *njuzu*, pool spirits, take a person under and send some back as healers if the family doesn't mourn: here, how some Clerics of the Hidden Domain and some **Revelators** of the River of Life are called.
- **The wanderers.** A *shave*, the spirit of someone who died far from home, chooses a host and gives a skill such as hunting or healing; unlike an ancestor, it can be refused.
- **The small people.** The *abatwa* of Nguni tradition are tiny, touchy hunters of the grass and anthills, with fixed rules for greeting them. The image may partly remember the San, who were pushed off that country, so play the abatwa as spirits and never as a picture of a people.
- **The Cape's Hidden.** The Khoekhoe Water Snake that keeps the springs, and the San's rain-animals, the bull and the cow of the rain. The San themselves are people, never fae, and much of what is written about their beliefs was taken down from ǀXam speakers in the 1870s and can't simply be read back onto 1668.
- **The deep.** In the ocean's deepest parts the Hidden have built a civilization of their own (see Peoples, Hearthfolk). It isn't the nagas' palaces or Ratu Kidul's court, which belong to living traditions and aren't Hidden. The Swahili sea *jini* may be its people: they behave in the game as Hidden creatures, though Swahili sailors count them among the jinn. Traders know only that some waters take a toll, and a captain who refuses it doesn't sail that sea again. Some of its people are Physicians, Immortalists whose Font drinks the heat of the fires on the sea floor in water the sun never reaches; one has come up a pearl diver's line at Faza asking what the sun is like. Europe's drowned-city legends (Atlantis, Ys, Lyonesse) are what people made of glimpses of it: sailors saw lights under the water and told them as a human city lost for its pride, because a human story was the only kind they had. The deep was never anyone's city.
- **The new border.** Mutapa's cities are growing into country that was always someone else's, where modern artifice meets the oldest things in the land (see Adventures and Hooks, The Border). For the Orang Laut and the dhow crews the edge is the deep water.
- **The calendar.** South of the equator the Wild Hunt rides through the southern dark half, the dry months. On the plateau it comes out of the river mist after the harvest, riding eland and buffalo with hunting dogs ahead; on the coast, sailors say it crosses the water in boats with no crew.

sections.heading: Life Here
sections.text:
Sofala is loud, new and rich, and most of its people came from somewhere else. The plateau keeps the older rhythm of rains, fields and beer, and the city keeps more of it than it admits.

**A day in Sofala.** The city wakes to the call to prayer from the old Swahili town, cockcrow from every yard and handclaps: here, as on the plateau, you clap to greet, softly for a friend and long for an elder. Women carry water and the day's grain home on their heads, and by first light the dhows are unloading at the fish market, where the catch goes straight into a row of Mutapan Cold Boxes. The guild's quarter rings with hammers by sunrise, and the journeymen eat at cook-shops whose cooks call the dishes in Shona, Swahili, Portuguese and Gujarati. At the hottest hour everyone stops under the shade trees, and the old men play *tsoro*, a race of seeds around rows of holes scooped in the ground. At night the quays stay lit by self-lighting lamps nobody bothers to turn off, and from the courtyards of the new quarter comes the sound of the mbira.

**Food and drink.** On the plateau the meal is *sadza*, a stiff porridge of finger millet or sorghum (maize is still a newcomer), eaten with the right hand with a relish of greens, beans, groundnuts or meat. Beer, brewed by women from millet or sorghum, is how a household says thank you, welcome and goodbye. Sofala adds what the sea brings: rice, coconut, fish and prawns, and palm wine at the end of the day.

**The year.** South of the equator the rains, November to March, decide everything.

- **The first fruits** (*marombo*), when the crops ripen in March or April: no one eats from the fields, children least of all, until the ancestors have had theirs. In 1668 the senior royal medium names the full moon of 28 March, at the flood in the light half, and Sofala shuts its workshops for the day.
- **The rain-asking** (*mukwerera*) comes before the rains: women leave porridge and tobacco out at sunset, and in the morning the whole district sings and dances around the medium until the spirit answers. It falls in the southern dark half, so people walk home together.
- **Everyone's holidays.** Sofala's Muslims keep the end of Ramadan on 15 March and its Catholics Easter on 1 April, and the city takes every holiday anyone offers it.
- **The bringing home** (*kurova guva*), a year after a death, ends grief in an all-night gathering, and everyone the dead person ever helped comes.

**Who helps.**

- **The king's field** (*zunde ramambo*). A chief's people work his field together for some days each month, as they always have, and its grain is for the hungry: widows, orphans, travelers and the year the rains fail. The king's own granary at Sofala feeds newcomers through their first month in the city, and with the sickness coming up from the coast it may be the most important building in Mutapa.
- **The work party** (*nhimbe*; Life in 1668, Neighbors). In Sofala the guild's journeymen raise a newcomer's house this way in a weekend, for the beer.
- **Lent cattle** (*kuronzera*). A family with cattle lends cows to one without, to milk and keep but not to sell. It is how a poor household gets on its feet, and how a rich one makes friends.

**What people love.** The mbira: iron keys over a gourd, played with the thumbs. A Portuguese friar heard it near Sofala eighty years ago and wrote of its "sweet and gentle harmony." Its best night is the *bira*, an all-night gathering where the mbira plays, the family's ancestors are asked to come and speak, and the beer and the dancing go on until dawn.

#### Hooks

- **The bira with no player.** A family in the new quarter is holding a bira to ask a grandfather's blessing on a wedding, and the mbira player they hired is stuck outside the city's newest gate. The beer is brewed, the guests are coming and the night is the flood.
- **The king's granary.** Grain is going missing from the king's granary at Sofala at night, and its keeper would rather know why than who.
- **The bringing home of a stranger.** A Goan sailor died in a Sofala lodging house a year ago, and his landlady means to hold his bringing home properly, which means somebody has to find out where home was.

sections.heading: Places
sections.text:
Each of the setting's own people here stands in the place where a party meets them, with what they want and how a table uses them. The cast of the Great Game and the Monsoon Road comes first. Each has a pregen sheet. The sheets are on the site, perceptualmechanics.com/euphonia.

#### Sofala

The empire's great city, its workshops, its bank and its door to the world, taken from the Portuguese in the 1640s and growing faster than anyone can govern it (The Lay of the Land; What's Happening in 1668). Life Here spends a day and a year in it.

**Simbarashe Moyo.** Mutapa's great artificer, about eighty, in his workshop in Sofala's old town with an iron construct at the door. A mentor or patron, and the man whose choice a party can force.
<!-- @at Sofala = Beira, Mozambique -->

He is a Mhizha: the man who showed that lightning is electricity, that electricity is its own force and that lightning is the purest form magical force takes in matter. Everything Mutapa makes runs on something he found. A table that wants to play him has his sheet among the pregens on the site (perceptualmechanics.com/euphonia).

He was a smith's son from the plateau, of the Moyo clan, whose totem is the heart. In his twenties he watched the first masters on the Dyke die of the sorting; in the 1630s he built a rod to call the lightning down safely, turned it sideways into the first Arc Gun, then turned his lightning into the forge that made platinum a metal (The Metal of White Fire). Then he noticed that the metal that makes one lamp behave like the next would make a piece of the Hidden behave at all, and he began building rooms inside the Hidden, one at a time, for the crafters who would come after him (Running Euphonia, Possible Futures, Basa Remhizha).

He has lost twice. The first time was to his own apprentice, Nyarai Soko, who wrote down how he did things so that anyone with the hands could learn them; that is the guild, and he has never quite forgiven it. The second time was to the court, which began selling his work abroad and sending his shewstones to every crowned head in the world. He fought both and lost both, and he still turns up to argue.

He lives in Sofala's old town, in the workshop he took when the city was taken, and goes to court as little as the king allows. The iron construct is at the door before anyone knocks. He wears a work coat with too many pockets and a burn on the left cuff he won't have mended. He works every day, on small things: the songs the guild's singing birds sing, a pair of speaking wires he would rather the world had than the shewstones, a better pump. He is courteous, quick and funny, and has no patience for flattery. He asks visitors to explain something simple, a lamp, a hinge, why a kettle sings, and listens to how they do it.

He writes letters. Every year a few go out in his own hand to people abroad who have opened a curiosity and closed it again, or asked a good question in a coffeehouse where a Mutapan factor was listening. Some of them answer. The guild reads the ones it catches, and the spymaster reads the ones the guild misses.

**His choice.** He has asked the court for passage abroad and hasn't said why. The book doesn't say what he chooses or when; it is the fifth turning point in Running Euphonia's Possible Futures, and it belongs to the table. By default he stays and keeps fighting at court until something forces his hand; the hooks below are the somethings. It can take many shapes: he stays and keeps fighting at court; he sails and gives the lightning to the world's natural philosophers as a science anyone can learn, which by his own rule it is; or he goes into the Hidden and closes the door behind him. Whichever it is, someone will try to stop him. The Shava house has already sent men to his workshop at night, the spymaster keeps a file on him and the guild would rather he stayed where it can see him.

**At the table.** He gives a party a scene. As a mentor he asks more than he answers, and what he teaches stays taught. As a patron he is the most dangerous commission in the setting: he pays in a retuned curiosity, a letter to the guild with his name on it or an honest answer, and he has built no weapon for anyone since the first Arc Gun. To a crown's crew he is the prize every ministry in Europe would most like to bring home.

*Hooks:*

- A letter in the great artificer's hand reaches a party member abroad, answering a question they asked a Mutapan lamp-tuner in passing a year ago. It invites them to Sofala. The guild has a copy.
- His construct has walked out of the workshop at night and is standing at the guild hall's door. Nobody sent it, and it won't move.
- The Shava house's men came back, and this time they took his notebook from the 1630s. He wants it back before the court learns it was ever gone.
- He wants passage on the party's ship, under another name, as far as Surat. He won't say where he goes after that.

**Shiri.** Mutapa's spymaster, who runs the foreign service from one room above the House of the Bird. A party meets her factor in Sofala or Hoerikwaggo and gets its orders under a soapstone-bird seal. A patron who pays on time, every time.
<!-- @at Sofala = Beira, Mozambique -->

She is a Counsellor (Spymaster), about forty-five. Her agents call her Shiri, "bird" in Shona, after the soapstone bird on her seal, and she has never corrected them. Her own name is in the ledgers of the House of the Bird (Mutapa's bank) and nowhere else.

She grew up at the fair at Dambarare, a customs officer's daughter, and by twelve spoke Shona, Swahili, Portuguese and enough Gujarati to know what a trader said when he thought no one at the scales could follow. As a clerk of correspondents' letters at the House of the Bird she noticed that the Bird's correspondents, read together, say what every court is about to do: who is borrowing for a fleet, who has stopped paying, who is buying platinum and at what price. The Bird made her its reader, and when the court began selling abroad, its reader became its spymaster.

She runs the thinnest service in the world from one room above the bank, with one window, a table and a bench. Her assets are a handful of factors in the ports, the Bird's correspondents and a few Mhizha abroad who retune curiosities in great houses and write home about what they see. She has never met most of them. Every report is answered by the next ship, even if the answer is one line, and every agent is paid on time, every time.

She belongs to the Back Stair, as every court's spymaster does; she is its only member whose king makes the stones. The others assume she can hear through the shewstones; she lets them assume it.

In 1668 she is watching four things: the London artificer and his English apprentice; who told Spain what its platina was; the shewstone push, which she and the great artificer are the two to see clearly; and above all the gate at Toledo and the warded blank, which she means to understand before Europe acts. She and Simbarashe Moyo agree about the stones and about little else. His choice is the thing she most fears and can least prevent, and she has a file on him as thick as any court's.

**At the table.** A party meets her factor first, and gets its orders by letter under the bird seal; a crew that does three jobs well is asked up the stairs, once, to the bench in the room above the bank. As a patron she pays in gold by the *mithqal* and in credit on the Bird, and never asks a party to do what it can't. As an opponent she seldom kills. She ruins credit: a factor stops honoring your paper, and a European crew discovers that nobody in any port will lend to it. On the fair's rest day she plays tsoro in the market at Sofala with whoever sits down, and loses on purpose to children.

*Hooks:*

- Her factor in Venice has stopped answering. She wants to know whether he is dead, turned or in love, and she wants the answer before the Sensa.
- A Mutapan factor in Lisbon has been seen going in at the Holy Office's side door. She wants him followed for a week, and stopped only if he goes in a second time.
- One of her Mhizha abroad has started writing home in a cipher she never gave him.
- She wants to know who is paying for the great artificer's passage. She doesn't say what she will do with the answer.

**Munyaradzi Shava.** Master of the Shava house, the merchant house that carries the king's shewstones abroad and now stands half a step behind the king's left shoulder. He keeps a counting room in Sofala's new quarter and a place at court, where he listens without blinking; it was his men who went to the great artificer's workshop at night. A lowland fever took his father and both his brothers when he was twenty-two and left him the house. He remembers loving them the way you remember a country you once visited, and keeps their three stools against the counting-room wall, where nobody else may sit. He wants a shewstone in every court on earth before the mediums or the old man can stop it, and the house safe for his daughter Rufaro, who is nine. The Great Game's villain on Mutapa's side, or its best-paying patron.
<!-- @at Sofala = Beira, Mozambique -->

**Dona Catarina de Sá.** An Afro-Portuguese prazo heiress who lost her land below Tete when Mutapa kept its mines, and now runs the platinum runners of Sofala. She spends the hottest hour at a cook-shop by the fish market, shelling prawns and asking after your family by name, though she has never met them. Nobody caught with platinum in Sofala can say where it came from, because she makes sure they never knew, and she pays her runners' widows. A villain or contact on the Monsoon Road; a Lisbon lawyer says a European court might honor her deed, and she hasn't decided whether she wants it back.
<!-- @at Sofala = Beira, Mozambique -->

**Tonderai Shumba.** The king's lion at Sofala's outermost gate, a Lionskin Guardian in a lion-helmed suit with a copper-wire mane. At dawn, when the merchant houses' carters line up to argue the fee, he agrees warmly that the road is theirs and keeps the gate shut. He has been posted to four gates without changing jobs, because the city keeps moving its edge outward, and wants one that stays put a whole season. An ally or a foil, and Sofala's new border in one man.
<!-- @at Sofala = Beira, Mozambique -->

**Nyarai Soko.** Master of the Mhizha Guild, who swept the great artificer's floor at fourteen and wrote down how he did things so that others could, which he has never quite forgiven. Find her at the guild hall in Sofala on entry day, reading each new journeyman's name aloud twice. She wants the guild's method written down so completely that it no longer needs Simbarashe, and she wants him to say she was right. A patron or foil, whose stamp is on every piece the guild sells.
<!-- @at Sofala = Beira, Mozambique -->

**Tapiwa Marufu.** An mbira player who plays every bira in Sofala's new quarter from dusk to dawn, and by day tunes the guild's singing birds to mbira songs the guild says it never taught him. He has a welcome in every household in the quarter and hears what each one is praying for. He wants to know who taught the birds his songs, since nobody living did.
<!-- @at Sofala = Beira, Mozambique -->

**Amai Rutendo Chigumba.** Keeper of the king's granary at Sofala, who decides who eats from it and has never once asked anyone's business. At dusk she stands at the granary door with a ladle and a pot of sadza; half the guild's journeymen ate from her pot in their first month in the city, and they still bring her the first of their wages. She wants the new granary's walls up before the rains and the sickness, and puts anyone who offers to help on the end of a hod. The best-loved person in Sofala.
<!-- @at Sofala = Beira, Mozambique -->

#### Hoerikwaggo

Mutapa's town under Table Mountain: the gate every European fleet must pass to reach the Indies, and the great flashpoint (What's Happening in 1668). The Cape is a different country, of winter rain and Khoekhoe grazing, which Mutapa took in 1650 by sea and by treaty (The Lay of the Land).

**Tsitsi.** The go-between at Hoerikwaggo, a Khoekhoe woman of twenty-five raised in the harbor town. Find her on the harbor steps when a ship comes in, translating for everyone at once, every word exact except, now and then, one. The town calls her Tsitsi, Shona for mercy; her own name she keeps to herself, and what she wants is her people's grazing, cattle and terms kept, whatever flag is in the bay. A contact or ally, owned by none of the parties who think they own her. In our history the go-between at the Cape was Krotoa, who lost her husband in 1668 and her place the year after.
<!-- @at Hoerikwaggo = Cape Town, South Africa -->

**Fadzai Shoko.** One of Mutapa's two healers at Hoerikwaggo, a Vitalist who treats the town under the mountain as one patient and the mountain as part of it, from a fever house on the slope with every shutter open at noon. When the sickness comes there will be more patients than she can reach, and she wants to talk over whom to treat first with someone who doesn't work for anyone. An ally or contact for the ship with the fever (see Hooks).
<!-- @at Hoerikwaggo = Cape Town, South Africa -->

#### The court on the plateau

The king rules from the old court in the north, near the royal graves and their mediums and above the mines and forges of the Dyke; each new king is installed there and lights the new fire (The Lay of the Land).

**Ambuya Rudo Gumbo.** The senior royal medium, through whom a king two centuries dead speaks on rain and war, and who has lately said things about the shewstones the living king didn't want to hear. A party meets her at court on the day the royal spirit is asked a question, or at home the next day shelling groundnuts, cross about it; she remembers nothing of what he says. She wants to be spoken to for an afternoon as herself. A patron or ally on the mediums' side of the question of who governs.
<!-- @at the court on the plateau = Mazowe, Zimbabwe -->

#### Muscat

The Ya'rubi imams took Muscat from the Portuguese and raid their posts down the Swahili coast. The imam, Sultan bin Saif, hires shipwrights, gunners and pilots (Who Holds Power).

**Rashid bin Khamis al-Ghafiri.** A Muscat dhow captain with the storm in his blood, an air elemental-blood (descended from an elemental that took a human shape and forgot) on his mother's side, who learned to tie winds into cord from her father on the Batinah coast. When the northeast monsoon brings the dhows in, he works every quay from Pate to Kilwa, selling fair winds by the knot to captains who swear they don't need them. A knot is a length of cord he has tied a wind into; untied aboard, it gives the ship a fair wind until he next sleeps. He wants to keep carrying dates and Gulf horses instead of guns for as long as the imam, Sultan bin Saif, lets him, and the imam's officers have started asking about his hold. A patron or rival on the Monsoon Road.
<!-- @at Muscat, Oman -->

#### Faza

The Swahili towns are Muslim trading towns built of coral stone, each with a foreign patron (The Lay of the Land; Who Holds Power). For the dhow crews the edge is the deep water (The Hidden Here).

**Mwalimu Bakari Shee.** A Bajuni pilot of Faza and a water elemental-blood like his grandmother; at fourteen he went over the side in a squall and came up three days later a mile out, breathing easily, with a promise to someone in the deep that he still keeps. Find him sitting on an upturned hull on the beach at Faza or the Lamu waterfront when a captain needs a pilot for deep water. He knows which waters take a toll, leaves a gift over certain soundings without explaining, and wants to be released from the promise, which he has never dared ask. An ally or contact; his pact is a Dreamlord's, with something in the deep.
<!-- @at Faza = Lamu, Kenya -->

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **Who governs?** A merchant house has quarreled with a royal medium, and the medium speaks for a king two centuries dead.
- **The great artificer's choice**, and whoever means to stop him making it (see Powers and Factions, The Mhizha Guild).
- **The platinum rush.** Every power's agents are on the Monsoon Road after Mutapan metal and secrets.
- **Oman's navy** is growing, Fort Jesus is watching the horizon and the Portuguese have no relief coming.
- **The south.** A young herder named Dombo is gathering followers under Mukombwe; in our history he breaks away in the 1680s and founds the Rozvi state. Whether he rises here, and who in Sofala is encouraging him, is the table's; by default he rises on our history's schedule, quietly paid by a merchant house that wants a second king to bargain with (see The World in 1668, The Mark).
- **Sofala.** Every European navy has priced the port, and Lisbon hasn't forgotten it was Portuguese.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The ship with the fever.** In our history smallpox reached the Cape by ship in 1713 and killed most of the Khoekhoen near it. A ship from Sofala has it in the hold now, and Mutapa has two healers at Hoerikwaggo. Whom they treat first decides what the Cape becomes.
- **The far chiefdoms.** A Cochoqua chief takes English muskets and Mutapan cattle in the same month, and both think he's theirs.
- **The cairn.** A Mutapan road crew has been ordered to clear the travelers' cairns for a new road, and none of them will touch a stone.
- **The missed wind.** A ship that sailed late is stuck in port for a season with a hold of Mutapan curiosities everyone in town wants; its captain needs it guarded until the wind turns.
- **A bottled jini**, one of the sea *jini*, is for sale on the Swahili coast. Its buyer wants to know what it does; its last owner wants it back before it asks for blood again.

data.name: The Ottomans, Persia and the Horn

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
Three old powers tied by water and rivalry. The Ottoman Empire besieges Venetian Crete. Safavid Persia's astrologers have just given its shah a new name and a better hour. In the Horn a Christian emperor rules from Gondar among Muslim and Oromo neighbors. Pilgrims sail to Mecca and silk runs from Isfahan to the Mediterranean. None of them is behind Europe in magic; all are older at it.

**The one thing to remember:** magic here is established, and the fight of 1668 is over who may touch it: preachers against Sufi lodges in Istanbul, clergy against astrologers in Isfahan, a church council deciding who belongs inside the wall at Gondar.

sections.heading: Playing Here
What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **Candia.** The siege of Venetian Crete enters what in our history is its last full year.
- **The second coronation.** On Nowruz, 20 March, Safi II is crowned **Solayman**. A comet follows; the astrologers disagree about what it means.
- **Razin on the Caspian.** Stenka Razin's Cossacks will raid the coast from Derbent to Baku, then sack the shah's palace town of Farahabad.
- **Gondar's council** segregates Muslims and the Beta Israel; Gondar's Muslims get their own quarter at **Addis Alem**.
- **Morocco.** Moulay al-Rashid, sultan at Fez since 1666, will break the Dila lodge in June and march on Marrakesh in July.
- **Mutapa** is a customer the Porte would rather tax than fight. Mustafa Remzi Efendi, who takes the measurements for the chief astrologer in Istanbul, has had a Mutapan device taken apart on his table.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
Plateaus more than desert. Persia's oasis towns live on underground channels; a town ends where its water does. Somali herders work the coast down to Mogadishu.

- **The heartland.** Anatolia's plateau and the Balkan plains feed Istanbul; Egypt's Nile feeds Istanbul and the holy cities and pays the Porte's bills.
- **Crete.** Candia's walls and countermines, under siege since 1648.
- **The Ethiopian highlands.** Flat-topped *amba* and deep gorges; the rains, June to September, close the roads.
- **The Hajj.** The pilgrim caravans leave Cairo and Damascus each year, and the Red Sea ships carry the rest to Jidda.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Porte.** Sultan Mehmed IV reigns and the Köprülü grand viziers govern; Fazıl Ahmed is pressing the siege of Candia in person. The chief astrologer answers for magic (see Powers and Factions, Institutions Beyond Europe). *It pays for:* sappers, powder and news from inside Candia's walls.
- **The provinces.** A pasha governs Ottoman Hungary from Buda; Baghdad has stayed Ottoman since 1639; Egypt's beys rule over its governor. The Regencies of North Africa govern themselves; in Algiers the corsair captains' guild, the *taifa*, sits in the government.
