Morocco, never Ottoman, is being united from Fez by Moulay al-Rashid, who buys muskets from any seller. A European consul in Algiers needs a go-between with the taifa, and pays one.
- **The shah.** Solayman, about 20, drinks hard and governs from the harem, which at the Safavid court is an institution of government with its own officers and treasury; his mother and three eunuchs decide what reaches him. The cleric Majlesi is rising. Access is what is for sale: a petition reaches the shah only through the harem's stewards (see Khadijeh Khatun, below).
- **Persia's edges.** Tabriz watches the Ottomans and Herat the Uzbeks; the Dutch trade at Bandar Abbas; Kandahar holds against the Mughals. The Armenians of **New Julfa**, Isfahan's suburb, ship the empire's silk from Amsterdam to Manila. Their houses hire guards and couriers for the roads to Bandar Abbas and Aleppo.
- **Gondar.** **Yohannes I**, about 28, rules the northwest well and the south hardly at all. The **Oromo** hold much of the old south and center under their own **gadaa** government. Ethiopia's Jews, the **Beta Israel**, are its landless masons and smiths. In the north, **Aksum**, the old capital, keeps the Church's oldest cathedral, where tradition says the Ark of the Covenant rests. The emperor is building his capital and hires masons, founders and Armenian go-betweens; he wants no Catholic priest in the country.
- **The Horn's others.** **Emir Hashim ibn Ali** rules walled Harar. The Ottomans hold the coast, but only Massawa has a governor. The Zaydi imam **al-Mutawakkil Ismaʿil** rules Sanaa on coffee shipped through Mocha; the Funj sultan **Badi II** rules Sennar. Each lives on a road (Harar's caravans to Zeila, Mocha's coffee, Sennar's road down the Nile), and each pays for guards and for news of the next road's tolls. Up the White Nile from Sennar, the Shilluk's reth holds the river as Nyikang's heir (Peoples, Divine-Bloods).

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
The region's learned magic is Hermetic, from the same root as the Children of the Emerald Tablet. Every faith here works (see Magic, Faith and Wisdom).

- **The science of letters** (*ʿilm al-ḥurūf*) works through the numerical values of the Arabic letters, the names of God and magic squares. Rulers wear talismanic shirts under armor. Hospitals here (al-Mansuri in Cairo, Istanbul's *darüşşifa*s) were teaching at the bedside centuries before Lanternhall.
- **The lodges and the preachers.** The Kadızadeli preachers condemn Sufi music, coffee and tobacco, and in 1666 Mehmed IV banned the Mevlevi whirling. The whirling is a working, a remembrance that opens the dervish to God, so the ban took magic off Istanbul's streets. The lodges still turn, behind closed doors (see Powers and Factions, The Brotherhoods of the Road).
- **The hour.** Persia's chief astrologer casts the "elections," the propitious moment for a journey or a coronation. An act begun at an elected hour carries that hour's stars to its end. A good hour doesn't win a battle; a bad one sours everything that follows, until someone begins the thing again. In play, a bad hour is story, not a mechanic (see the Court Astrologer's Astrolabe, in Characters). After famine and earthquake, the court crowned the shah again. A Zoroastrian was set on the throne first to take the bad stars; here it worked, and that man is still somewhere in Isfahan.
- **The däbtära** of Ethiopia, unordained church scholars, write God's secret names (*asmat*) on the skin of an animal killed in the patient's place.
- **The tabot.** Every Orthodox church is consecrated by its *tabot*, a copy of the tablets of the Law. A church's tabot anchors its priests' holy work; a church without one is just a building.

**At the table.** A court astrologer is an NPC of the trade. A party hires one for 25 GP or for a favor owed.

- **Electing the hour.** The astrologer spends 10 minutes and names an hour within the next day for one venture: a journey, a battle or a negotiation the DM agrees is one undertaking. An astrologer elects one hour a day.
- **The benefit.** If the venture begins within that hour, one creature the hirer names who takes part gains Heroic Inspiration. If that creature already has it, the hirer names another who takes part.
- **A late start.** If the venture doesn't begin within the hour, the benefit is lost and the fee is still owed.
- **The Astrolabe.** The Court Astrologer's Astrolabe (see Characters) finds the day's auspicious hour, a separate benefit; neither needs the other.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Persia's Hidden are the pari. The Horn has its own, and in the Ethiopian highlands the Church names the demons and keeps the prayers against them.

- **The pari**, whose homeland is Persia, behave in the game as Hidden creatures, though the learned count them among the jinn. They carry people off to **Paristan**, sometimes to a pari wedding. Farrokh of Isfahan (see Places, Isfahan) is of their people; by default he has forgotten, as most hearthfolk have, and only the wedding reminds him.
- **The Āl**, the *albastı*, is a thin old woman with a clay nose who carries off a new mother's liver within forty days of birth. Iron, onions, garlic and prayer guard the forty days. She is a low pari that took a demon's name.
- **The ghul** haunts the desert, takes any shape but keeps its ass's hooves and calls travelers by name.
- **The children Eve hid.** In an Ethiopian tale Eve hid some of her children from God. Those beings are the Hidden there, humanity's own siblings, placated with hospitality rather than driven out.
- **The edge.** Past the last garden of an oasis town, or the waterless country between wells. Persians reckon Paristan nearest at Nowruz, and the Wild Hunt rides through the northern dark half (see Running Euphonia, Running the Hidden). The Horn keeps its own dates: its dark half is the dry season, from the end of the rains at Meskel until they return, the same months the armies march. In Persia the Hunt looks like a royal hunt, horsemen in silk with hawks on their wrists and hunting cheetahs riding pillion; in the Horn it comes as a caravan that travels by night and never makes camp.

> **The *buda* charge is not the Hidden, and not true.** Ethiopian highlanders accuse artisans, above all smiths and the Beta Israel, of *buda*: the evil eye, and the power to become a hyena by night. The accusation is false, a prejudice the game shows and a party can expose, never a monster to hunt.

sections.heading: Life Here
sections.text:
Three old civilizations, four calendars and one habit in common: the guest is fed first.

**A day in Isfahan.** The call to prayer from the shah's mosque on the Maidan starts the day, though the bakers have been at their ovens an hour by then, slapping flat bread onto the hot walls of the *tanur*. The bazaar opens behind the great portal at the Maidan's north end, a covered street for every trade, and the women of the city fill the bathhouses in the mornings, when the baths are theirs, for washing, gossip and matchmaking. Water comes down the river and through the underground channels; ice cut in winter and sold all summer chills the sherbet. At dusk the drum house above the bazaar portal plays the sun down, and the men go to the coffeehouses around the Maidan for chess, poetry and the storyteller. On summer nights whole families sleep on the roofs.

**Food and drink.** In Isfahan, steamed rice (*chelow*) under a stew, flat bread, yogurt, herbs and white cheese, and the melons the whole empire envies; sherbet of lemon, sour cherry or rosewater over ice. In Istanbul the poor and the students eat their soup at the imarets, and the street sells sesame bread rings (*simit*) by day and, on winter nights, *boza*, thick fermented millet. In Gondar it's *injera*, the sour flatbread of teff, with a stew (*wät*), barley beer (*tälla*) and honey wine (*tej*), and the Church's fasts keep meat off the table on Wednesdays and Fridays.

**The year.**

- **Ramadan,** 14 February to 14 March: the fast breaks at sunset, the streets of Istanbul fill with food and music, and every quarter has its **Karagöz**, the shadow-puppet clown, behind a lit screen. Mid-Ramadan falls at the flood, so the screens go up with iron nails.
- **Nowruz,** 20 March, five days after the end of Ramadan this year. The guilds and the grandees set up tents and booths on the Maidan and hand out sweets and drinks to the city for days, and children go around their elders for gifts. In 1668 the moon is at the half that night, so the tide turns from ebb to flood with the year, at the hour the astrologers chose for the shah's new reign (see What's Happening in 1668).
- **Ashura,** 20 June: the reciters tell Husayn's death at Karbala and the city weeps together. It is a day of mourning, and it is how Isfahan teaches its children to grieve.
- **Meskel,** 24 September by the Frankish calendar (17 Mäskäräm), ends the rains in Gondar with a great bonfire, the *demera*, decked with yellow daisies. People mark their foreheads with its ash and read the coming year in the way it falls. This year it burns at the flood, as the Horn's dark half begins. **Timkat,** the Epiphany, follows on 16 January 1669, when every church's tabot goes down to the water.

**Who helps.**

- **The waqf** (Life in 1668, Neighbors). Istanbul has one for nearly everything. Beyond the imarets there are waqfs that give poor brides their wedding dresses, ice to the poor in summer, loans without interest, shoes to poor students and winter fodder to the wild animals on the hills; one pays for what a servant breaks, so that he isn't beaten for it, and one takes children on picnics. A party meets them as a meal, a bed or a debt paid by someone two centuries dead.
- **The mahbär.** In Gondar, neighbors form an association in a saint's name and meet each month on the saint's day, each member hosting in turn with bread and tälla. A family in trouble goes to its mahbär before it goes to anyone else.

**What people love.** The storyteller. In the coffeehouses of Isfahan a *naqqal* tells the *Shahnameh*, the Book of Kings, a few battles a night; listeners pay what they can, and he always stops with Rostam's hand on his sword, so that they come back. The women of the city have their own tellers, on the roofs on summer nights.

#### Hooks

- **The fortieth night.** Abbas-qoli the Teller has told Rostam and Sohrab in a coffeehouse off the Maidan for forty nights and fallen ill before the ending. His daughter has it word for word, the coffeehouse has never let a woman tell, and a guest in green in the corner cares very much how it ends (Golnar; see Places, Isfahan).
- **The trousseau.** An Istanbul waqf that dresses poor brides has a bride, a wedding at the Feast of the Sacrifice on 22 May and no money, because its trustee has been borrowing from it. The party has until the wedding.
- **The mahbär's turn.** A poor widow's turn to host her mahbär in Gondar has come around, and her storeroom is empty. Her neighbor Wälättä Śellase knows and can't be seen to help; the party has to help her host it without anyone, least of all her, knowing she was helped.

sections.heading: Places
sections.text:
Each of the setting's own people here stands in the place where a party meets them, with what they want and how a table uses them. The Isfahan cast comes first (Farrokh, Golnar, Shushan Ghukasian, Khodadad, Khadijeh Khatun and Abbas-qoli): they are one cast and can be run as one adventure. Each has a pregen sheet. The sheets are on the site, perceptualmechanics.com/euphonia.

#### Isfahan

The shah's city, where Solayman governs from the harem and the Armenians of New Julfa, its suburb, ship the empire's silk (Who Holds Power). Life Here spends a day and a year in it.

**Farrokh of Isfahan.** The pari-touched elf (see The Hidden Here), who went to a pari wedding at Nowruz, ate at the feast and came back three years later in the wedding robe, green silk gone sea-gray at the hems. After the evening prayer he sits in the corner of a coffeehouse off the Maidan, letting a water pipe bubble that he doesn't inhale. He wants the way back in and can't leave it alone. He can tell by looking who else has been to the wedding and come back, so the families of the taken find him: an ally or contact for the pari wedding (see Hooks).
<!-- @at Isfahan, Iran -->

**Golnar.** A pari of the bride's family at the wedding Farrokh ran from, holding a shape in Isfahan to get the painted glass cup back, and remembering every minute of what she is. She sits by a fountain on the Maidan at dusk, in a green nobody else seems to notice; when she sits at your table, every water flask you carry is suddenly full of rosewater. She wants the cup back unbroken and Farrokh returned to the feast of his own free will, which she thinks kinder than the other way, and she knows where Shushan Ghukasian's son is and won't say. A villain or foil, polite, patient and bound by every promise she makes.
<!-- @at Isfahan, Iran -->

**Shushan Ghukasian.** The widowed head of a New Julfa silk house with partners in Surat, Venice and Amsterdam, who hires crews for the Bandar Abbas and Surat run and pays in credit good from Amsterdam to Manila. Find her in her counting room off the Vank cathedral square, reading a bill of exchange, a manifest and your faces in that order. Her younger son went to a pari wedding at Nowruz with a flute and hasn't come back; she has paid a priest, a dervish and an astrologer, and decided it's time for people who carry swords. The patron of the pari wedding (see Hooks), and a Monsoon Road employer afterward.
<!-- @at New Julfa = Isfahan, Iran -->

**Khodadad the Dyer.** The Zoroastrian dyer who was set on the throne before the second coronation to take the bad stars off the shah (see Magic Here); it worked, and as far as anyone can tell he still has them. He's knee-deep in a dye vat in Isfahan's Zoroastrian quarter, arms blue to the elbow, hoping you're a customer; when he hears who sent you, he sits down in the dye. He wants to be forgotten or, failing that, for his daughter's wedding to go ahead with nothing going wrong at it. The heart of the substitute (see Hooks): one court faction wants him safe and quiet, another wants him back on the throne for an afternoon.
<!-- @at Isfahan, Iran -->

**Khadijeh Khatun.** Stewardess of the shah's mother's household, called the Key, who decides which letters, petitions and rumors go in to the women who decide what reaches the shah. Meet her in a garden pavilion of the royal harem, through a screen, with sherbet already poured for the number of visitors she was told to expect. She has someone in every great house in Isfahan, usually a cook, and wants her nephew placed in the chancery and her own name kept out of every European's travel book. A patron or rival for a Great Game at Isfahan.
<!-- @at Isfahan, Iran -->

**Abbas-qoli the Teller.** A naqqal of Isfahan, who tells the *Shahnameh* in a coffeehouse off the Maidan with a stick for a sword and can make a room of grown men cry over Sohrab. After the evening prayer he is on his stool, two tables from Farrokh of Isfahan, collecting coppers in a cloth cap and refusing to say what happens tomorrow. His daughter Parvaneh tells it better than he does, to the women of the quarter on the roofs on summer nights, and what he wants is one hall where they can both tell it. A contact who hears everything a coffeehouse says, and the best way to spend an evening in Isfahan.
<!-- @at Isfahan, Iran -->

#### Istanbul

The Porte's city, where the Kadızadeli preachers condemn Sufi music, coffee and tobacco and the Mevlevi whirling has been banned since 1666 (Magic Here). Istanbul has a waqf for nearly everything (Life Here).

**Mustafa Remzi Efendi.** He picks the hour at which the sultan acts. The chief astrologer, the *müneccimbaşı*, is the empire's minister of magic; the new chief is Ahmed Dede, and Remzi, the senior astrologer under him, does the measuring, on a terrace of the Topkapı an hour before dawn, astrolabe at arm's length, while the court waits in the cold for his finger to lift. The Kadızadeli preachers want him gone and the Köprülü viziers need him; he wants to be left alone long enough to finish tables the Frankish astronomers will have to copy. A patron or mentor, with a Mutapan device in parts on his table.
<!-- @at Istanbul, Turkey -->

**Hafız Ömer.** A young Kadızadeli preacher in Istanbul, honest, learned and certain that the lodges, the coffee and the talisman-makers are innovations the Prophet never knew. His prayers are answered, and so are the dervishes', which he doesn't discuss; he would close the lodges and carry a dervish's shopping home on the way. He wants the lodges shut by law before his followers shut them with torches. A foil or rival.
<!-- @at Istanbul, Turkey -->

**Saliha Hatun.** A widow of Üsküdar who left her husband's fortune to a waqf that dresses poor brides and keeps her street's fountain cold in summer. She receives after the afternoon prayer behind a screen, with the waqf's deed on a cushion beside her. Her nephew, the trustee, has started to borrow from it (the trousseau, under Life Here's Hooks).
<!-- @at Üsküdar = Istanbul, Turkey -->

**Ferhad Usta.** An elf of Istanbul, second master of the confectionery in the Topkapı's kitchens, whose grandmother, the family says, was a pari. His violet sherbet is cooled with Uludağ snow, and three viziers' cooks have failed to copy his *zülbiye* helva. He wants the next Feast of the Sacrifice's helva to be the best the sultan has ever tasted, and has started to dream of a sweeter table than this world sets, which frightens him. A patron with the palace's ear.
<!-- @at Istanbul, Turkey -->

#### Algiers

In Algiers the corsair captains' guild, the *taifa*, sits in the government, and a European consul needs a go-between with it (Who Holds Power). A janissary agha governs and the corsair captains bring in the money (Trouble Brewing).

**Yusuf Rais.** A captain of the *taifa*, Algiers' corsair captains' guild, born Tom Penhale of Falmouth. Meet him at the taifa's counting house by the mole, pricing every name on a ransom list in three currencies without looking up. He takes ships, ransoms what he takes and buys Muslim captives back out of Malta and Livorno, and wants both sets of books balanced, the guild's and his own, with nobody reading the second. A patron or rival for any ransom job (see Hooks).
<!-- @at Algiers, Algeria -->

#### Gondar

Yohannes I is building his capital here, and the council's decree moves Muslims and the Beta Israel out of the Christian quarters this year (Who Holds Power; Trouble Brewing). Gondar's food, its Meskel and its mahbär are in Life Here.

**Wäldä Mika'el.** A *däbtära* of Gondar, an unordained church scholar, cantor and poet who writes God's secret names on healing scrolls for Christian, Muslim and Beta Israel clients alike; he turns up in any courtyard where a child is sick. He wants to go to Enfraz and argue with Zera Yacob, the old scholar there who tests every religion by reason. An ally or teacher, and a good friend to have when a *buda* charge is made.
<!-- @at Gondar, Ethiopia -->

**Wälättä Śellase.** A widow of Gondar whose tej is the best in the city, and who hosts the mahbär of St Mary on the twenty-first of each month, with priests, masons and a däbtära arguing on one bench. She knows what every household in her quarter is short of, and which of her neighbors the council's decree is about to move. A host, and the person to ask before you try to help anyone in Gondar.
<!-- @at Gondar, Ethiopia -->

#### Cairo

Egypt's beys rule over its governor (Who Holds Power). Its hospital, al-Mansuri, was teaching at the bedside centuries before Lanternhall (Magic Here).

**Nafisa al-Qalyubiyya.** A physician of al-Mansuri, the Cairo hospital that has taught at the bedside for nearly four hundred years, who runs its plague service and finds Lanternhall's fame puzzling. She noticed in 1651 what Lanternhall noticed, that a patient cured by magic catches the same fever again, and wants her notes read by someone in Basel who will take them seriously. A mentor or contact for any Physician.
<!-- @at Cairo, Egypt -->

#### Tabriz

Tabriz watches the Ottomans (Who Holds Power). Iron, onions, garlic and prayer guard the forty days after a birth against the Āl (The Hidden Here).

**Nane Gulbahar.** A Tabriz midwife who keeps the forty days after a birth against the Āl, and has never lost a mother to her. She sits through the night across a new mother's doorway, an iron sickle on her knees; when something thin with a clay nose looks around the gate, she says its name without getting up. She wants an apprentice with younger knees who isn't afraid of the dark. A mentor or ally, and a Hidden Killer by another name.
<!-- @at Tabriz, Iran -->

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **Candia's end.** In our history the city surrenders in September 1669, and every power with a man inside wants something out first. If nobody acts, the garrison marches out with its arms and whatever else is in the citadel passes to the grand vizier.
- **The preachers' reach.** Their next targets are the sultan's chief astrologer, with his timekeepers, and the talisman-makers. If nobody stops them, the palace loses the people who time its acts, and the lodges lose their last protectors at court. A party is hired to guard an astrologer, to find what a preacher's patron is paying or to move a lodge's instruments out of the city.
- **The new hour.** One faction at Isfahan needs it to hold, another needs it to fail; the next disaster will be read as a verdict. The proof either way is one man (see Khodadad the Dyer), and both factions are looking for him.
- **Gondar's wall.** The council's decree moves Muslims and the Beta Israel out of the Christian quarters this year, and in our history the remaining Catholics are expelled to Sennar in 1669. It breaks over a family that won't move, a mason the emperor still needs or a *buda* charge made to hurry a neighbor out.
- **The Regencies.** In Algiers a janissary agha governs and the corsair captains bring in the money. In our history an English squadron burns ships in the harbor in 1671, the corsairs kill the agha and one of their own rules as dey. Until then each side is collecting friends, and each wants the richest captives in its own hands.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The citadel.** A Venetian commander and a grand vizier each want something in Candia's citadel that neither will name, and the party is hired by both.
- **The ransom.** A broker carries a Livorno merchant's ransom to Algiers, and the taifa has just sold the captive on.
- **The substitute.** The man who carried the shah's bad stars off the throne is loose in Isfahan, and someone wants them back on the shah.
- **The pari wedding.** A New Julfa merchant's son went to one at Nowruz and hasn't come back; his family pays well.
- **The *buda* charge.** A Beta Israel mason is accused after a child sickens, and the party has a day to show what really happened.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
Africa's Atlantic shore is crowded with strong states: Sahel cavalry kingdoms, Yoruba and Akan forest kingdoms, a sacred king at Benin and, south of the equator, Kongo, Catholic for 170 years and broken since 1665. Fever keeps European armies at the shore; the ships go to Brazil (see The Americas). Every company here also ships the region's charms and carvings to Europe's ministers of magic, and Soyo's count is asking about Mutapa.

**The one thing to remember:** the Europeans are tenants. Every fort stands on ground an African ruler rents out, and what the coast sells is decided ashore: gold, copper, cloth and, more and more, people.

sections.heading: Playing Here
What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The slave trade is growing,** fed by Kongo's civil war. On the coast the question for a king, a broker or a company is who you sell to, and who you sell. **Who resists:** Muslim scholars who refuse to sell Muslims to Christians; Benin, which restricts the sale of men; and the people who run.
- **Oyo** looks southwest, toward Allada.
- **Soyo's man holds São Salvador,** barely.
- **The regalia.** Kongo's crown and scepter are in Lisbon.
- **The Dutch** will soon buy captives at Loango.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
- **North of the equator** the bands run east to west: the Sahel and its desert port, Timbuktu, cavalry savanna, forest towns and shrines, then surf where canoemen ferry every cargo to the ships. The **tsetse fly** kills horses, so cavalry can raid the forest but can't live in it.
- **South of it the rivers are the roads,** though falls block the Congo below the Tio markets at Malebo Pool; the Kwanza is Portugal's road inland.
- **The harmattan**, the dusty Saharan wind, blows roughly November to March: the caravan and campaign season.
- **Fever** kills newcomers from Europe at catastrophic rates.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Yoruba** share one language and one holy city, **Ife**, whose king is the **Ooni**; their crowned kings trace their lines to Oduduwa, who came down from heaven there (Peoples, Divine-Bloods). **Oyo** is the rising power; its **Alaafin** isn't absolute, since the seven councilors of the **Oyo Mesi** choose him and can order him to take his own life. Its southwestern neighbor **Allada** sells captives through Offra and Whydah. Oyo buys horses from the north and pays well for anyone who can keep them alive.
- **Benin's oba** is a sacred king secluded in his brass-plaqued palace in Benin City while his chiefs take the power he doesn't use. A party needs one of those chiefs as its sponsor to enter the city or trade in it.
- **The Akan.** **Denkyira** keeps a gold treasury, the *Sikadan*; **Akwamu**, behind Accra, is rising on musketeers. Both buy muskets and powder with gold, and both hire gunsmiths.
- **The Sahel.** **Bornu** faces a revolt; **Kano** braces against the **Kwararafa**; **the Arma** rule Timbuktu and stopped answering to Morocco in 1660. Kano hires riders; the Arma sell caravans their protection.
- **Kongo.** At Mbwila in 1665 Portuguese Luanda's army killed the king and much of the nobility. The **Kinlaza** **Álvaro VIII** holds São Salvador because Soyo put him there; his kinsman Pedro III is counting his guards. Each claimant needs the regalia, a bishop's blessing and Soyo's muskets, and will promise a great deal for any one of them.
- **Soyo.** Count **Paulo da Silva** rules Kongo's only port province from a capital with a fortified sacred wood, **Nfinda Ngula**, that no army has taken. He buys Dutch guns with ivory and captives, and wants a second ally who isn't Portuguese.
- **Portuguese Angola.** Luanda, Benguela and river forts, run by a junta since 1667. Inland, **Matamba** has been contested since Queen Njinga died, and **Kasanje**, an Imbangala war-state, sells captives to Luanda. **Loango**'s **Vili** merchants carry copper and cloth to Malebo Pool. Luanda's governors make their fortunes from captives and pay for the wars that produce them; the Vili pay porters and guides.
- **The tenants.** The **Dutch** hold **Elmina**, the **English** **Cape Coast Castle** and the **Danes** **Christiansborg** (see Powers and Factions, The Chartered Companies). African armies decide which company keeps its forts. A factor pays for whatever keeps his landlord content: gifts, powder and news of a rival company's debts.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Every tradition here is a Wisdom tradition or a learned one, and most are both (see Magic, Faith and Wisdom).

- **The Yoruba kingdoms** are a power whose Wisdom tradition makes them a match for any court's magic. In the field it looks like **spirit riding**: when Oyo's cavalry rides, some of its riders are ridden by the orisha.
- **Ifá** is learned Wisdom. A *babaláwo*, "father of secrets," casts palm nuts to find one of 256 *odu* and prescribes sacrifice; kings consult it before every great decision.
- **The Ogboni's brass staffs**, cast in pairs and joined by a chain, are said to hold the Earth itself, where an image would only show it. An oath sworn on them binds.
- **Timbuktu's family libraries** survived conquest, and Katsina's scholars know the science of letters.
- **Kongo's word for holy.** In Kikongo, "holy" is *nkisi*, a spirit-charged object, and a priest is an *nganga*, a healer. The Church runs on noble lay teachers, the *mestres*, and the bishop in Luanda ordains almost no Kongolese, so a mestre casts as a Cleric with no ordination at all.
- **The nganga** heals, divines, guards against the *ndoki*, the witch, and makes *minkisi*: pots, horns and bundles that house a spirit. Oath *minkisi* seal treaties. Italian Capuchins burn minkisi, but the Capuchins' charms and the nganga's both work; that's the problem.
- **The Imbangala** anoint themselves with *maji a samba*, said to make a warrior invulnerable while the warrior keeps the camp's law, the *ijila*. It works like an oath: break the law and it fails. The accounts come from outsiders who wanted them monstrous.
- **The book of the year.** Dapper's *Description of Africa*, out in Amsterdam in 1668, shows Europe Benin's brass palace and Loango's minkisi as both thing and spirit, and Europe's ministers of magic are reading it.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Nearly all of this is later record of living belief, kept today in Africa and in Palo, Candomblé Angola and Vodou.

- **The owners of the land.** Every forest, river and rock has owners, and an earth priest bargains with them. This is the region's village edge, and the Hidden Killers watch it.
- **The calendar.** West Africa keeps the northern calendar, so the Hunt's raiding season falls in the harmattan, when the caravans and the armies are on the road too. Soyo and Luanda keep the southern calendar, so the Wild Hunt rides through the southern winter (the dry season). In the savanna it rides out as horsemen with drums; in the forest it comes on foot between the trees, and a village knows it is near when the night insects stop.
- **The teachers.** The Akan **mmoatia**, forest folk about a foot high with backward feet, teach herbs to priests; whoever takes a Yoruba **egbere**'s little mat grows rich. Here the Hidden teach professions.
- **The bisimbi** are Kongo's Hidden, guardians of pools, streams and rocks, seen as a person, a snake or a spark. Every pool has one, and a village asks before it draws. **Kianda**, the Mbundu spirit of the sea, takes offerings thrown into the waves.
- **Not the Hidden:** the orisha, who are gods, and Kongo's ancestors, who don't ride with the Hunt.

sections.heading: Life Here
sections.text:
From the Sahel to Kongo, a stranger is somebody's guest before the day is out. The market is where the news, the prices and the matches are made, and women run most of it.

**A day in Oyo Ile.** The palace drums greet the Alaafin before dawn, and the city answers with greetings: in Oyo nobody passes anybody without one, and a young man lies flat before an elder. Families live in great compounds of rooms around courtyards, a lineage to a compound, the weavers at narrow looms in the shade and the women's indigo pots dark to the brim. Women carry their goods to the market outside the palace wall, where each trade has its row; men work the yam fields outside the city walls and come home at dusk. After dark the night market opens by the light of palm-oil lamps, a good place for courting, and in the courtyards someone starts a story with a song in it, and the children sing the answers.

**Food and drink.** Pounded yam (*iyan*), beaten in a mortar until it's smooth, with a soup of greens and melon seed in palm oil; bean cakes fried in the market; and palm wine. The first thing a host offers is kola, split and shared, and to refuse it is to refuse the welcome. In Kongo the bread is millet, and palm wine is tapped from the top of the tree, sweet in the morning, sharp by evening and vinegar by the end of the week.

**The year.**

- **The new yam,** in August: nobody in Oyo eats new yam until the first has been offered for the king and the town, and then everybody eats it at once.
- **Egungun.** The masked ancestors come back to town for a festival of days, whirling in layered cloth, and families greet their own dead dancing in the street. Nobody touches an Egungun.
- **St James's Day,** 25 July, is Kongo's greatest feast, for the saint who rode at Afonso I's side. The nobles come to the court, or to Mbanza Soyo for the count, and dance the *sangamento*, the war dance with sword and shield, in Kongo cloth and Portuguese silk, to drums and ivory horns. In 1668 it falls two nights after the full moon, at the flood, in Soyo's dark half.

**Who helps.**

- **The esusu** (Life in 1668, Neighbors). Oyo's market circles pay in every market day, every fourth day, and each time one member takes the pot: a loom, a wedding or a brother bought back. The circle's collector is the most trusted person in the market, and the most watched.
- **The mother of the market** (*iyaloja*) speaks for the market women at the palace, settles their quarrels and says what's fair; a trader cheated in Oyo goes to her before any chief.

**What people love.** *Ayo*, the board game of seeds and pits, played fast and loud in every patch of shade; the talking drum, which can say a person's praise names; and *oríkì*, the praise poems every family has (Ayoka; see Places, Oyo Ile). In Kongo, it's the evening palm wine under the plaza's great tree.

#### Hooks

- **The esusu's turn.** The collector of a market circle at Oyo Ile vanished the night before a widow's turn to take the pot, which she needs for her daughter's wedding. He's no thief: he went to the forest's edge for something and didn't come back.
- **The Egungun cloth.** A family's Egungun costume, its ancestor's cloth, was sold to a Dutch factor for a European cabinet of curiosities, and the festival is in five days. The ship is still at Offra.
- **The feast at Soyo.** Count Paulo wants St James's Day to go off with guests from São Salvador, Loango and the Dutch lodge at one feast and no blood spilled. The party seats the table, and the flood brings guests nobody invited.

sections.heading: Places
sections.text:
Each of the setting's own people here stands in the place where a party meets them, with what they want and how a table uses them. Each has a pregen sheet. The sheets are on the site, perceptualmechanics.com/euphonia.

#### Oyo Ile

Oyo is the rising power, and its Alaafin isn't absolute: the seven councilors of the Oyo Mesi choose him (Who Holds Power). Life Here spends a day and a year in Oyo Ile.

**Akinwale.** A front-rank horseman of Oyo's cavalry who is ridden by his orisha in battle and remembers none of it. In the dry season he is in the horse lines outside Oyo Ile, rubbing down a Nupe warhorse that cost more than his house; he looks at your horse's eyes before he looks at yours. He wants that horse alive through one more rainy season, and to hear from someone who saw it what he was laughing at in the ford. An ally or contact.
<!-- @at Oyo Ile = Ilorin, Nigeria -->

**Olaniyi.** Master of the Alaafin's horse, sworn into the Ogboni, who knows to the animal how many mounts Oyo has, how many it can buy from Nupe and how many the forest will kill; before the dry-season campaign he lives in the royal stables at Oyo Ile, a tally-stick in each hand. He is the patron of the horse (see Hooks), and would forgive the one who can do it almost anything.
<!-- @at Oyo Ile = Ilorin, Nigeria -->

**Ayoka.** A chanter of *oríkì*, the praise poetry of Oyo's families, who knows every lineage's glories and the parts it leaves out. She greets a stranger with a line of praise for their grandfather, made up on the spot, and trades what she knows for a story she hasn't heard. She wants the *oríkì* of a family nobody in Oyo has heard of, and to be the first to chant it.
<!-- @at Oyo Ile = Ilorin, Nigeria -->

**Iya Adunni.** The mother of the palace market at Oyo Ile, who settles every quarrel in it before sundown from a stool where the cloth row crosses the pepper row. The palace doesn't overturn her verdicts. She wants a Mutapan singing bird for the night market, one of the kind that sings when a hand goes into the wrong basket, and will trade a great deal of what she knows for it.
<!-- @at Oyo Ile = Ilorin, Nigeria -->

#### Soyo

Count Paulo da Silva rules Kongo's only port province from a capital with a fortified sacred wood, Nfinda Ngula, that no army has taken (Who Holds Power). On St James's Day the nobles come to Mbanza Soyo for the count (Life Here).

**Dom Garcia Nsaku.** A Soyo shield-bearer who carries Count Paulo da Silva's letters to people who would rather not receive them, and comes back. He hears Mass from the Capuchins and stops at the nganga's door on the way home to ask after the count's oath-bundle, and sees no contradiction. He wants to learn whether Soyo means to reunite Kongo, rule it or keep it broken before he is asked to fight for the answer. An ally or patron, and Soyo's man on the road if Count Paulo sends to Sofala.
<!-- @at Mbanza Soyo = Soyo, Angola -->

**Ndona Nsimba.** A nganga of Soyo who heals, divines, guards against the ndoki and makes the oath minkisi that seal the count's treaties, at her compound on the edge of the sacred wood of Nfinda Ngula. She and the Capuchin heal the same fevers in the same streets under an arrangement neither admits to, and she wants him to stop burning her work and start asking what it's for. An ally or teacher; lords who break an oath sworn on one of her bundles have been known to sicken.
<!-- @at Nfinda Ngula = Soyo, Angola -->

**Dona Leonor Mvemba.** A Kongo noblewoman widowed at Mbwila, who swore over her husband's body to bring the king's crown and scepter home from Lisbon, and the oath took. She receives visitors in a borrowed house in Mbanza Soyo, in her late husband's best cloak, as if the kingdom were still whole. The patron of the crown in Lisbon (see Hooks), honest that what her house does with the crown afterward is her house's business.
<!-- @at Mbanza Soyo = Soyo, Angola -->

**Ndona Mvita.** A palm-wine seller of Mbanza Soyo, whose bench under the plaza's great tree is the one place in the province where the Capuchin, the nganga, the Dutch factor and the count's shield-bearers drink together; she repeats nothing she hears. Her son is a mestre who teaches the faith in the villages, and she wants him ordained a priest, which the bishop in Luanda won't do for a Kongolese. A peacemaker, and the person who knows who is quarreling with whom.
<!-- @at Mbanza Soyo = Soyo, Angola -->

#### Loango

Loango's Vili merchants carry copper and cloth to Malebo Pool, and pay porters and guides (Who Holds Power). The Dutch will soon buy captives there (What's Happening in 1668).

**Buatu Makaya.** A Vili merchant of Loango who carries copper and cloth to Malebo Pool and speaks the language of every valley on the road, including some no one taught him. One of the languages he dreams in belongs to no valley he has found, and he wants to find it. A contact, and the best guide on the copper road for a party that wants to arrive with its manners intact.
<!-- @at Loango = Pointe-Noire, Congo (Brazzaville) -->

#### Benin City

Benin's oba is a sacred king secluded in his brass-plaqued palace while his chiefs take the power he doesn't use, and a party needs one of those chiefs as its sponsor to enter the city (Who Holds Power).

**Osaretin.** A master of the oba's guild of brass-casters in Benin City, who casts the court's history in metal and can read a room's ranks from where people stand. He has heard that Europe's ministers of magic are reading about Benin's palace in Dapper's new book, and wants to see it and find out what the Dutch got wrong. A contact at the oba's court, and a reason to carry a book from Amsterdam.
<!-- @at Benin City, Nigeria -->

#### Accra

Akwamu, behind Accra, is rising on musketeers (Who Holds Power). Every forest, river and rock has owners; that is the region's village edge, and the Hidden Killers watch it (The Hidden Here).

**Akosua Nyarko.** An Akan hunter who walks the forest's edge behind Accra for her village, keeps the owners' rules and deals with what doesn't. She has met the mmoatia three times and wants to learn what they teach the priests without paying the priests' price. An ally or guide for a game on the Border, for a fair fee and the promise that you'll do exactly as she says at the shrines.
<!-- @at the forest's edge = Accra, Ghana -->

#### Timbuktu

The Arma rule Timbuktu and stopped answering to Morocco in 1660 (Who Holds Power). Its family libraries survived conquest (Magic Here), and Morocco's new sultan will want the city back (Trouble Brewing).

**Alfa Mahmud Gurdu.** Keeper of a Timbuktu family library near the Sankore mosque, and a master of the science of letters, who corrects a student's grammar without opening his eyes. His grandfather walled up a room when the Moroccans carried the scholars away, the family is still unwalling it shelf by shelf, and he wants a copyist with a steady hand and a good memory. A mentor or patron who pays in knowledge, which he considers the more generous currency.
<!-- @at Timbuktu, Mali -->

#### Offra

Allada, Oyo's southwestern neighbor, sells captives through Offra and Whydah (Who Holds Power); the roads at Offra are one of the region's Hooks.

**Sossi.** A market woman of Allada who has sold everything she can sell and walked to the beach at Offra to buy her brother back before the company ship sails. She sits by a company lodge counting cowries on a mat, in her best cloth, never once looking at the ship. The patron of the roads at Offra (see Hooks), who will owe a party for the rest of her life and pay it.
<!-- @at Offra = Cotonou, Benin -->

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **Kitombo is coming.** In our history Pedro III kills Álvaro VIII in January 1669, a new king calls in Portugal against Soyo and in 1670 Soyo destroys the Portuguese army with Dutch cannon from its sacred wood. Here it's the table's; by default it runs as in our history. Before then everyone is buying: Pedro III wants Álvaro's guards, Soyo wants cannon and Luanda wants a king who will sign over the copper mines. A party can sell, carry or stop any of the three.
- **The Kwararafa.** In our history they break Kano again in 1671. Kano's walls need work and its king needs riders, and a party can bring him either, or carry the warning he doesn't want to hear.
- **Morocco's new sultan will want Timbuktu back** (see The Ottomans, Persia and the Horn). The Arma haven't decided whether to send tribute, hide the treasury or find another protector, and each of their factions will pay a messenger. The family libraries have been through one conquest and are deciding what to wall up.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The horse.** Oyo's master of horse wants someone who can keep a horse alive past the tsetse line, and every kingdom south of it wants that person gone.
- **The mat.** A trader at Ijebu market is suddenly, inexplicably rich, and the egbere who lost the mat wants it back.
- **The roads at Offra.** A company ship is loading captives, and a family ashore has come to buy one of them back before it sails.
- **The crown in Lisbon.** A Kongo noble hires the party to bring the regalia home and give their house a claim no other could ignore.
- **The Mutapan question.** Soyo's envoys went to Dutch Brazil in the 1640s, and Count Paulo wants to know whether they should go to Sofala next.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
India in 1668 is two political worlds under one monsoon. The north is Mughal: the richest state in the world, ten years into Aurangzeb's reign. The far south is a crowd of heirs to Vijayanagara, fighting every season over rice and cloth. Between them stand the Deccan sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda and a Maratha raja building a kingdom in the hills. The Europeans trade on sufferance, and at Surat the agents of every court change ships for Mutapa.

**The one thing to remember:** in India permission is the currency. In the north the emperor is pious and licenses magic the way he enforces prayer; in the south every king claims the name of an emperor without an empire, and what rules is the price of cloth and rice.

sections.heading: Playing Here
What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **Bombay**, Catherine of Braganza's dowry to Charles II, is passing to the English East India Company.
- **The Deccan.** Shivaji is home; Bijapur and Golconda stand between him and the Mughals.
- **The platinum rush.** Surat is where the agents bound down the Monsoon Road change ships.
- **The French arrive.** The new French company opens its first factory at Surat this year, and every broker in the city is deciding what to charge it.
- **The road to Assam.** The Ahoms retook Guwahati last year. A Mughal army under Ram Singh of Amber is marching east to take it back, and the ninth Sikh Guru travels with it.
- **The famine's trade.** In the famine of 1659 to 1661 the Dutch shipped some six thousand people from this coast, and the ships still sail.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
- **The monsoons** bring most of the year's rain: the southwest from June, and on the Coromandel coast the northeast from October to December. When one fails, famine follows and plague follows famine. Food goes further in a district with a priest, a druid or a go-between with the Hidden to purify the grain (see Magic, Faith and Wisdom), so a lean year there is hungry rather than deadly.
- **The north.** The Gangetic plain, from Agra past Patna, is the heart of Mughal farming. Bengal, governed from Dhaka, is rich in cloth and silk; the Sundarbans at the Ganges mouth are mangrove and man-eating tigers. The Terai, the malarial marsh at the Himalaya's foot, walls out armies; the Tharu live in it well.
- **The south.** The Kaveri delta is the Tamil rice bowl; Thanjavur sits on it and everyone else wants it. At Madurai the temple is landlord and bank. Kerala, the green strip between hills and sea, has no village edge: houses stand in their own compounds, and the edge is each household's sacred grove and snake grove.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The emperor.** Aurangzeb (Alamgir), at Delhi, won a war of succession in 1658 and deposed his father, Shah Jahan. Each city's *muhtasib*, the censor, polices magic until the commissioned *Fatawa-e-Alamgiri* sets the rules down (see Powers and Factions, Institutions Beyond Europe). The dynasty came by way of Kabul and rules Rajput houses bound by marriage (many of them of the Sun's or the Moon's line, and Mewar's too proud to give the Mughals a daughter: Peoples, Divine-Bloods), Sikhs whose fifth Guru was executed at Lahore and a mostly Hindu population. The court grants *farmans*, written leave to trade or to practice, and every company keeps an agent at Delhi to seek one.
- **The Marathas.** Shivaji sacked Surat in 1664 and escaped Aurangzeb's court in 1666. He isn't crowned yet, and he is at peace, for now, with the Mughal viceroy at Aurangabad. He is rebuilding his forts while the peace lasts, and pays for gunners and for news of Mughal garrisons.
- **The Deccan sultanates.** Bijapur holds its southern forts through Maratha captains. Golconda holds the coast at Masulipatnam, and its mines are nearly the world's only source of diamonds. The sultan claims every large stone, so the best diamonds leave with smugglers.
- **The southern kings.** At Madurai, young Chokkanatha Nayak lost to Mysore in 1667; his seventy-two poligars are deciding whom to obey. At Thanjavur old Vijayaraghava Nayak is broke and quarrels with his Danish tenants over the rent. The last Vijayanagara emperor, Sriranga III, is a guest in the western hills. Madurai needs soldiers it can trust more than its poligars; Thanjavur needs money and will sign almost anything to get it.
- **Kerala's kings.** The Zamorin of Calicut is the strongest; Cochin's raja owes his throne to the Dutch. Most houses pass property to sisters' children. The Zamorin sells pepper to anyone who isn't Dutch and pays for ways past the Dutch ships.
- **The money.** Gujarati merchants finance much of the ocean's trade by *hundi*, the bill of exchange (see Powers and Factions, The Trading Nations). A *hundi* drawn at Surat is paid at Mocha, Agra or Malacca, so a party can travel on paper.
- **The companies** (see Powers and Factions, The Chartered Companies). The Dutch have the Portuguese ports in the south; the English have Surat and Madras, the Danes Tranquebar and the French arrive this year. Each factory hires its interpreters, brokers and guards locally, and none may fortify without the local ruler's leave.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Under Aurangzeb, practicing magic takes a permit, a patron or a pious reason. The south has no such license; there the holy are simply everywhere.

- **Learned magic** is the Islamic world's Hermeticism, its science of letters and talismans older than Europe's (see Magic, Learned Magic).
- **Every faith's holy work:** a Sufi at a shrine, a Brahman, a village goddess's priest, a Sikh, a Jain, a St Thomas Christian.
- **The Naths**, Shaiva yogis (see Powers and Factions, Seekers of Immortality), pursue a deathless body through yoga and alchemy. Most are practitioners of a living tradition. The powers folk belief credits them with, from weather control to flight, are real only in a few: the Sandhyānāthāha, a small inner current among them.
- **Kalaripayattu.** Nair and Thiyya fighters train in the *kalari* under a *gurukkal*, who teaches the vital points (*marmam*) only to the most trusted pupils; a Monk's Stunning Strike is a touch to the right point.
- **Mutapan curiosities** reach Surat on the Monsoon Road. A Mughal noble with a self-lighting lamp makes the same statement as a Viennese countess with one in her salon: that the owner can buy what Europe can't make.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
South Asia's spirits belong to living religions; much of the record of village belief was written by British officials who called non-Brahman worship "demonolatry."

- **The pari** are the fae of the Persian and Urdu world and the Mughal court's own Hidden: beautiful, morally mixed, Muslim or not.
- **Yakshas** are spirits of trees, lakes and towns who guard buried treasure; a delve for a yaksha's hoard can start under a city.
- **The *cur*.** Sangam poetry knows the *cur*, beings of devastating force who live in mountains, forests and waters, nobody's dead and nobody's gods. Here they are the greatest of the Tamil Hidden, past the fields. When one seizes a girl, her family calls the Velan, who dances and is possessed.
- **Keeping them out.** The *gramadevata*, village guardians and often goddesses, both send epidemics and stop them. In the Tamil country Ayyanar keeps the boundary; the potter-priests who make his terracotta horses are the nearest thing here to Hidden Killers.
- **Not the Hidden:** the gods, the theyyam deities, the Kanara coast's bhutas, the snake groves' nagas and the jinn. A South Asian spirit is likelier to enter a person than carry them off.
- **The raiding season** follows the northern dark half. Theyyam's season, late October to May, matches it almost exactly, so the god-dancers are out on the nights the Hunt rides. On the plains the Hunt comes as a wedding procession with elephants, torches and no bride; in the Tamil country the *cur* bring it down from the hills.

sections.heading: Life Here
sections.text:
India keeps more calendars than anywhere on earth, and on one of them something is always being celebrated. What doesn't change is the guest: the betel leaf at the door, and water for anyone who asks.

**A day in Madurai.** Before dawn the women of every house wash the doorstep and draw a *kolam* on it in rice flour, a new pattern each morning, which the ants have eaten by noon. Drums and pipes wake the goddess and her husband in the great temple, and the streets around it, laid out in squares within squares, fill with flower-sellers, pilgrims and pots. The temple is landlord and bank here, and its tank is the city's bath. The weavers work in the cool of the morning; by noon everyone is indoors, and the market wakes again in the evening under the pillared hall the late Nayak built. At night the god and goddess go out in procession to music, and half the street follows.

**Food and drink.** Rice, always, with a sour tamarind broth, lentils, vegetables and curd, served on a banana leaf and eaten with the right hand; buttermilk spiced with ginger in the heat; and betel leaf and areca nut after the meal and for every guest. In summer the temples and the well-off keep sheds of water and buttermilk on the roads, free to anyone walking. In the north the bread is wheat, baked on a griddle.

**The year.**

- **The Chithirai festival** is Madurai's: the wedding of the goddess Meenakshi to Sundareswarar, and her brother Alagar coming down from his hill to the Vaigai. The late Thirumalai Nayak joined the two into one festival within living memory, so that the villages would come in and help pull the great chariots. Alagar enters the river at the full moon of Chithirai, on 26 April 1668: the flood, in the last week of the dark half, with half the Tamil country camped on the riverbank.
- **Pongal,** in January, when the new rice is boiled in new pots until it froths over and everyone shouts "Pongal!" as it does; the next day the cattle get their horns painted.
- **Diwali,** at the new moon of 4 November, puts a lamp in every doorway on the darkest night of the season, at the ebb.

**Who helps.**

- **The chatram.** A pilgrims' rest house on the road, endowed by a king, a queen or a merchant, with cooked rice for whoever comes until midnight, a well and a place to sleep. On the Alagar road at festival time they cook day and night.
- **The langar.** Every Sikh congregation from Lahore to Dhaka feeds whoever sits down in the row. The ninth Guru is on the road in Bengal and Assam this year, and the sangats along his way feed whoever follows.
- **The hospital for animals.** At Surat the Jain and Hindu merchants keep a hospital for old and hurt animals: lame horses, cows past work, birds with broken wings, all fed and doctored to the end of their days.

**What people love.** Music at the temple door at dawn; *pallanguzhi*, the seed-and-pit board game women play on the veranda through the afternoon heat; and the epics told in the temple hall in the evenings, a few verses a night.

#### Hooks

- **The full moon at the river.** Chitra Pournami falls at the flood in the dark half this year, with a hundred thousand people asleep on the Vaigai's sand, and Ayyanar's potter-priests need every hand at the boundary that night (Ponni; see Places, Madurai).
- **Rice for the road.** A chatram on the Alagar road has rice for three days of a festival that lasts ten, because the village endowed to feed it has paid nothing since Mysore's war. The rice exists; it's behind three poligars' tolls.
- **The horse that won't go back.** A Company factor's lame horse was taken in at the hospital for animals at Surat and healed, and the hospital won't return it to a man who'll ride it into the ground. The factor needs a horse for the road, and the hospital needs a home for this one.

sections.heading: Places
sections.text:
Each of the setting's own people here stands in the place where a party meets them, with what they want and how a table uses them. Surat, the Monsoon Road's port, comes first. Each has a pregen sheet. The sheets are on the site, perceptualmechanics.com/euphonia.

#### Surat

Surat is where the agents bound down the Monsoon Road change ships, and the new French company opens its first factory there this year (What's Happening in 1668). Its Jain and Hindu merchants keep a hospital for animals (Life Here).

**Manekbai Parekh.** A Jain shroff's widow who runs her late husband's banking house in Surat and writes hundis honored from Mocha to Malacca, doing sums aloud in Gujarati faster than the English president's writer can on paper. She'll stake a party's voyage at a rate that depends on how much she likes them, and she likes very few; she wants her grandson to take the house before her husband's brothers do. A Monsoon Road patron.
<!-- @at Surat, India -->

**Abdul Wahid.** The Surat *muhtasib*'s clerk, who reads every foreigner's permit to practice magic and checks whether the official who signed it is still in office. He is honest, pious, underpaid and very good at his job, and wants to be the first clerk in Surat to read the emperor's new law book and find that it agrees with him. A foil for a permit nobody will name (see Hooks), and the worst man a smuggler can meet.
<!-- @at Surat, India -->

#### Calicut

The Zamorin of Calicut is the strongest of Kerala's kings, and sells pepper to anyone who isn't Dutch (Who Holds Power). Kerala has no village edge: the edge is each household's sacred grove and snake grove (The Lay of the Land).

**Kesavan Vaidyan.** A Malabar surgeon whose family craft is the nose rebuilt from the patient's own skin, and whose knife floats while his hands stay folded in his lap. Patients from both sides of the nose-cutting wars between Mysore and Madurai pass each other on his road without speaking; he charges the poor in rice and the poligars in gold, and gives both the same attention. He wants to see a nose he rebuilt twenty years ago and know that it held. A mentor or ally for any Physician.
<!-- @at Malabar = Kozhikode, India -->

**Kunhi Ayesha.** A Mappila pepper broker on the Calicut beach, who sells the Zamorin's officers news of every ship and every ship news of the Zamorin's officers. She can repeat word for word what a Dutch captain said three tables away. A contact, at a price she names after she has heard why you ask.
<!-- @at Calicut = Kozhikode, India -->

#### The Western Ghats

Shivaji is rebuilding his forts while his peace with the Mughal viceroy at Aurangabad lasts (Who Holds Power). In our history it lasts until 1670 (Trouble Brewing).

**Rakhmabai Deshmukh.** A Maratha deshmukh's widow who took the fort's keys from her husband's belt before the funeral and holds his hill fort in the Western Ghats for Shivaji. Find her on the gate bastion at dusk, counting the Mughal patrol fires on the plain, or at a truce table, winning. She wants the peace with the viceroy to last one more monsoon, until the cistern is cut and the granary full. A patron or rival, who plays chess with the enemy and wins in the margins.
<!-- @at the Western Ghats = Pune, India -->

#### Aurangabad

The Mughal viceroy of the Deccan sits at Aurangabad, at peace with Shivaji for now (Who Holds Power).

**Kunwar Ratan Singh.** A younger prince of a minor Hada Rajput house, serving in the Mughal army of the Deccan at Aurangabad, who fences like water and has never lost his temper in public. Rakhmabai Deshmukh has beaten him at chess twice across a truce table and he would like a third game; what he wants most is land of his own rather than his elder brother's. A rival, a love interest or a gracious enemy.
<!-- @at Aurangabad, Maharashtra, India -->

#### Kollur

Golconda's mines are nearly the world's only source of diamonds. The sultan claims every large stone, so the best diamonds leave with smugglers (Who Holds Power).

**Ammakka.** A dwarf diamond appraiser of Golconda, of a family that says it came from the treasure-keeping yakshas, who is testing whether a diamond can do for magic what platinum does for Mutapa. Her trials so far are inconclusive and twice explosive, the notebook lives in a pot of rice and she wants a clean answer with nobody from three crowns watching. A contact or patron for the untested stone (see Hooks).
<!-- @at Kollur = Amaravati, India -->

#### Madurai

At Madurai the temple is landlord and bank, and young Chokkanatha Nayak's seventy-two poligars are deciding whom to obey (The Lay of the Land; Who Holds Power). Life Here spends a day and a year in it.

**Ponni.** A potter-priest's daughter of seventeen near Madurai, who helps make Ayyanar's terracotta horses and has started riding out behind them at the boundary on dark-half nights, with a sickle and a clay lamp. She has better hands for clay than either brother, and wants her father to let her make one horse that is hers alone. Quietly furious about almost everything, and a Hidden Killer just starting out.
<!-- @at the Ayyanar shrine = Madurai, India -->

**Perundevi.** Keeper of the chatram her mother endowed on the Alagar road outside Madurai, who has cooked for every Chithirai festival since she was nine. The village that owes the chatram its rice hasn't paid since Mysore's war, and she means to feed the festival anyway. The patron of the rice for the road (see Life Here).
<!-- @at Madurai, India -->

#### Delhi

Aurangzeb holds court at Delhi, and every company keeps an agent there to seek a *farman* (Who Holds Power).

**Saadat Ali.** A singer of the imperial court at Delhi, out of work since the emperor stopped hearing music. He sings every night in a walled garden outside the Ajmeri Gate for a patron behind a screen who pays in gold of a reign nobody can name, and comes home at dawn thinner each week. He wants to be asked back. The singer of the garden (see Hooks).
<!-- @at Delhi, India -->

#### The pilgrim road

Above the Ganges plain the Naths, Shaiva yogis, pursue a deathless body through yoga and alchemy, and in a few of them, the Sandhyānāthāha, the powers folk belief credits them with are real (Magic Here).

**Amritnath.** A yogi of the Sandhyānāthāha who has stopped aging and no longer needs food, water or air, and takes all three out of courtesy. At dawn he sits at his *dhuni* on the pilgrim road above the Ganges plain, and lets the raja's men who come to ask how to live forever wait until noon. He gives the old inoculation against smallpox to anyone who sits still, and wants the last *siddhi*, the deathless body. A mentor, or a foil to Lanternhall's Ilyanor Sael, who stopped reaching for the same thing.
<!-- @at the pilgrim road = Dehra Dun, India -->

#### Dhaka

Bengal, governed from Dhaka, is rich in cloth and silk (The Lay of the Land). Every Sikh congregation from Lahore to Dhaka feeds whoever sits down in the row (Life Here).

**Mai Raji.** The cook of the langar at the Sikh sangat in Dhaka, who has fed Mughal soldiers, Bengali boatmen, Portuguese deserters and an Armenian merchant at one sitting, in one line, and sets whoever is nearest to wash the pots. She wants news of the ninth Guru's party on the road to Assam, where her nephew rides as a cook, and whoever brings it eats free for a month. A host, and the safest table in Bengal.
<!-- @at Dhaka, Bangladesh -->

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The license.** Until the law book is finished, a foreigner's permit is only as good as the official who signed it. When an official falls, every permit he signed is void that day, and the companies pay for warning of who falls next.
- **The slavers.** The Arakanese and Portuguese slavers of the Bengal coast lost their base at Chittagong to Shaista Khan in 1666 and kept their ships. They raid from the river mouths now, and a delta village pays for a watch, a ransom or a pilot who knows where the captives are sold.
- **The emperor's seal.** Sriranga III has nothing left to give but legitimacy, and three kings want to borrow it. Whoever brings him to their court, willing or carried, can issue grants in the name of Vijayanagara.
- **The peace in the Deccan.** Shivaji and the Mughal viceroy are at peace, and each is using it to repair forts. In our history it lasts until 1670. A raid by either side's captains, ordered or not, ends it sooner.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **A permit nobody will name.** A Company factor needs the court's license for something its employers won't describe, and the *muhtasib*'s clerk wants to see it first.
- **A curse in a Company town.** A Nath yogi was refused alms at a factory gate, and the factor's well has gone dry. Whether he is one of the Sandhyānāthāha or the well was failing anyway, nobody at the factory can tell, and the yogi wants an apology from someone too proud to give it.
- **The untested stone.** A foreign natural philosopher wants to know whether a Golconda diamond could do for some art what platinum does for Mutapa's. The sultan won't sell, and the Dutch and English factors are both watching the buyer.
- **The garden.** A dismissed court singer performs every night in a garden outside Delhi's walls for a patron nobody has seen by day. His wife wants him home before the morning he doesn't come back.
- **The painter for sale.** On a Batavia-bound ship out of Pulicat is someone who can paint any pattern on cloth. A friend wants them bought back before it sails, and the VOC doesn't sell cargo twice.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
The Manchus took Beijing in 1644 and are still finishing the conquest: the emperor is fourteen and Ming loyalists hold Taiwan. Japan has shut its doors. To the south, river kingdoms hold the mainland and port sultanates the islands, which the Dutch East India Company (VOC) is breaking one by one. A court party comes here after a Jesuit's letters, a company's cargo or a ministry of magic older than any in Europe.

**The one thing to remember:** in China magic is a branch of government, and in December the emperor will test whose sky is right; the islands are losing a war one port at a time.

> **Further in.** Someone at the Astronomical Bureau chose the day each Ming prince's tomb was sealed.

sections.heading: Playing Here
What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The gnomon trials.** On 27–29 December the emperor will set the Jesuit Ferdinand Verbiest against Yang Guangxian to predict the noon shadow. In our history Verbiest wins and the Jesuits get the Bureau back.
- **The coast.** The clearance is in force and officials are petitioning to lift it; in our history it's eased in 1669 and lifted after Taiwan falls in 1683.
- **Makassar burns.** Hasanuddin signed the Treaty of Bongaya in 1667 and went back to war. On 12 October the VOC and its Bugis allies will win a great battle under the walls, and the brick fortress of Somba Opu will still stand.
- **The walls are quiet.** The Nguyễn walls have held for a generation, with cannon bought through Portuguese Macau.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text: The monsoon (see Mutapa and the Indian Ocean) brings the junks south and takes them home. Since 1661 the Qing have cleared a strip of the southeast coast 15 to 20 miles deep, forcing its people inland to starve the loyalists; watch-posts mark the line. Tigers come close enough to Seoul that roads need armed escorts. On the mainland the rivers make the kingdoms; the islands are joined by their seas, and cutting down a village's sago is how the VOC starves it.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Kangxi Emperor** has yet to break the regent Oboi. He is skeptical of elixirs and prefers to test claims. Oboi's party and the emperor's each want proof against the other; in our history the emperor arrests Oboi in 1669. The Manchus, whose old capital is Mukden, rule a Han majority.
- **The Three Feudatories,** former Ming generals, hold the south as near-autonomous fiefs, Wu Sangui from Kunming and Shang Kexi from Canton among them. They keep their own armies and revenues, and hire without asking Beijing.
- **Koxinga's heirs** rule Taiwan as the Kingdom of Tungning from Chengtian, modern Tainan, on the western plain. The mountains and the east coast are still the Formosan nations' own: the Atayal, the Amis, the Paiwan and their neighbors, who trade with Chengtian when it suits them and fight it when it doesn't. Tungning pays for rice, iron and powder run past the cleared coast.
- **Joseon Korea**, ruled from Seoul, pays tribute to a dynasty its scholars consider barbarian. Its yearly embassies to Beijing buy books, calendars and news, and carry home more than the Qing know.
- **The Tokugawa shoguns** rule Japan from Edo; the emperor at Kyoto, of Amaterasu's line (Peoples, Divine-Bloods), reigns and keeps the rites. Christianity is banned. Trade runs through four gates only: Nagasaki (the Dutch on Dejima, and the Chinese), Tsushima (Korea), Satsuma (Ryukyu) and Matsumae (the Ainu). At each gate the interpreters are the people to know: Nagasaki's write down the world's news from the Dutch every year, for the shogun.
- **The mainland kings.** Narai of Ayutthaya keeps Persian ministers and French bishops at court. Pye Min rules Burma from Ava. In Đại Việt the **Trịnh** lord rules from Thang Long (Hanoi) and the **Nguyễn** lord the south. Narai hires foreigners for his guard, his ships and his treasury, and both Vietnamese lords buy cannon and gun-founders.
- **The VOC** rules from Batavia, where about half the people are enslaved (see Powers and Factions, The Chartered Companies). It holds Malacca, Ambon and the Bandas, and its *hongi* fleets cut down spice trees outside its control. Its factors are the likeliest buyers of a Mutapan device east of the Cape.
- **The port sultans.** Hasanuddin of Gowa holds Makassar against the VOC and the Bugis prince Arung Palakka. Aceh's queen, Sultanah Safiatuddin, has kept Aceh free for twenty-seven years and buys cannon and books with pepper. Spain holds Manila, and its galleon carries American silver to the junks. Makassar pays for powder, gunners and any ship that will run the Dutch blockade.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
China's learned magic is its own school, the talisman-writing of the Daoists (see Magic, Learned Magic). The Qing Code's statute against "sorcerers and heterodox arts" makes unlicensed magic the crime here too.

- **The Astronomical Bureau** is China's ministry of magic (see Powers and Factions, Institutions Beyond Europe): calendar, omens, tombs and the days for ceremonies and burials. Rome's interest in who wins it back makes it a Great Game prize.
- **Daoist priests.** The Zhengyi exorcise and write talismans; the Quanzhen are celibate monks of internal alchemy.
- **The Qiu Xian Zhe**, the fallen court alchemists (see Powers and Factions, Seekers of Immortality), believe the old imperial tombs hold the recipes their predecessors were disgraced for.
- **Korea's *mudang*** mediate with the spirits; the state taxes and despises them.
- **Japan.** *Onmyōdō*, the court art of calendar and divination, is licensed to the heirs of Abe no Seimei; village *yamabushi* quarrel with the onmyōji over who may divine.
- **The south.** Under Theravada kings a Cleric is most often a monk. The Muslim ports' learned magic is the science of letters. The Malay *bomoh* heals, reads the land and works sorcery, calling on Sanskrit mantras, local spirits and Allah together. The *babaylan*, the Philippine spirit-mediums, led a rising against Spanish clergy as recently as 1663. Đại Việt ranks its village guardians by royal certificate, the way a ministry licenses a wizard.

sections.heading: Angkor
sections.text:
Angkor Wat was built for Vishnu and became a Theravada sanctuary; in the gallery called the Thousand Buddhas pilgrims have carved prayers since 1541, among them a Japanese pilgrim in 1632 who believed this was the Buddha's own garden.

**At the table.** Angkor doesn't check the label: it answered Vishnu's priests, it answers the Buddha's monks and it answered a Japanese pilgrim who thought he was somewhere else.

- **Prayer carries.** A creature that keeps a night's vigil in the Thousand Buddhas gains Heroic Inspiration at dawn. The vigil runs from dusk to dawn, awake and in prayer, and gives none of the benefits of a Short or Long Rest. Any creature that prays can keep it, whatever it calls what it prays to.
- **One vigil a visit.** A creature gains this once per visit. A new visit begins when the creature has finished a Long Rest more than a day's travel from Angkor; leaving the moat and coming back doesn't start one.
- **Answers.** A divination spell cast inside the moat (*Augury*, *Divination*, *Commune*) works as written, and the answer comes from whatever the caster truly serves. The DM answers in that power's voice. A caster who serves something other than what they profess learns it from the answer.
- **No court inside the moat.** The neak ta and the naga keep the Hidden from holding court within Angkor's waters. The Wild Hunt rides around the moat, never across it.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Most of what's "known" comes from literati story collections and later ethnography, not practitioners.

- **Fox spirits.** The *huli jing* is seducer or devoted wife, trickster or model of virtue. Foxes may be the greatest of China's Hidden.
- **The Wutong**, five sinister gods of Jiangnan, are handsome gentlemen who give husbands sudden wealth in exchange for their wives, then take it back at any slight.
- **The hidden world.** Japan has its own, the *kakuriyo*, the realm of the kami and the dead, and it isn't the Hidden's. A child lost at dusk is *kamikakushi*, "hidden by the kami," taken by a local god or a *tengu*, and here sometimes the Hidden, not a kami, did the hiding: the Border's oldest story in a Japanese mountain village.
- **Hidden on terms.** The Khmer *neak ta* and the Thai and Lao *phi ban* guard a village, a tree or a hill, and here they are beings of the Hidden who made terms: a spirit house, offerings and a district to keep. That is how a village here keeps the rest out.
- **The orang bunian**, the Malay "hidden people," keep clans and kings in the hills and forests. People ask leave before entering their places and don't whistle there.
- **Not Hidden:** Burma's nats, the nagas of living Hindu and Buddhist traditions, and the hantu and pontianak, who are the dead.
- **Not Hidden: Ratu Kidul**, Queen of the Southern Sea, is a court institution. Mataram's founder won her help by making himself and all his heirs her husbands, and on Java's south coast no one wears her green near the water.
- **Against them** stand the Zhengyi exorcists, the Khmer *kru* and the Malay *pawang*, nearest kin to the Hidden Killers.
- **The line through the middle.** The equator runs through Sumatra and Borneo, so Aceh's Hunt rides in the northern dark half and Mataram's in the southern. In China it comes down the road as an official's retinue, lanterns and bearers and no one in the chair; in Japan's mountain villages it is fires moving along the ridge; in Khmer and Thai villages it rides past the spirit houses and can't cross a district whose spirit made terms.

sections.heading: Life Here
sections.text:
Most people here live by rice, the family and the almanac. The day runs on the drum tower and the market, the year on the moon, and a good day for a wedding is something you look up.

**A day in Suzhou.** Suzhou, on the Grand Canal, is the city the rest of China copies: its silk, its gardens, its opera, its way with a crab. The night watch beats its last drum before dawn, and by first light the vegetable boats are tied up along the canals and the looms are going. The best embroidery in Jiangnan is women's work, and the best of it is signed and priced like painting. By midmorning the teahouses by the Chang Gate are full, and a storyteller with a fan and a wooden clapper is three weeks into the same novel, stopping at the best moment every afternoon on purpose. The gentry walk their gardens; the boatwomen row everyone else. In the evening Kunqu, the opera of Suzhou's own countryside, is sung in courtyards, on hired boats and by apprentices practicing on the bridges. The city lost sons to the Manchu conquest and still grumbles about the queue, and it sings anyway.

**Food and drink.** Rice, and tea with everything. Suzhou's autumn is for crabs from the lakes, eaten with ginger and warm yellow wine, and a crab party in the tenth month is how old friends stay friends. Beijing eats wheat: noodles, steamed buns and mutton from the Mongol trade. Joseon eats rice with soy pastes and salted, pickled cabbage and radish; red pepper has only lately come over from Japan, and most kitchens don't trust it yet. Edo has fallen for buckwheat noodles from cheap shops. The mainland south eats rice with fish sauce and fermented fish paste, and the islands eat sago, rice and their own pepper.

**The year.** Dates are New Style, worked from the moons of 1668; the Bureau's own almanac may differ by a day, which is this year's whole argument.

- **New Year,** 12 February. China, Joseon and Đại Việt (where it is Tết) start the year on the same new moon. Debts are settled before it, doors get fresh red couplets, firecrackers drive off last year's ills and everybody turns a year older at once.
- **The Lantern Festival,** 26 February, the first full moon: lanterns hung with riddles, dragon dances and the one night a respectable woman walks the streets after dark. It falls in the dark half, at the flood, so every Hidden Killer in Jiangnan works it.
- **Bon,** the middle of the seventh month (late August in 1668), in Japan: the dead come home for three nights. Families light lanterns to bring them in and float them out again, and the whole village dances in a ring in the street.
- **Mid-Autumn,** 20 September, the full moon. Moon cakes, family and, in Suzhou, Tiger Hill: the whole city spreads mats on the rocks, pipes and drums sound from a hundred spots at moonrise, the strings take over as the night wears on, and in the small hours, when the crowd has thinned, one singer climbs onto a rock and sings with no instrument at all, and nobody claps.
- **The floating lights,** on Ayutthaya's rivers at the full moon of the twelfth month, when the floods go down (18 November in 1668): the river covered in little lamps, to thank the water. It falls in the dark half, at the flood, and the spirit houses get a second offering that night.

**Who helps.** The lineage first: the Fan family's charitable estate in Suzhou has fed its widows, paid for its daughters' weddings and buried its dead since 1050, and every lineage with land tries to copy it. Past the lineage, the merchants' and gentry's benevolent societies buy coffins for the poor and bury the unclaimed dead, and China's first foundling hall, opened in 1655, takes in babies left at its gate. In a Joseon village the *gye*, a society of neighbors, pools rice and coin for each member's wedding or funeral. Under the Theravada kings the monastery teaches the boys and feeds anyone who asks, and a family making merit builds a *sala*, an open pavilion by the road, where any traveler may sleep.

**What people love.** The almanac. Every household buys the Bureau's almanac and checks it before marrying, moving house, cutting cloth or washing hair, which is why the trials in December matter to people who will never see Beijing. After that, stories: the storyteller in the teahouse, the opera in the courtyard, the water puppets of Đại Việt, whose dragons swim across the village pond spitting fireworks while the village eats on the bank. And crickets: a good fighting cricket in a clay pot is worth more than the man carrying it.

**The Formosan nations at home.** In an Amis village on the east coast the house belongs to its women. Land, name and house come down from mother to daughter, the eldest sister runs the household, a husband moves in with his wife's family, and a wife ends a marriage by setting his things outside the door.
