The men's age-sets do the heavy work and keep the young men in order, and when the harvest is in, the village dances in its age-sets for days. In the Atayal mountains a woman's facial tattoo is earned at the loom, and a girl who weaves well is spoken of the way a Suzhou family speaks of a scholar.

#### Hooks

- **The lucky day.** A Suzhou silk family set their daughter's wedding for New Year's week by Yang Guangxian's almanac. If the shadow falls the Jesuits' way in December, the new almanac calls the day unlucky, and both mothers are ready to call the wedding off. The couple want a day both almanacs agree on, and someone to make both mothers believe it.
- **The last song.** The old man whose lone song ends Mid-Autumn night on Tiger Hill has lost his voice, and swears a fox took it in trade for something he won't name. The crowd wants its song, and the teahouse singer Wang Yuezhen has been asked to stand in. The fox's price is for the table to find; by default, the fox wants to be asked politely and to sing the song herself.
- **One lantern too many.** At Bon in a mountain village in Japan, the lanterns that bring the dead home light one more guest than the village has graves. The guest is polite, hungry and very glad to be home, and nobody can remember her name.

sections.heading: Places
sections.text:
Each of the setting's own people here stands in the place where a party meets them, with what they want and how a table uses them. Lu Qingxu, Gu Wenyuan, Shen Xuanji and Hu Lanxin come first, in Beijing: they are the cast of the Tomb Road, the tomb-robbing game in Adventures and Hooks. Each has a pregen sheet except Nang Bua. The sheets are on the site, perceptualmechanics.com/euphonia.

#### Beijing

The Manchus' capital since 1644 and the Astronomical Bureau's, where on 27–29 December the emperor will set Verbiest against Yang Guangxian to predict the noon shadow (What's Happening in 1668). The trials throw a calendar clerk out with a sealing date that doesn't add up, and the Tomb Road begins (Adventures and Hooks, The Tomb Road).

**Lu Qingxu.** The last of a line of Ming court alchemists, one of the Qiu Xian Zhe (see Powers and Factions, Seekers of Immortality), in Daoist dress that keeps the queue off his head and the questions off his past. Find him at a hill hermitage with a luopan on the table and the Bureau's old sealing calendar open beside it, or at the last door of a tomb by lamplight. He carries a red pill from the batch his teacher died of, and wants to learn whether the batch was wrong, or the teacher. An ally or mentor who digs where the sealing dates don't add up: the Tomb Road's fallen alchemist.
<!-- @at the hill hermitage = Beijing, China -->

**Gu Wenyuan.** A dragonborn calendar clerk of Yang Guangxian's Astronomical Bureau, who will be out of work the day the shadow falls the Jesuits' way and has found a Ming prince's sealing date that doesn't add up. At night he is at the observatory on the city wall, or in a teahouse nearby doing long division on a tea bill with his sleeve pulled down over the scales on his wrist. He wants to prove the arithmetic wrong before anyone burns the records, mostly so someone will know he was right. The clerk (see Hooks) who opens the Tomb Road: a patron or a fellow delver.
<!-- @at the observatory = Beijing, China -->

**Shen Xuanji.** A fallen court alchemist, seventy-four and looking forty-five, who compounds mineral elixirs for rich men in Beijing. He sees visitors by introduction only, after dark, in the back room of a medicine shop near the Drum Tower that smells of mercury. His illusions are first-rate and his elixirs are mercury; he has decided Lu Qingxu's teacher found something real, and he wants to be young, actually. The Tomb Road's villain, always one tomb ahead.
<!-- @at Beijing, China -->

**Hu Lanxin.** A fox spirit in a woman's shape who remembers what she is, and is after the same tomb the party is, for the fox-jade buried with a prince who once loved her. Meet her already inside a sealed Ming tomb when the party breaks through, sitting on the coffin eating their dried plums and asking what took them so long. She is honest about everything except her age, wants the jade back because it's hers and wants to know whether he was buried holding it. A rival or love interest on the Tomb Road.
<!-- @at the sealed Ming tomb = Beijing, China -->

**Brother Joris Vanhove.** A Flemish Jesuit lay brother in Beijing who can cast a cannon, mend a clock and compute a noon shadow, and is checking every figure he can before December. He likes the Bureau's Chinese astronomers better than the Portuguese fathers, thinks the gnomon trial the most honest test he'll ever see, and is terrified. A contact or ally for the witness (see Hooks).
<!-- @at Beijing, China -->

#### Mount Song

The mountain of the Shaolin monastery, whose fighting monks are among the region's natural fits (Playing Here).

**Shi Yuanjing.** A Shaolin fighting monk the abbot sends down alone with a staff to meet whatever official comes up the valley road, because he is calm, polite and plainly impossible to arrest; he reached the gate tower's lintel on Mount Song by walking three steps up its face. His ordination certificate dates from the last Ming years, and no Qing clerk has asked to see it yet. He wants not to have to decide what he'll do when the governor tells the monks to stop drilling; until then, an ally or teacher.
<!-- @at Mount Song = Luoyang, China -->

#### Suzhou

On the Grand Canal, the city the rest of China copies. Life Here spends a day and a year in it, and its last song on Tiger Hill is that section's second hook.

**Wang Yuezhen.** A Suzhou *tanci* singer who has told the same love story in a teahouse by the Chang Gate every afternoon for eleven weeks, stopping each day on the best line. Everyone talks under the music, so she knows the city's business. A contact for anything in Suzhou, and the singer asked to stand in for the last song on Tiger Hill, if the fox allows it (see Life Here).
<!-- @at the Chang Gate = Suzhou, Jiangsu, China -->

#### Taiwan's east coast

The mountains and the east coast are still the Formosan nations' own, who trade with Tungning's Chengtian when it suits them and fight it when it doesn't (Who Holds Power). In an Amis village here the house belongs to its women (Life Here).

**Panay.** An Amis woman, the eldest sister of her house on Taiwan's east coast, who runs its fields, its rice and its marriages, and feeds whoever came along the coast that day. She wants Chengtian's soldiers kept on their own side of the mountains. A host and an ally, and the first open door on the east coast.
<!-- @at the east coast = Hualien, Taiwan -->

#### Seoul

Joseon's capital, paying tribute to a dynasty its scholars consider barbarian (Who Holds Power). Tigers come close enough that the roads need armed escorts (The Lay of the Land).

**Ok Rye-hwa.** A Korean *mudang* outside Seoul's walls, who bargains with the spirits for her neighbors, pays the state's tax on shamans and is despised by the scholars who send for her at night. At a *gut* she dances barefoot on the blades of two fodder-choppers in a general's hat. She wants her daughter to inherit the drum and the clients without the contempt. An ally or contact for any game in Joseon.
<!-- @at Seoul, South Korea -->

#### Edo

The Tokugawa shoguns rule Japan from here, and trade comes in through four gates only (Who Holds Power). Edo has fallen for buckwheat noodles from cheap shops (Life Here).

**Kichibei.** A tempura seller at the foot of Nihonbashi in Edo, a century before the city takes to the dish; his batter came from a Nagasaki cook who learned it in a Portuguese kitchen before the ban. Since spring he has been losing customers to a second stall across the bridge, whose fish is never out of season and whose owner nobody has seen in daylight, and he wants to know what is frying there. A source of every rumor on the Tōkaidō.
<!-- @at Edo = Tokyo, Japan -->

#### The mountain shrine

A mountain province of Japan, where a child lost at dusk is *kamikakushi*, hidden by the kami, and sometimes the Hidden did the hiding (The Hidden Here).

**Tachibana Chiyo.** A shrine priestess in a mountain province of Japan, an angel-touched divine-blood (Peoples, Divine-Bloods) born with the light in her, who is sent for when a child is lost at dusk (see The Hidden Here). She wants the province to send a second priestess before a child is lost on a night when she is already out. An ally for a child hidden by the kami, or by something that isn't one.
<!-- @at the mountain shrine = Tsuruoka, Japan -->

#### Thang Long

The Trịnh lord rules Đại Việt from here and buys cannon and gun-founders (Who Holds Power). In its villages the water puppets' dragons swim across the pond spitting fireworks (Life Here).

**Đào Thị Lựu.** The head of a water-puppet guild in a village outside Thang Long, the first woman to keep the guild's book and swear its oath, which forbids teaching the tricks to anyone who might marry out of the village. She taught them to her daughters anyway and dared the elders to say so. She wants her troupe to play for the Trịnh lord's court at New Year. A host, a contact and a way into court.
<!-- @at Thang Long = Hanoi, Vietnam -->

#### Ayutthaya

Narai's city, whose court keeps Persian ministers and French bishops and hires foreigners for its guard, its ships and its treasury (Who Holds Power). At the full moon of the twelfth month its rivers are covered in floating lights (Life Here).

**Nang Bua.** A river pilot of Ayutthaya, who takes foreign ships from the bar up the Chao Phraya to the city in a narrow boat with a red awning, and tells each captain which of King Narai's ministers to visit first, and with what gift. The captains pay her, and so do two of the ministers and the Japanese quarter. She wants a boat of her own for her daughter before the ministers' quarrel sinks them all. The way into Narai's court for a party that arrives by sea.
<!-- @at Ayutthaya, Thailand -->

#### Angkor

Built for Vishnu and now a Theravada sanctuary, Angkor answers whoever prays in it; what a vigil and a divination do inside the moat is told above (see Angkor).

**Chea Sok.** A Khmer former monk called by spirit illness at Angkor, who sees the temple as the world-mountain it was built to be and guides pilgrims through it by night, describing with complete calm the five peaks above the central tower that nobody else can see. He wants to know why the mountain answered a Japanese pilgrim who thought he was somewhere else. A mentor or contact for any game at Angkor (see Angkor).
<!-- @at Angkor = Siem Reap, Cambodia -->

#### Makassar

Hasanuddin holds it against the VOC and the Bugis prince Arung Palakka (Who Holds Power). On 12 October they win a great battle under its walls, and the brick fortress of Somba Opu still stands (What's Happening in 1668).

**Daeng Calla.** A Makassarese halfling smuggler with a share in a padewakang, who moves Mutapan curiosities without a ministry stamp and carries letters out through the lines at Somba Opu, smiling at a Dutch boarding officer and telling him the long crate is rattan. Her lamps drift every month, and she wants someone with Mutapan training aboard. An ally or contact for the last sortie (see Hooks); her grandmother says the family came from the *orang bunian*, and she says that explains the hiding and nothing else.
<!-- @at Makassar, Indonesia -->

#### Aceh

Sultanah Safiatuddin has kept Aceh free for twenty-seven years and buys cannon and books with pepper (Who Holds Power).

**Teungku Fatimah.** A scholar of the science of letters at the court of Aceh's queen, Sultanah Safiatuddin, who writes the talismans on the port's walls and is one reason the Dutch knock before entering. She wants a book of letters she has only seen quoted, said to be in a Bohra library in Surat, and pays for books in pepper, generously. A Monsoon Road patron.
<!-- @at Aceh = Banda Aceh, Indonesia -->

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The trials.** Two parties at court need the shadow to fall their way in December, and both want witnesses and leverage. Left alone, the shadow falls where the arithmetic says. Before then each side pays for anyone who can move a gnomon, buy a timekeeper or keep one honest.
- **The tombs.** The Ming princes' tombs lie in valleys the new dynasty ignores, and more than one crew is on its way. The first crew through a door meets whatever the sealing day was chosen to hold in.
- **Ainu Mosir**, Hokkaido, is Ainu land, with its own chiefs and its own religion, and bad Matsumae exchange rates are turning trade toward war. In our history the Ainu leader Shakushain raises that war in 1669. A party can carry the grievance to Edo, run rice north or sell either side its news.
- **The delta.** Vietnamese settlers are moving onto Khmer land, the Khmer are burning them out and two courts are watching. A party is hired to escort a settler convoy, to find a burned village's survivors or to carry one court's letter to the other.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The clerk.** A calendar clerk who expects to lose his place at the Bureau in December has found a sealing date that doesn't add up, and wants its tomb opened before Yang's people burn the records.
- **The witness.** A court back in Europe wants its own eyes at the gnomon trials, and both the Jesuits and Yang's party would rather it saw something else.
- **A Wutong gift.** A Jiangnan family grew rich overnight, and the wife wants the bargain broken before the Wutong come for her.
- **The lamp in Nagasaki.** A Dutch factor on Dejima has a Mutapan lamp to sell to the shogun's men, and the company would rather nobody knew where he got it.
- **Seedlings.** Someone is offering nutmeg seedlings from outside the Dutch plots. A Company rival wants them; the *hongi* fleet wants the seller.
- **The last sortie.** Somba Opu needs a message, or a prince, got out through the Bugis lines, and Arung Palakka's scouts know every path.
