sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
The Americas in 1668 are continents of Indigenous powers with European footholds on their edges. Wisdom medicine and divinity blunted each epidemic, so the nations are far stronger than the record has them. In the north the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, in the middle of the Beaver Wars, is the power in front, and the colonies live on its permission. In the south the Inca state never fell: the huacas rose, the Sapa Inca rules from Cusco again and the conquest became a standing war, with Potosí, Spain's silver mountain, on the front line. Between them the Itza at Nojpetén have kept Spain out since Cortés passed through in 1525. What ties the continents together is Spain, stretched across both, and the metal it has been throwing into the Chocó's rivers.

**The one thing to remember:** the Andes are at war, and the world is about to join it. The Inca and Spain fight across the roof of the world, with Spain's silver on the front line and its platina thinly guarded in the Chocó, and everyone else sells to both. Everywhere else the Europeans are small: in the north the diplomacy that matters runs through Onondaga rather than Quebec.

sections.heading: Playing Here
What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The Beaver Wars** go on, moving west. The Dutch who sold the guns have been gone since 1664.
- **Nojpetén** stands. In our history it falls in 1697.
- **The Caribbean.** In July, Henry Morgan will sail from Port Royal and take Portobelo.
- **A new viceroy** marches on Laicacota's rebel silver camp, leaving his wife to govern Lima; see Adventures and Hooks, The High Ground, for the war's 1668.
- **The siege line.** Spain holds Potosí; the Inca hold its approaches and Huancavelica's mercury, so every ounce Spain refines is on Inca sufferance.
- **The platina.** Every ministry of magic now knows what Spain was dumping until 1667 (in our history Spain didn't meet platina until about 1690), and an English squadron at Port Royal is asking how well Spain holds New Granada.
- **The Chocó.** Spain hasn't secured it. The Wounaan have moved upriver from the missionaries; mining families from Popayán push in.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
- **The eastern woodlands.** Palisaded Iroquoian longhouse towns stand in fields of maize, beans and squash that women own and work. The fur front has moved west past the Great Lakes.
- **Mexico and the Caribbean.** Mexico City is still digging out from its 1629 flood; the Maya lowlands are a managed forest garden. Spain's treasure fleets gather at Havana.
- **The vertical Andes.** Each community holds fields at several heights, and freeze-dried potatoes, *chuño*, keep for years, so the high ground can outlast a siege. ✦ The map's Inca state is the book's: in ours it ended at Vilcabamba in 1572, and no atlas draws the high ground it kept.
- **Potosí.** Some 120,000 people live about 13,000 feet up under Cerro Rico, where nothing grows. Everything comes in on llama trains, mercury from Huancavelica among it, and contraband silver leaks out to Buenos Aires. ✦ On the map Potosí is a Spanish town inside a contested ring, not a border; in ours all the country around it was Spain's.
- **The Chocó.** Pacific rainforest with up to 43 feet of rain a year. The rivers are the only roads: the Atrato north to the Caribbean, the San Juan south to the Pacific. The gravel bars hold gold, mixed with grains of a "little silver" that won't pan out.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Haudenosaunee.** Five Nations under the Great Law of Peace. A Grand Council of 50 chiefs, the Onondaga its Firekeepers, decides by consensus. **Clan Mothers choose the chiefs and can remove them.** A party that wants passage, trade or peace asks at Onondaga, through a speaker the council accepts, with wampum.
- **New France and the English.** Quebec's casters hold Paris's license. The English hold New York (Dutch until 1664), Virginia, New England, Barbados and Jamaica: smaller than in our history, with no reach inland. Both pay for furs and interpreters, and neither moves inland without a nation's leave.
- **Nojpetén.** The Itza capital, on an island in Lake Petén Itzá, under a king titled *Aj Kan Ek'*. Their prophecy says it isn't yet time to convert, and here their gods' answer is why the friars keep failing. The Itza receive envoys and send them home, and trade for iron tools through Maya towns that left Spanish rule.
- **The Sapa Inca.** The son of the Sun, here literally: Inti's son by blood (a divine-blood: Peoples, Divine-Bloods), and the succession goes to whichever royal son the Sun answers. He rules by bargaining with the huacas (mountains, springs, stones, oracles and the mummified dead), which now answer back. He is **Cusi Túpac Yupanqui** (KOO-see TOO-pahk yoo-PAHN-kee), of Manco Inca's line: the fourth Sapa Inca since Vilcabamba held in 1572, named for joy, splendor and honor, as his house's kings always are. He pays outsiders in cloth, silver and safe roads for work his own officers can't do in a Spanish town.
- **Spain.** In Mexico City and Lima viceroys rule with the Church, and in Peru the Archbishop's campaign against "idolatry" is at its height. The viceroys pay in silver and offices for news from the Inca side of the line.
- **The Mapuche.** Independent by treaty since 1641. Spain's frontier south of Santiago is an army post paid for from Peru. Horses, cloth and captives cross that frontier both ways, and both sides pay the go-betweens who arrange it.
- **Brazil and Palmares.** Portugal's Brazil, governed from Salvador, runs on sugar worked by enslaved Africans. In the hills of Pernambuco the *quilombo* of Palmares, free since about 1605, holds fortified towns under an elected king. Palmares trades with its neighbors for powder and salt, and takes in anyone who reaches it.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
The Americas' advantage is Wisdom medicine and divinity (see Magic, Faith and Wisdom). **The catch:** a magical cure isn't immunity (see Powers and Factions, Lanternhall and the Healers), so every healed town is exposed again when the sickness returns.

- **Medicine.** Haudenosaunee medicine societies have members, songs and obligations; their rites are private, the Confederacy asks that the masks not be shown, and the book doesn't depict them. Cinchona bark from Loja cures malaria; Kallawaya healers of the Bolivian highlands carry a pharmacopoeia of about 980 plants.
- **The huacas rose.** During Taki Onqoy (c. 1564–72) followers said the huacas had left stones and lakes to enter human bodies. Here they did. Keepers speak for each, and weather is a weapon.
- **The jaibaná.** Emberá and Wounaan specialists of the Chocó, men and women, who capture *jai*, the animating force of everything and of disease, and are hired to "open" a river for settlement.
- **Platina.** Spain can't separate the platinum grains from Chocó gold, so until 1667 it stored them and threw them back into the rivers under a notary's certificate, lest anyone fake gold with them. Since the crown's order of 1667, royal officials seal the grains in barrels and send them away under guard. The order hasn't reached every camp. Where the crown has no official, miners still throw the platina back, and smugglers have started buying it. How the powers found out: The World in 1668, The Mark.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Many peoples' Hidden, not one.

- **The Jogah** (Haudenosaunee). Little people of caves and stream banks. Drumming with no drummer means they want tobacco. Their stories are told only in winter.
- **The wendigo** (Cree *wīhtikōw*, Ojibwe *wiindigoo*). What a person becomes when hunger breaks the duty to share, rather than a horror monster. Many people don't speak of it lightly, and a table that brings it in can take it the same way.
- **Owners of places.** The Maya *aluxes* guard a field; the Emberá *wãndra*, "jealous and surly," live at the Chocó's headwaters and can take jaguar form. In the Andes the people of the old age, ancestors in caves, sicken those who neglect them.
- **The fat-stealer.** The Andean *pishtaco* is the fairy turned inside out: the dangerous stranger is European, cutting people open for their fat.
- **The edge** half fits. The beings past an Iroquoian palisade are kin; in the Andes the edge runs up and down a mountain, between a community's floors. The Hidden Killers patrol the colonies' villages; each nation keeps its own protectors on its own terms.
- **The Hunt** keeps the northern dark half above the equator and the southern below it. In the eastern woodlands it comes on foot and by canoe, fast and silent; on the plains and in New Mexico it rides horses, which few of the plains peoples have yet; in the Andes it comes down from the high country with a llama train behind it.

sections.heading: Life Here
sections.text:
Life here runs on the land's own calendars, the corn, the potato, the cane and the rains, and on what people owe each other. Most of it happens far from any European, and has for a long time.

**A day at Onondaga.** The Firekeepers' town stands on its hill inside a palisade: bark longhouses, each the home of a line of sisters, their daughters, their husbands and their children, two families to a fire down a central aisle. The women and girls are in the fields at first light, among the corn, beans and squash, which are theirs; the men are hunting, trading, in council or away at the war. The old sit with the small children and teach them what everything is called. Every visitor eats first, at any hour, before anyone asks what they came for, and a kettle of corn soup is always on for it. Summer evenings the young men play lacrosse on the flats below the town; winter evenings are for the stories, which may only be told when the snow is down.

**Food and drink.** In the woodlands: corn soup, hominy, cornbread baked in the husk with beans or berries in it, venison, lake fish and, in June, wild strawberries. In the Andes: potatoes in hundreds of kinds, *chuño* freeze-dried for the lean years, quinoa, *charki*, guinea pig for a feast and *aqha*, the maize beer the world calls chicha, at every work party. Mexico City drinks chocolate at all hours, in every house that can afford it and some that can't. Brazil eats cassava flour with everything, and Palmares grows its own.

**The year.**

- **Midwinter,** at Onondaga and in every Haudenosaunee town, at the first new moon after the solstice (mid-January in 1668). People go from house to house telling their dreams in riddles, and whoever guesses a dream must give the dreamer what it asked for. The two halves of the town play the peach-stone game against each other for days, and everyone bets.
- **The strawberries,** in June: the first fruit of the year, crushed into a drink that everyone shares, with thanks.
- **Inti Raymi,** at the June solstice in Cusco: the Sapa Inca, who is the Sun's son here, greets his father at dawn in the great square.
- **Situa,** in Cusco at the first new moon after the September equinox (6 October in 1668): the city sends its sickness away. A hundred runners carry it out toward each of the four quarters and wash it off in the rivers, the whole city bathes at dawn, doorposts are smeared with *sankhu*, the festival bread, and strangers wait outside the city until they are called back for four days of feasting. Here, for a season, the sickness does go.

**Who helps.** When a Haudenosaunee family loses someone, the clans across the fire come to condole: they wipe the mourners' tears, clear their ears and open their throats, so that grief doesn't take their minds, with the words that made the League in the first place. In the Andes nobody works alone: at a *mink'a* (Life in 1668, Neighbors) the whole community turns out for one field, and the household that called it feeds everyone and pours the *aqha*. The Sapa Inca's storehouses feed the widows, the orphans and the old, and this war the families of his runners. In Salvador and Recife the Black brotherhoods of Our Lady of the Rosary nurse their sick, bury their dead with candles and a sung Mass, and save coin in a locked chest to buy their members free.

**What people love.** Lacrosse: the Creator's game, played by whole towns against each other, sometimes for a sick person's recovery, always with the old men arguing on the sidelines. In the Andes, the panpipes and the *harawi*, the love songs and the songs of parting, sung at every leave-taking on the war's roads. In New Spain, processions, chocolate and gossip, in that order.

#### Hooks

- **The dream nobody can guess.** At Midwinter an old woman of the Turtle Clan has told her dream in riddles at every house in Onondaga and nobody has guessed it. Until someone does, it can't be given to her, and she's getting thinner.
- **The *mink'a*.** A widow's field above the Apurímac must be dug before the frost, the men are at the front and the *aqha* is already brewing. The party is the work party, and the whole village has come to watch.
- **The brotherhood's chest.** The Rosary brotherhood in Salvador has saved eleven years to buy one of its sisters free, and the day before the sale her owner raised the price. The brothers want someone to argue him, shame him or bargain him back to his word before the feast of the Rosary in October.

sections.heading: Places
sections.text:
Each of the setting's own people here stands in the place where a party meets them, with what they want and how a table uses them. The High Ground's cast comes first. Each has a pregen sheet. The sheets are on the site, perceptualmechanics.com/euphonia.

#### The Apurímac front

The Inca and Spain fight across the roof of the world (At a Glance), and the men of the villages above the Apurímac are away at the front (Life Here). Weather is a weapon here, because keepers speak for the huacas (Magic Here).

**Kusi Wallpa.** The Sapa Inca's senior staff officer on the Apurímac front, who reads Spanish columns by their dust and empties the storehouses on their road before they arrive. Find him on a cold rock above a column's road, a khipu across his knees and a runner waiting. He hires outsiders for what a khipu can't do (reading a Spanish captain, buying a mule-driver, finding who in Potosí sells powder to both sides) and pays in cloth, safe roads and his word. The patron of an Inca start in The High Ground, who wants the Spanish column turned back before the harvest, with as few of his own counted out of the khipu as he can manage.
<!-- @at the Apurímac front = Abancay, Peru -->

**Waman Illa.** A storm-priest of the high valleys above the Apurímac, struck by lightning as a boy herder, who keeps a huaca that rose in the Taki Onqoy years and speaks for it to the Sapa Inca's officers, and for them to it. Officers climb to his shelf above the Apurímac crossing with khipus of the Spanish column and leave with rain, and a list of what the huaca wants in return; he offers everyone coca while they decide whether to pay. He wants to see the war end before the huaca decides it likes it. A patron or ally for an Inca start in The High Ground (see Adventures and Hooks).
<!-- @at the Apurímac crossing = Abancay, Peru -->

#### The roads

The war's roads run between the lines, and the *harawi*, the songs of parting, are sung at every leave-taking on them (Life Here).

**Willka Mamani.** A Kallawaya healer of Charazani who walks the war's roads with close to a thousand plants in his head, treating Inca runners and Spanish muleteers alike. He goes between the lines with a mule and a woven bag of medicines, stopping wherever someone is sick. Both armies let him through because both need him, and he sells each exactly as much news of the other; he wants the road kept open to healers whoever wins, and has asked both commanders to swear it. A mentor, and the best guide across the line alive.
<!-- @at Charazani = Puerto Acosta, Bolivia -->

#### Lima

The viceroy rules Peru from here with the Church, and the Archbishop's campaign against "idolatry" is at its height (Who Holds Power). This year the new viceroy marches on Laicacota and leaves his wife to govern the city (What's Happening in 1668).

**Licenciado Diego Ruiz de Lezcano.** A visitor-general of idolatries for the Archbishop of Lima, who burns the mummified dead and the stones that speak, and whose prayers work, which he takes as proof. He sets up at a table in a highland plaza with a notary, soldiers and a bonfire laid but not yet lit, calling the village's ancestors by name in a gentle voice and writing down who doesn't answer. He is sincere, learned and kind to children, and wants one village where the stone stays silent after he has prayed over it. A villain for the visitations (see Trouble Brewing), and a frightened man.
<!-- @at Lima, Peru -->

#### Cusco

The Sapa Inca rules from Cusco again (At a Glance). At the June solstice he greets his father the Sun in the great square, and at Situa the city sends its sickness away (Life Here).

**Chuqui Ocllo.** A brewer of Cusco whose house's *aqha* is poured at Situa and at half the *mink'a* gatherings in the valley, keeping track out loud of who owes whom a day's work, back three harvests. She has fed the Sapa Inca's officers, a captured Spanish muleteer and a huaca's keeper at one bench without anyone leaving hungry or angry, and wants her son home from the Apurímac front in time to dig his own field. A host and a contact who knows everyone in Cusco, and what they owe.
<!-- @at Cusco, Peru -->

#### Onondaga

The Firekeepers' town, where a party that wants passage, trade or peace asks the Grand Council, through a speaker the council accepts, with wampum (Who Holds Power). Life Here spends a day and a Midwinter in it.

**Ganonhsese.** An Onondaga Clan Mother, among the Firekeepers of the Haudenosaunee, who chooses her clan's chief for the Grand Council and can remove him. Find her in her longhouse at Onondaga in winter, shelling beans with her daughters while a council chief explains himself to her. The patron of the drumming (see Hooks), who pays in the Confederacy's remembering.
<!-- @at Onondaga = Syracuse, United States of America -->

#### The Eastern Door

The Confederacy's door on the trail from Albany, whose new English masters will sell the Haudenosaunee guns at a price that includes a say in whom they fight next (Trouble Brewing).

**Kawennanoron.** A Mohawk matron of the Wolf Clan, of the Keepers of the Eastern Door, whose longhouse stands nearest the trail from Albany, so every traveler eats her corn soup before anyone else's. She decides which guest gets which bowl and what the council hears about each, and she wants the Albany traders to stop carrying rum up the trail before the next council. A host, and the gate into the Confederacy from the east.
<!-- @at the Eastern Door = Schenectady, United States of America -->

#### Mille Lacs

Dakota country, west of the Great Lakes. The fur front has moved west past the lakes (The Lay of the Land), and the Beaver Wars are moving west with it (What's Happening in 1668).

**Čhaŋté Wašté Wiŋ.** A Dakota druid of the lake country around Mille Lacs who hunts bison on foot with her people and takes the bison's shape, a fact about her rather than a secret. She lets the young men tell her story wrong, and wants a good harvest, a quiet winter and no black-robed visitors; she has seen one Frenchman, at a distance, carrying a kettle, and has not felt the lack. An ally or mentor on her own ground, where she has enough to do.
<!-- @at Mille Lacs = Brainerd, United States of America -->

#### Mexico City

New Spain's viceroy rules here with the Church (Who Holds Power), in a city still digging out from its 1629 flood (The Lay of the Land) that drinks chocolate at all hours (Life Here).

**Doña Isabel Cuauhtzin.** A Nahua cacica of a noble Xochimilco family who paints portrait miniatures for the viceroy's court in Mexico City, and so holds the likeness of everyone worth scrying in New Spain. She keeps her family's lawsuit over their Xochimilco lands going in Spanish, and has started, very quietly, painting her likenesses slightly wrong. A contact for a Great Game in New Spain; three services want her sketchbooks.
<!-- @at Mexico City, Mexico -->

#### Nojpetén

The Itza capital, on an island in Lake Petén Itzá, has kept Spain out since 1525 (At a Glance), and a Spanish road is being surveyed toward the lake (Trouble Brewing).

**Aj K'in Kuch.** An Itza priest who reads the k'atun count for the Aj Kan Ek' at Nojpetén, and has seen, past the edge of the world, why it is not yet time; he tells a friar politely and precisely that he has come twenty-nine years too early. He wants the surveyor never to arrive, and the count kept by more than one reader in case he does. A patron or mentor for the survey (see Hooks).
<!-- @at Nojpetén = Flores, Guatemala -->

#### Chocó

Pacific rainforest whose rivers are the only roads, and whose gravel bars hold gold mixed with platina (The Lay of the Land). The Wounaan have moved upriver from the missionaries, and mining families from Popayán push in (What's Happening in 1668).

**Kima Ismare.** A Wounaan *jaibaná* of the upper San Juan, hired by her people to keep a river shut against the mining families from Popayán, who have hired another jaibaná to open it. She has kept it shut six years from under her stilt house, and wants to outlast her rival, a man she trained and is not proud of. A patron or foil for opening the river (see Hooks), paid in fish, cloth and the right to be cross with everyone.
<!-- @at the upper San Juan = Quibdo, Colombia -->

#### Palmares

The *quilombo* in the hills of Pernambuco, free since about 1605, holds fortified towns under an elected king and takes in anyone who reaches it (Who Holds Power; see Powers and Factions, The Free Towns).

**Ana Kitumba.** A captain of Palmares, born free behind the palisade at Macaco after her mother came up from a Pernambuco sugar mill with a baby and nothing else. At dusk she walks the palisade greeting every sentry by name; by day she sits at council in the king's house. She wants a child of hers to grow old in Palmares without having to fight for it. An ally or patron.
<!-- @at Palmares = Rio Largo, Brazil -->

#### Porto Calvo

Pernambuco's sugar country, below the hills of Palmares. Portugal's Brazil runs on sugar worked by enslaved Africans (Who Holds Power).

**Brás Furtado.** A *capitão-do-mato*, a hunter of people who escaped slavery, whom the sugar planters of Pernambuco hire to lead their expeditions against Palmares, naming the price per head without looking up. He has studied every expedition that failed against Palmares and knows why each did, which is why Ana Kitumba knows his name. A villain from a hard part of the record; a table chooses how much of him to use.
<!-- @at Porto Calvo = Barreiros, Brazil -->

#### Salvador

Portugal's Brazil is governed from Salvador (Who Holds Power), where the Black brotherhoods of Our Lady of the Rosary save coin in a locked chest to buy their members free (Life Here). The brotherhood's chest is that section's third hook.

**Domingas da Costa.** A free woman from Angola who sells cooked food from a tray in Salvador's lower city and keeps the key to the Rosary brotherhood's chest. She bought her own freedom a coin at a time and has helped buy six others since; the seventh is in Life Here's hooks. A patron of the brotherhood's chest, who pays in food, favors and a welcome in every Black brotherhood on the coast.
<!-- @at Salvador, Brazil -->

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The guns.** The Dutch who armed the Confederacy are gone. Albany's new English masters will sell guns, at a price that includes a say in whom the Confederacy fights next.
- **The kivas and the road.** Santa Fe burns kivas, and a Tewa religious leader named Po'pay is watching; whether and when the Pueblos rise is the table's; by default, as in our history, in August 1680. To the south, Itza priests read the prophecy as a Spanish road is surveyed toward the lake.
- **The visitations.** Lima's extirpators, burning mummies, are reaching villages whose huacas talk back.
- **Florida.** Spain's missions run west from St Augustine through Timucua and Apalachee country, and the mission towns owe labor drafts to carry maize to the coast. The Timucua rose against the drafts in 1656 and were crushed; the Apalachee are counting. In our history English buccaneers under Robert Searle sack St Augustine this May. A party can carry a grievance to Havana, warn the presidio or sell the presidio's weakness in Port Royal.
- **The continental war.** If New Granada and Cartagena fall easily, the first navy up the Atrato takes the metal. The Wounaan and the Emberá know the rivers, and every fleet that comes will need a guide or will take one.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The drumming.** In a Haudenosaunee town the drumming has started with no drummer, and nobody left tobacco. A Clan Mother wants to know who neglected the Jogah before winter's stories can be told.
- **The mission's price.** A Jesuit healer will lay hands on a dying Wendat village only after baptism. A medicine society would do it for nothing, if someone can carry word past the mission.
- **The survey.** A Spanish surveyor wants guides to Lake Petén Itzá. An Itza priest wants him never to arrive.
- **The notary's barrels.** A season's platina sits in sealed barrels at a river camp, waiting for the crown's canoes, and a smuggler out of Cartagena wants it first.
- **Opening the river.** A mining company has hired a jaibaná to open a river, and the Wounaan have hired another to keep it shut.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
Oceania is a sea of islands, and the sea is the road: its peoples navigated to Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa centuries ago. Europe has a few charts, a VOC verdict that Australia is worthless and a Jesuit mission bound for Guam. On Pohnpei, in the eastern Carolines, tradition says two sorcerer brothers raised the basalt city of Nan Madol by magic. In Euphonia, they did, and the Monsoon Road has started asking how.

**The one thing to remember:** Pohnpei shows what a society can build with spells instead of brick, and what it risks by relying on them alone.

sections.heading: Playing Here
What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **Guam.** The Jesuit San Vitores sails for the Marianas to plant Spain's first lasting presence among the Chamorro; in our history thirty years of war follow.
- **Aotearoa.** Pā-building in the Waikato has paused; in our history fighting resumes in the early 1700s.
- **Australia.** Whether Makassar trepang fishers have reached Arnhem Land is the DM's call; by default not yet, and the first praus come within a generation.
- **The Monsoon Road** reaches this far; its agents have put Wisdom-built places on their list.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
- **High islands and atolls.** Volcanic islands like Pohnpei feed many people; atolls rise a few feet from the sea.
- **Nan Madol.** Off Pohnpei's coast, a complex of artificial basalt islets, tombs and channels; its first chiefly tomb stands over 25 feet high. It's the region's great site and holds the chiefly dead; nobody goes in without leave from the people who keep it (see Places, Nan Madol).
- **Wayfinding.** Navigators hold a star compass of 32 houses and read several swells at once; Carolinians imagine the canoe as still and the islands moving past it. It's a science, taught in ranked, initiated schools.
- **Australia.** A continent of Country: every part named, sung, owned and cared for under Law.
- **New Guinea.** One of the world's first farming centers, at Kuk.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **Pohnpei.** The Saudeleur dynasty ruled from Nan Madol until Isokelekel of Kosrae overthrew it, by tradition about 1628; power is now split among chiefdoms under **Nahnmwarki** titles. Priests, the *samworo*, mediate with the gods and work sorcery. The chiefs hold the titles and the priests the rites, and the stones answer neither by right. A visitor needs a chief's leave to land and the priests' leave to go near Nan Madol.
- **Aotearoa.** *Hapū*, the working political and land-holding units, within *iwi*, under *rangatira* whose authority rests on descent, ability and *mana*. *Tapu* restricts persons of rank, burial grounds and certain acts. A visiting party is called onto the marae and hosted; what it can ask after that depends on what it brought and who speaks for it.
- **Tonga.** The Tuʻi Tonga is a sacred paramount, of the sky god Tangaloa's line (Peoples, Divine-Bloods), whose chiefly network reaches Samoa and Fiji. Tongan canoes carry tribute, brides and craftsmen between the three island groups, and a place in one is how a party travels. In Samoa, authority sits with the *matai*, the titled heads each family chooses, meeting in village councils; in Fiji, with the chiefs of ranked lineages, some of them married into the Tongan network.
- **Tahiti and the Society Islands.** Chiefs and priests allied around ʻOro's temple on Raʻiātea; the traveling ʻarioi mock the chiefs. The ʻarioi are fed wherever they land, and a party in their company is fed with them.
- **Hawaiʻi.** Rival paramount chiefs, whose genealogies run back to the gods (Peoples, Divine-Bloods), and *kapu*, sacred law whose breaking means death unless the offender reaches a place of refuge. A chief at war wants canoes, fighters and a kahuna's reading of the day.
- **Aboriginal Australia.** About 250 language groups; authority rests with senior men and women by knowledge and age, not with a ruler. The book sets no play here. These lines mark what a ship's crew would be walking into: owned country, entered by its owners' leave.
- **New Guinea.** Hundreds of peoples and languages, from highland valleys farmed for thousands of years to the Sepik and the coasts. Authority rests with clan elders and with big men, who win followers by giving more than they receive at exchange feasts. Coastal peoples trade along the shore by canoe, clay pots and shell valuables for sago and timber. The book sets no play inland; a ship that lands is the guest of whoever owns the beach.
- **The outsiders.** Spain's Manila galleons water at Guam; the VOC has charted nothing it wants to buy. The galleon pays for water, food and a pilot, and stays as few days as it can.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
- **Mana.** The nearest Oceanic word to what this book calls Prime, the first matter that magic runs on (see Magic, Prime and the Threshold): spiritual power, authority and prestige, inherited, and gained or lost through action.
- **Pohnpei builds with spells.** Olisihpa and Olosohpa raised Nan Madol's basalt, and the samworo and the stone-raisers after them have kept it and built on it. Pohnpei's sea walls, canals and islets are all kept this way, and few people are left who can do it (see Trouble Brewing). Rites at stone altars, *pei*, secure land and sea.
- **Experts.** A Māori *tohunga* is an expert, not only a priest; Hawaiian *kāhuna* include healers and sorcerers.
- **Australia's healers.** *Ngangkari* treat harms to the spirit. The making of "clever" men and women is restricted knowledge and stays off the page.
- **The sea's otherworlds.** Pulotu and Hawaiki lie across the sea, not up or down: the blessed isles at the mouth of the River of Life, which a Revelator walks (see The Plenum). Nobody in Europe has asked whether Prime, like mana, can be lost.

**At the table.** Nan Madol's basalt was asked into place, and it still answers to asking.

- **Leave.** Working stone at Nan Madol takes leave from two hands: a Nahnmwarki's for the place and the samworo's for the rite. Each is asked for separately, and each is given for one named work.
- **Without leave,** a spell or feature that moves, shapes or breaks stone or earth inside Nan Madol (*Stone Shape*, *Move Earth*, *Passwall*, *Wall of Stone*, a Shaper's features) fails, and the slot or use is spent.
- **With leave,** stone raised or shaped there can't be dispelled. Once it is permanent (a *Wall of Stone* held for the spell's full duration, or *Stone Shape*), it stands until someone with leave asks it down.
- **Elsewhere on Pohnpei** the same spells work as written. Only Nan Madol asks.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Each people has its own Hidden, mostly recorded after contact; much is restricted by rank, gender, initiation or clan.

- **The patupaiarehe** (Aotearoa). The closest Pacific figure to the Hidden: a people of the misty hilltops, fair-skinned and never tattooed. Their flutes entrance a woman and can call her back at will. Dawn defeats them; firelight, cooking smoke and red ochre keep them off.
- **Taniwha.** Guardians or dangers of particular rivers, lakes and seas, closer to dragons than fairies.
- **The menehune** (Hawaiʻi). Night builders who must finish by dawn.
- **Eni** (Pohnpei). Gods and owners of places; they keep no court and steal no children.
- **The Hunt by sea.** The Wild Hunt crosses the sea of islands in canoes that land at night where the fires are out, and in Aotearoa it comes down off the hills in the mist with the patupaiarehe's flutes. It keeps the dark half of its own hemisphere: the northern on Pohnpei and Hawaiʻi, the southern in Aotearoa and Tahiti.
- **Country isn't the Hidden.** The Dreaming is Law and ongoing creation, not an otherworld, and mapping it onto the Hidden misrepresents it. Nor does the village edge fit Country, where every place is someone's home ground; in Aotearoa the patupaiarehe's hills were the edges of settlement, but still Māori land.

sections.heading: Life Here
sections.text:
Across the sea of islands a life is the garden, the reef, the canoe and the feast, and a person is known by how well they feed their guests.

**A day on Pohnpei.** Morning in a farmstead on the green slopes: the yam gardens and the breadfruit, children sent up the trees, women working the reef flats with hand nets at low tide and men out past the reef in canoes. Breadfruit that can't be eaten fresh goes into leaf-lined pits to ferment, against a bad year. In the evening everyone who matters, and everyone else, goes to the feast house, where *sakau*, the kava root, is pounded on an old basalt stone with a ringing knock you can hear across the valley, squeezed through hibiscus bark and served by rank. The first cup goes to the highest title in the house. "The cup doesn't come to you," people say. "You go to the cup."

**Food and drink.** Breadfruit, yams, taro, coconut and fish, everywhere. Kava is drunk in a circle from Pohnpei to Tonga, Samoa, Fiji and Hawaiʻi, and the circle is where the talking gets done. Hawaiʻi eats poi, pounded taro, and fish from stone-walled fishponds on the shore; Aotearoa eats *kūmara*, the sweet potato, kept in pits through winter, fern root, and birds preserved in their own fat, all cooked in the earth oven.

**The year.**

- **The yam feasts** on Pohnpei, at the height of the yam season (September to November): prize yams carried on poles to the Nahnmwarki's feast house, decorated with fern, and the whole chiefdom arguing for a month about whose was biggest.
- **Makahiki** in Hawaiʻi, from the evening the Pleiades first rise at sunset (late October or early November) for four months. War is kapu, offerings go around the island behind Lono's standard and everyone plays: boxing, wrestling, canoe races, surfing, *ʻulu maika* stone-bowling and races on sleds down stone-paved slides.
- **Matariki** in Aotearoa, when the Pleiades rise before dawn in midwinter (late June): the new year. The names of the year's dead are called to the stars, the first of the stored food is offered and there is feasting and kite-flying. It falls in the southern dark half, so the pā's fires burn high that night for two reasons.
- **The ʻinasi** on Tongatapu, the first-fruits presentation to the Tuʻi Tonga, when yams, mats and kava come in from every island under him (Fusipala keeps the count; see Places, Tonga).

**Who helps.** In Hawaiʻi the *puʻuhonua*, the place of refuge, is mercy written into law: a kapu-breaker or a beaten warrior who reaches one is safe, and goes home absolved. In Aotearoa a hapū's mana rests on *manaakitanga*, how well it looks after its guests: a visiting party is called on by a woman's voice, wept over for its dead, fed until it can't move, and remembered. Children are raised by grandparents and aunts as readily as by their parents, openly, and everyone knows whose they are. On Pohnpei the chief's feast goes back out: what comes in on poles leaves in baskets.

**What people love.** In Hawaiʻi, surfing, by chiefs and commoners, men and women, with bets on the beach. In Tahiti, the ʻarioi, who make chiefs laugh at themselves (see Places, Tahiti). In Aotearoa, string games, kites and the long speeches on the marae, judged like poetry. In Australia, every few summers, when the bunya pines of the Bunya Mountains bear heavily, their custodians send word and nations come from hundreds of miles for weeks of feasting on the nuts, trading, arranging marriages and settling what needs settling. What else happens there is theirs, and stays off the page.

#### Hooks

- **The biggest yam.** Two Pohnpei families each swear their prize yam is the largest in the chiefdom, the Nahnmwarki's feast is in three days and one of the yams has gone missing from its pole overnight. Both families have fed the party already.
- **The stranger in the surf.** At Makahiki a chief's daughter has bet her canoe on a surfing match against a stranger nobody saw arrive, who rides the waves at night and leaves no footprints on the sand. She wants to win fairly, and she wants to know who he is first.
- **The guests are early.** A Waikato hapū is hosting a great gathering, the guests are two days early and the kūmara pits are low after a lean year. The party has two days to find food for three hundred, because the hapū's mana is on the table.

sections.heading: Places
sections.text:
Each of the setting's own people here stands in the place where a party meets them, with what they want and how a table uses them. Sehpin, Kilimoar, Lihpahnu and Tinashe Gumbo come first: they are one cast on Pohnpei. Each has a pregen sheet. The sheets are on the site, perceptualmechanics.com/euphonia.

#### Nan Madol

Off Pohnpei's coast, basalt islets, tombs and channels raised by magic, which hold the chiefly dead; nobody goes in without leave from the people who keep it (The Lay of the Land). What working its stone takes is in Magic Here.

**Sehpin.** A yam-grower's child the basalt answered at fifteen, now one of the few left who can raise a course at Nan Madol, and the keeper of the chiefly dead behind the walls. Find them waist-deep in the shallows at dusk with a palm on a fallen column, or at the feast house the day the prize yams come in. A Nahnmwarki asks for their work and so do the samworo, and neither has it by right; Sehpin wants to stop being asked to choose. A patron or mentor: when traders off the Monsoon Road ask how the stones were raised, Sehpin tells them the truth, that you ask, and they write it down as if it were a lie (see Hooks).
<!-- @at Nan Madol = Palikir, Federated States of Micronesia -->

**Kilimoar.** A *samworo*, a priest of Pohnpei, who made Sehpin listen to the basalt for a year before letting them touch it. He keeps to the old teachers' stones at Salapwuk, or goes to Nan Madol at night to lay offerings on a *pei* the chiefs have forgotten. He wants the rites kept by someone after him, and not sold, and would rather Sehpin kept them than built sea walls for a chief. A mentor or rival; when a Monsoon Road trader asked to buy the method, he laughed so long the trader left.
<!-- @at Salapwuk = Palikir, Federated States of Micronesia -->

#### Pohnpei

A high island under Nahnmwarki chiefs, where a visitor needs a chief's leave to land (Who Holds Power). Life Here spends a day on it, and its biggest yam is that section's first hook.

**Lihpahnu.** Sehpin's elder sister, who grows the family's prize yams for the chiefs' feasts and considers this the family's real work. She's up to her elbows in red earth above the lagoon, or at the feast house the night the yams come in on poles. She loves Sehpin, finds the stones a little showy and wants to grow a yam so large the Nahnmwarki remembers her name and not her sibling's. Anyone who wants Sehpin goes through her kitchen, and she feeds them first and asks questions after.
<!-- @at Pohnpei = Palikir, Federated States of Micronesia -->

**Tinashe Gumbo.** A Mutapan Mhizha, grandson of the royal medium Ambuya Rudo Gumbo, who came out along the Monsoon Road to learn how Pohnpei's stones were raised, and whether the method can be bought. He waits at the edge of a Nahnmwarki's feast house for leave to see Nan Madol at night, his construct holding a sunshade over him while he asks every passing child the Pohnpeian word for something. He has watched Sehpin talk a column into a wall and is no longer sure what he came to buy. A rival or contact, and the trader of the stones (see Hooks).
<!-- @at Pohnpei = Palikir, Federated States of Micronesia -->

**Sarongelug.** A *palu*, a master navigator of the Carolinian wayfinding schools on Polowat, who holds the star compass and the swells in his head. A Dutch captain offered him a year's silver for a passage no chart shows, and he told the captain, kindly, that the school doesn't sell and the captain couldn't pay. He wants one more voyage to Guam before the Spanish change it. A mentor or contact for a navigator for hire (see Hooks).
<!-- @at Pohnpei = Palikir, Federated States of Micronesia -->

#### Guam

Spain's Manila galleons water at Guam (Who Holds Power), and in June the Jesuit San Vitores lands there, welcomed by the chief Kepuha (Trouble Brewing).

**Asiga.** A Chamorro *makåhna* in Hagåtña, a healer and speaker to the ancestors, who will watch San Vitores's mission come ashore in June, studying the black-robed men the way she'd study a new plant. Chief Kepuha has welcomed the Jesuits and she respects Kepuha; she hasn't decided whether to be the priests' best friend or their worst problem, and wants her curious daughter not to decide anything quickly. A contact or foil for the mission (see Trouble Brewing).
<!-- @at Hagåtña = Agana, Guam -->

#### Tonga

The Tuʻi Tonga is a sacred paramount whose chiefly network reaches Samoa and Fiji, and Tongan canoes carry tribute, brides and craftsmen between the three (Who Holds Power). On Tongatapu the ʻinasi brings him the first fruits of every island under him (Life Here).

**Fusipala.** A woman of a chiefly house at Lapaha on Tongatapu who keeps the order of the *ʻinasi*, the first-fruits presentation to the Tuʻi Tonga: whose yams, mats and kava go where, and what it means when a chief sends less. The Tuʻi Tonga is sacred and doesn't count things, so she counts them for him, with a knotted cord in her lap, and wants to know which chief is sending short on purpose this year. A patron who hires strangers when a canoe goes missing, because a stranger can ask what a chief can't.
<!-- @at Lapaha = Nukualofa, Tonga -->

#### Tahiti

Chiefs and priests are allied around ʻOro's temple on Raʻiātea, and the traveling ʻarioi mock the chiefs and are fed wherever they land (Who Holds Power).

**Tetua.** A young ʻarioi of ʻOro's society from Raʻiātea, whose troupe mocks the chiefs in dance and verse and is fed handsomely for it. She can imitate a chief's walk so exactly that his own sons can't breathe, and she wants the next grade of the society, and its leg tattoos, before the troupe sails for the other islands. A contact who hears what chiefs say when they think the performers are only performing.
<!-- @at Tahiti = Papeete, French Polynesia -->

#### Kona

On Hawaiʻi Island, where rival paramount chiefs rule under kapu (Who Holds Power) and Makahiki brings four months of games, surfing among them (Life Here). The stranger in the surf is that section's second hook.

**Hoʻolulu.** A *kahuna lāʻau lapaʻau* of Kona on Hawaiʻi Island, a healer by plants and prayer who studied twenty years before he was let near a patient, and who hurries for no one. He has treated the warriors of three rival chiefs and been thanked by all three, and wants an apprentice patient enough to learn a plant's prayer before its use. A mentor or ally; when no plant answers, he goes up the mountain and asks why.
<!-- @at Kona = Kailua-Kona, United States of America -->

**Kalehua.** A chief's daughter of Kona on Hawaiʻi Island, who has won the Makahiki surfing three years running and composes the chants that tease whoever she beats. She wants a match against someone worth beating. An ally, and the chief's daughter in the hook (see Life Here).
<!-- @at Kona = Kailua-Kona, United States of America -->

#### The Waikato

Pā-building in the Waikato has paused (What's Happening in 1668), and patupaiarehe flutes sound on the misty ridges (The Hidden Here). A Waikato hapū's early guests are Life Here's third hook.

**Kaiawa.** A *tohunga* of a Waikato hapū who heals with the waters that run toward Hawaiki and keeps the pā's fires lit when patupaiarehe flutes sound on the ridge. She wants the flutes off her ridge for good, is ready to go up and ask what that would cost, and tells anyone who'll listen that a pause is not a peace. A mentor or ally for the flute (see Hooks).
<!-- @at the Waikato = Hamilton, New Zealand -->

**Hinewai.** The *kaikaranga* of a Waikato hapū, whose call brings every visiting party onto the marae, so hers is the first voice anyone hears on arriving. She is Kaiawa's cousin, and thinks Kaiawa should come down off the ridge and eat something. A host and an ally for a party that arrives properly.
<!-- @at the Waikato = Hamilton, New Zealand -->

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The mission.** San Vitores lands on Guam in June, and the chief Kepuha welcomes him. In our history a chief named Matapang kills him in 1672 and thirty years of war follow. The welcome wears out as baptized infants die and the holy water is blamed.
- **The method.** Traders off the Monsoon Road keep asking how Nan Madol's stones were raised and whether the method can be bought. Each refusal raises the offer, and a chief short of allies may sell what the priests refused.
- **The few who can.** Pohnpei's sea walls, canals and islets were raised by asking and are mended the same way. Only a handful of people can still raise a course, and nobody on the island has had to cut and haul basalt in living memory. If the few are bought, drowned or set against each other, the walls go unmended and the sea takes the taro pits first.
- **The fortified hills.** The Waikato's pā-building has paused. In our history the fighting resumes in the early 1700s. Here a disputed eel weir, a slight at a gathering or a woman lost to the flutes and blamed on a neighbor could start it sooner.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The stones.** A trader off the Monsoon Road wants a Nahnmwarki's permission to see Nan Madol at night, and the samworo want to know who is paying him.
- **The flute.** A patupaiarehe's flute sounds on a misty ridge, and a woman keeps walking toward it. The cooking fires are the only ward, and the mist is coming down.
- **A navigator for hire.** A Dutch captain wants a wayfinder for a passage his charts don't show; the school he asks doesn't sell.
- **The galleon's chaplain.** A Jesuit at Guam has written to Madrid about Pohnpei's stones, and a court wants the letter before the minister of magic reads it.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
From the Volga to the Pacific and the Arctic shore, Russia, China and Persia meet peoples who have run this ground for millennia: Uzbek khans in the oasis cities, Kazakh khans on the grass, the Dzungars' Buddhist steppe state with cannon, and Russia's fur collectors on the Pacific. The little beaked beasts the griffin legends grew from are alive here.

**The one thing to remember:** there is no edge here. Herders and reindeer peoples move through their whole country on a planned round, and the spirits live where the people do. Every empire is trying to fix them in place.

> **Further in.** The Taymyr, in the far north, is one of the few places on earth that could match Mutapa's platinum. The metal lies under the tundra at the edge of Russia's fur tribute. Nobody has looked yet.

sections.heading: Playing Here
What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **Razin on the Yaik.** Stenka Razin's Cossacks took the fort at Yaitsk last summer and wintered there. In spring they sail for the Persian coast, and the tsar's troops retake the town behind them. The Yaik Cossacks who let him in are waiting to learn what that costs.
- **The Dzungars.** Sengge broke the last Altan Khan in 1667 and now tells Russia's forts on the Yenisei that the peoples they tax are his. The forts' Cossacks have started skirmishing with his men.
- **The Kazakhs** have fought the Dzungars since the 1640s, and this year's raiding season opens when the grass does.
- **The Amur.** A fugitive, Nikifor Chernigovsky, who fled after the killing of a Siberian governor, holds the rebuilt fort at Albazin with a hundred outlaws and takes tribute from Daur villages the Qing count as theirs. The tsar hasn't decided whether to hang him or thank him.
- **Bukhara.** About 500 Indian merchant-bankers lend from its caravanserais, and this year's loans decide which khan can pay his riders.
- **Siberia.** Sable tribute has fallen from up to 22 pelts a man to about 3, yet furs are more than a tenth of Russia's revenue, so the forts take hostages to make up the count.
- **The far northeast.** The Chukchi remain undefeated.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
- **The grass sea.** Grassland and semi-desert from the Black Sea to Manchuria.
- **The zud** is the winter disaster that kills the herds; the answer is *otor*, a move onto a distant community's reserve pasture, calling in an old debt.
- **The Gobi.** On Khalkha land; its red sandstones are fossil beds of *Protoceratops*, sheep-sized, beaked and frilled, and here the living animal still nests among the bones.
- **The oases.** Bukhara and Samarkand on the Zarafshan; Khiva in Khwarazm.
- **Siberia and the Arctic.** Taiga, bog, tundra and sea ice. The rivers are the roads.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Uzbek khanates.** Chinggisid khans. In Bukhara a *quriltai* elects the Janid khan and Naqshbandi Sufi shaykhs confirm him. The khan, Abd al-Aziz, pays scholars and builders, and pays guards for the Samarkand road.
- **The Kazakhs.** Three *zhuz* under Chinggisid khans (the *töre*, of Heaven's line: Peoples, Divine-Bloods), with *biys*, judges of oral customary law. Their capital is Turkestan, at the shrine of Ahmed Yasawi. A *biy* settles a feud with a fine in livestock, and a party with a claim against a Kazakh takes it to one.
- **The Dzungars.** The Oirat khanate, ruled in 1668 by Sengge from the Ili valley. It is Buddhist, mines metals, makes its own guns and farms as well as herds. Sengge's younger brother has been a monk in Tibet since childhood. Sengge hires gunsmiths and miners, and has told Russia's forts to stop taking tribute from peoples he counts as his.
- **The Kalmyks.** Oirats who took the lower Volga in the 1630s: a Buddhist khanate around Russian Astrakhan, allied with Russia. The tsar pays them to ride against the Crimean Tatars, and they sell horses by the thousand at Astrakhan.
- **Russia.** River forts from Tobolsk to Yakutsk and Okhotsk, on the Pacific, collect *yasak*, fur tribute, from every Indigenous man aged 18 to 50, often by holding hostages. The country between the forts belongs to the peoples who pay it, or refuse: the Khanty and Mansi on the Ob, the Nenets on the tundra, the Sakha on the Lena. A fort's governor hires anyone who can guide, interpret or carry the tsar's mail to the next fort.
- **The Qing** to the east, the border with Russia undrawn. The Qing want Russia's deserters and tribute-takers off the Amur, and rely on the Daur and Solon to report them.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
- **The Buddhist campaign against shamans** is live. Mongol law bans shamanizing and the *ongon*, images that house ancestor and helping spirits, and burns them in public. Shamans hold out in the northern forests.
- **Learned magic.** Bukhara "the Noble" is a city of madrasas and of the Islamic science of letters (see Magic, Learned Magic).
- **The Siberian shaman.** A dead shaman's spirit chooses the next with an illness that lasts until the call is accepted. The three worlds the shaman travels hang on the Tree a Revelator walks (see The Plenum).
- **The naturalist.** Nurbibi, a steppe gnome (see Places, The Gobi), is the first to study the steppe's little monsters as animals, and the courts' cabinets want specimens.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Much of this was recorded late, and Buddhism, Islam and Orthodoxy have reclassified many of these beings.

- **The *ezen*** (Mongol). "Owners" of a mountain, spring or pasture, who sicken those who pollute, dig or kill wantonly. Travelers add a stone to the *ovoo* at a pass.
- **The *albasty*** (Kazakh, Kyrgyz and others). The same being as the Persian Āl (a low pari), here a childbirth demon with long tangled hair, said to steal a mother's lungs where Persians say her liver. A specialist drives her off by announcing "a hero has arrived."
- **Pari.** Beautiful beings who take human lovers and possess the chosen: the nearest match here to European fairies.
- **Killers and the Hunt.** With no village, riders and guards keep watch. To herders the Wild Hunt looks like raiders: horsemen on pale horses who drive off the herd and take the night guard. The steppe's own riders ride out against it.

sections.heading: Life Here
sections.text:
Out here home is a felt tent, a birch-bark tent or a reindeer-hide one, and it moves. A camp goes where the grass, the fish or the herd goes, on a round its grandparents rode, and it carries its welcome with it.

**A day in a Kazakh camp.** A few related yurts on the summer pasture. The mares are milked every couple of hours from before dawn, and the milk goes into a big leather bag to become *kymyz*, mare's-milk kumys; anyone who comes into the yurt gives the churn-stick a few strokes before sitting down. Men and boys ride herd, the old men judge disputes in the shade and the girls race the boys and win. A stranger who rides in unannounced is "God's guest" and gets the best of everything; the most honored guest at a feast is served the sheep's head and must share it out, with a word for each person. In the evening someone tunes a *dombra*, and if two singers are in camp, everyone stays up.

**Food and drink.** Kumys, mutton, horsemeat sausage for the winter and *qurt*, dried curd balls that keep for a season in a saddlebag. The Mongols drink brick tea boiled with milk and salt. Bukhara eats *osh*, rice cooked with mutton, carrots and onions in one great pot, with flat bread from the clay oven and melons from Khwarazm that travelers write home about. The Sakha drink kumys and eat their own butter; the Khanty and the Nenets eat reindeer and river fish, raw and frozen in winter, and cloudberries in summer.

**The year.**

- **Nauryz,** the new year at the March equinox, across the Turkic and Persian world. New clothes, a visit to every tent, quarrels forgiven and a swing hung between poles where the young people are allowed to sit close.
- **Crow Day,** for the Khanty and the Mansi, when the first crows come back with snow still on the ground (late March or early April). The crow wakes the spring and looks after mothers and children; the first woman to see one, people say, will have the year's first baby.
- **The first kumys,** in late spring, when the mares have foaled: the camp's first bag of the year is shared out with a blessing, and the summer has begun.
- **Ysyakh,** the Sakha new year, at midsummer on the meadows of the Lena. The eldest, in white, pours kumys to the fire and asks blessing for everyone; the hitching posts are hung with horsehair, carved wooden cups of kumys go around and the *osuokhai*, the great circle dance, goes on all night under a sun that barely sets, one singer improvising and the whole circle answering.

**Who helps.** When the zud kills a family's herd, the relatives each give animals so that it can start again; the Kazakhs call it *zhylu*, "warmth." A yurt to raise or a flock to shear in a day calls an *asar*: the neighbors come, the work is done by evening and the household feeds them. In Bukhara, Nadir Divan-Beghi's lodge by the great pond at Lyab-i Hauz, built in 1620, houses wandering Sufis and feeds travelers, and the city sits under the old trees around the water in the evenings to watch the water-carriers fill their skins.

**What people love.** The *aitys*: two singers, often a man and a woman, dueling in improvised verse before the whole camp until one runs out of answers. *Qyz quu*, "chase the girl": a young man chases a young woman on horseback, and if he catches her he may kiss her; if he doesn't, she chases him back with a whip. The goat-dragging match at every feast, the eagle hunters' talk, a good horse.

#### Hooks

- **The warmth.** A late storm killed a young widow's whole herd. Her clan has given what it can and it isn't enough to see her through winter, and three days' ride away is an uncle who owes her husband a horse and his honor. The party carries the *zhylu*.
- **The singer at the feast.** At a wedding feast a stranger challenges the camp's best singer to an aitys and wins every round, and as his forfeit asks for the bride's first dance. He is very handsome, he has no shadow by firelight and the camp's singer wants a rematch.
- **Tribute day.** A Sakha bride's wedding falls on the day the *yasak* collectors come to her camp. The families want the wedding kept, the Cossacks fed and sent on their way before anyone notices that the bride's brother is the man they're looking for.

sections.heading: Places
sections.text:
Each of the setting's own people here stands in the place where a party meets them, with what they want and how a table uses them. Aisulu, Kenzhe, Zhamal-apa and Gaukhar come first: they share one Kazakh camp. Each has a pregen sheet. The sheets are on the site, perceptualmechanics.com/euphonia.

#### The Kazakh camp

The Kazakhs have fought the Dzungars since the 1640s, and this year's raiding season opens when the grass does (What's Happening in 1668). Life Here spends a day in a Kazakh camp, and the night watch is this camp's (Hooks).

**Aisulu.** A Kazakh *batyr* of giant blood, a goliath who rides watch for her camp against Dzungar raiders and the Wild Hunt alike. Find her on a ridge of the autumn pasture at dusk, standing in her stirrups a head taller than any rider on the line, a golden eagle on her arm. On the steppe the camp's own riders ride out against the Hunt and she rides first; she hasn't told the camp that the Hunt's best rider has her brother's laugh. An ally who wants her brother Kenzhe home and himself again, and knows the second is harder.
<!-- @at the autumn pasture = Taldyqorghan, Kazakhstan -->

**Kenzhe.** Aisulu's brother, a Kazakh rider taken by the pari three winters ago, who came back riding ahead of the Wild Hunt and takes people rather than killing them. In the dark half he waits just past a camp's watch fires, smiling his old smile and calling the watch by their childhood names. He isn't cruel: he takes people the way you'd carry a friend out of a burning yurt, and he wants to bring his sister across because he truly believes she'd be happier there. A villain or foil; the camp still sets a bowl for him at feasts, and something empties it.
<!-- @at the camp = Taldyqorghan, Kazakhstan -->

**Zhamal-apa.** A Kazakh midwife of the same camp, a Hedge Witch who drives the albasty off birthing mothers by announcing that a hero has arrived, and pays for each healing out of her own body when there is nothing else to take it from (the Hedge Witch's way; *The Classes*, Physician). She shouts "The hero has come!" so convincingly that the hero, Aisulu, ducks into the yurt looking embarrassed. The camp's mullah calls it superstition; she says the mullah has never had a baby. A mentor or ally, who wants the camp to winter where a midwife can be reached.
<!-- @at the camp = Taldyqorghan, Kazakhstan -->

**Gaukhar.** A Kazakh *aqyn*, a singer of improvised verse, from Aisulu's camp, whom nobody on the autumn pasture has beaten in an aitys in six years. She sings the bride out of her mother's yurt at every wedding in the valley, and she knows every family's quarrels because she has put them in verse. The camp's singer in the hook (see Life Here).
<!-- @at the autumn pasture = Taldyqorghan, Kazakhstan -->

#### The Gobi

On Khalkha land, where the red sandstones are fossil beds of *Protoceratops*, sheep-sized, beaked and frilled, and the living animal still nests among the bones (The Lay of the Land).

**Nurbibi.** A steppe gnome, the first to study the griffins' kin as animals rather than legends, nine days into a watch in a felt blind on a ridge of red sandstone; she has watched one brood its eggs on warm quartz and written "a mother" in a careful hand, with the date. Buyers in Bukhara, Moscow and London court her notebooks, and she wants the little monsters described properly before a cabinet gives them a Latin name and the wrong diet. A contact or ally, and the naturalist of the specimen hook, if the table likes.
<!-- @at the red sandstone ridge = Dalandzadgad, Mongolia -->

#### Bukhara

Bukhara "the Noble," a city of madrasas and of the science of letters (Magic Here), where about 500 Indian merchant-bankers lend from the caravanserais (What's Happening in 1668).

**Bibi Oysha.** A Bukharan *otin*, a woman teacher, who writes the protective talismans for her father's Naqshbandi lodge and teaches the science of letters to girls the madrasas won't take. She has outlived half the scholars who said a woman couldn't do it, and wants one of her girls admitted to read in a madrasa library with the door open. A mentor or patron, and the reason the lodge's shelter holds.
<!-- @at Bukhara, Uzbekistan -->

**Lala Sukhdev.** A Multani moneylender, one of some five hundred Indian bankers in Bukhara's caravanserais, who weighs a herder's silver on a hand scale and turns the beam so the herder can read it. He'll advance a party anything against a bill on Surat, and the Bukhara buyer who wants Nurbibi's live beast writes his offers through him. He wants to go home to Multan rich enough to stay, and can't until the cousin who is to take over his clients comes, and the cousin keeps not coming. A patron or contact.
<!-- @at Bukhara, Uzbekistan -->

#### Ili valley

Sengge rules the Dzungars from here; the khanate is Buddhist, mines metals and makes its own guns (Who Holds Power). His half-brothers are counting their men (Trouble Brewing).

**Tseren Dorji.** A *zaisang*, a Dzungar noble official in the khan's tent in the Ili valley, who has watched Sengge's half-brothers count their men and wants Sengge's brother home from Tibet before they move. He needs someone to carry a letter, and an argument, to teachers in Tibet who can't be ordered, and pays in good Dzungar guns. The patron of the vow (see Hooks), who wants the monk home and the khan alive, in that order if it can't be both.
<!-- @at the Ili valley = Yining, China -->

#### Erdene Zuu

A Khalkha Buddhist monastery, under a law that bans shamanizing and the *ongon* and burns them in public (Magic Here).

**Gelong Tsereng.** A Khalkha Buddhist monk of Erdene Zuu who heals the sick on the herding round and burns the shamans' *ongon* because the law says to, and has stopped arguing about what the images hold. He sets a felt *ongon* on the coals, then bandages the hand of the woman who made it, and keeps one he couldn't burn in a box under his bed. A foil or ally, who has asked twice for a younger monk to take over the round and been refused.
<!-- @at Erdene Zuu = Arvaikheer, Mongolia -->

#### Astrakhan

The Kalmyks' Buddhist khanate lies around Russian Astrakhan, and they sell horses by the thousand there (Who Holds Power).

**Avetik of Julfa.** A New Julfa merchant's younger son sent to Astrakhan to learn the silk trade, who learned nard, the Persian backgammon, instead and wins more from Kalmyk princes than his father makes on silk. He keeps a board in the Armenian merchants' yard in Astrakhan and plays in the Kalmyk camps across the Volga in summer, and he wants enough winnings to buy a ship of his own before his father stops writing. Comic relief or a rival; his father's letters get shorter every season.
<!-- @at Astrakhan, Russia -->

#### Tobolsk

Russia's river forts run from Tobolsk to Yakutsk and Okhotsk and collect *yasak*, fur tribute, often by holding hostages (Who Holds Power). Sable tribute has fallen from up to 22 pelts a man to about 3 (What's Happening in 1668).

**Avdotya Shchukina.** A Cossack widow who runs a sable-smuggling family from the back room of her late husband's tavern below the Tobolsk kremlin, pouring kvass for a governor's clerk with one hand and sliding him a pelt with her foot. She buys furs from both sides and lights a candle for every runner she has lost. A villain or contact, who wants her youngest son out of the trade and a long way from Tobolsk, and will pay a party to take him.
<!-- @at Tobolsk, Russia -->

#### The upper Lena

Siberian taiga, where the rivers are the roads (The Lay of the Land) and a dead shaman's spirit chooses the next with an illness that lasts until the call is accepted (Magic Here).

**Iliqa.** An Evenki shaman of the upper Lena, chosen by a dead shaman's spirit through an illness that lasted three winters, who walks the Tree's three worlds for her clan. On tribute day she is at the Yakutsk fort's gate, asking to see the hostage house, where her nephew is held; the fort wants fur, and she gives exactly as many sables as the forest can spare, which is never enough. An ally or mentor for the hostage (see Hooks).
<!-- @at the upper Lena = Kirensk, Russia -->

#### Yakutsk

Russia's fort on the Lena, in the Sakha's country (Who Holds Power). Ysyakh, the Sakha new year, is danced at midsummer on the Lena's meadows, and tribute day is Life Here's third hook.

**Sardaana.** A Sakha singer of the Lena meadows who leads the osuokhai at Ysyakh, and has kept a circle dancing from dusk to the next noon. She pays her family's fur tribute and resents every pelt, and wants this year's circle large enough for the fort to hear. A host and a contact on the Lena, and the bride's cousin on tribute day (see Life Here).
<!-- @at the Lena meadows = Yakutsk, Russia -->

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The succession.** Sengge's half-brothers are counting their men, and his brother Galdan is a monk in Tibet, bound by a vow. In our history they kill Sengge in his tent in 1670 and Galdan comes home to avenge him. A party can carry the warning, guard the tent or bring the monk.
- **The tribute.** The sable is running out and the forts keep their hostages anyway. A fort that can't make its count takes more hostages; a clan that can't pay moves out of reach or burns the fort.
- **The red alert.** The hunt for Mutapa's metal hasn't turned north yet. When a court learns what lies in the rivers of the Taymyr, Russia's tribute country becomes worth an expedition, and the Nenets and Nganasan who live there become guides or obstacles to it.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The specimen.** A naturalist has a live griffin-kin, and buyers in Bukhara, Moscow and London want it before anyone learns what it eats.
- **The hostage.** A clan leader's son is held at a Russian fort until the furs come in, and this year's furs won't.
- **The vow.** A Dzungar noble wants Sengge's brother brought home from Tibet before Sengge's rivals move, and the monk's vow and his teachers stand in the way.
- **The night watch.** A camp's night guards have started vanishing, and the watch says the rider who took them called them by their childhood names. Aisulu wants her brother Kenzhe brought back alive; the elders want the watch kept whole, whatever it costs him.
